questions.answer: If accuracy is 1, every example is classified correctly, so for a standard loss like cross-entropy the lower bound on per-example loss is 0, approached as the predicted probability of the true class tends to 1. The upper bound, however, is not tightly constrained by accuracy alone: a correct prediction only requires the true class to have the largest probability, so its probability can be just over the decision threshold, meaning the loss can still be moderately large. For binary classification the predicted true-class probability lies in (0.5, 1], giving loss in [0, log 2). So the loss is bounded below by 0 but can be as high as log 2 per example while still being correct.

questions.question: We have two models, 85% and 82% accuracy. Which do you pick?
questions.answer: Accuracy alone is insufficient; I would first confirm the difference is statistically significant given the test set size and not within noise. I would check that the metric matches the business objective and examine class-conditional performance, calibration, precision/recall tradeoffs, and robustness across slices. I would also weigh model complexity, latency, interpretability, and maintenance cost, since a 3-point gain may not justify a heavier or less stable model. Ultimately the choice depends on the deployment context, not the headline number.

questions.question: How do you handle missing data in Pandas?
questions.answer: In Pandas, start by detecting missing values with isna() or isnull() and summarizing them per column. Options include dropping rows or columns via dropna() when missingness is sparse or non-informative, or imputing with fillna() using a constant, mean, median, mode, or forward/backward fill for time series. For principled handling I would consider the missingness mechanism (MCAR, MAR, MNAR) and use model-based imputation such as scikit-learn's SimpleImputer, KNNImputer, or IterativeImputer within a pipeline to avoid leakage. Adding a binary indicator column for was-missing can preserve signal when missingness itself is predictive.

questions.question: Explain self-attention. What is its computational complexity, and what are your options when contexts get long?
questions.answer: Self-attention lets each token compute query, key, and value vectors, scores every pair via scaled dot products, softmaxes those into weights, and returns a weighted sum of values, so every position can attend to every other in one layer. Its time and memory complexity is O(n^2 d) in sequence length n, which becomes the bottleneck for long contexts. Options to scale include IO-aware exact kernels like FlashAttention (same complexity, far less memory traffic), sparse or sliding-window attention that restricts which pairs interact, linear-attention and state-space models that drop to O(n), and retrieval or chunking so the model never sees the full sequence at once. KV-cache reduction (GQA, MLA, quantization) attacks the memory side at inference.

questions.question: What is the relationship between cross-entropy, KL divergence and perplexity, and why is cross-entropy the training loss for language models?
questions.answer: Cross-entropy measures the average negative log-probability the model assigns to the true tokens, and it equals the data's entropy plus the KL divergence from the true distribution to the model's, so minimizing cross-entropy minimizes that KL gap. Perplexity is simply the exponential of the per-token cross-entropy, interpretable as the effective branching factor, or how many equally likely choices the model is confused among. Cross-entropy is the training loss because maximizing the likelihood of the observed tokens is exactly minimizing cross-entropy, and it is smooth, decomposable per token, and provides well-behaved gradients through the softmax. KL to the fixed data distribution differs from cross-entropy only by the constant data entropy, so the two have the same gradient.

questions.question: What is the effect of adjusting an LLM's context window size?
questions.answer: Enlarging the context window lets the model condition on more tokens, improving tasks that need long documents, extended dialogue, or many retrieved chunks, but it increases attention compute (quadratically) and KV-cache memory (linearly) at inference. If the model was not trained or adapted for the longer length, quality degrades through positional extrapolation failures and lost-in-the-middle effects, so more context is not automatically better. A larger window also widens the surface for distracting or conflicting content, which can increase hallucination if retrieval is noisy. Shrinking the window saves cost and latency but risks truncating needed information, so the size is a cost-quality trade-off tied to the task.

questions.question: You are building a production agent that calls tools (function calling). What makes the loop reliable enough to ship?
questions.answer: Reliability comes mostly from the engineering around the model, not the prompt alone. Validate every tool call against a strict schema before executing, treat tool outputs as untrusted, and return errors as structured, actionable observations so the model can recover; add bounded retries with backoff for transient failures and caps on self-correction to avoid loops. Bound the loop with step and cost budgets, loop detection, and an explicit termination and verification condition, and make tools idempotent so retries are safe. Gate irreversible actions behind human approval, scope permissions to the task, and instrument everything with full tracing plus an offline evaluation suite so regressions are caught before shipping.

questions.question: How would you build an LLM-powered enterprise search system?
questions.answer: Index enterprise content through permission-aware connectors that pull documents and their ACLs from source systems into a hybrid store (lexical plus dense embeddings) with incremental sync to stay fresh. At query time, resolve the user's identity and groups, retrieve candidates with ACL filtering so results respect source permissions, rerank with a cross-encoder and behavioral signals, and have an LLM synthesize a grounded, cited answer with inline links back to sources. Add query understanding for acronyms and jargon, and a knowledge graph of people and entities to improve ranking beyond raw similarity. Enforce defense-in-depth on permissions, defaulting to deny, and log queries for relevance tuning. Tradeoffs are retrieval recall versus precision, index-time versus query-time permission enforcement, and the latency and cost of LLM synthesis, so stream the answer and cache common queries.

questions.question: Design the serving stack for a ChatGPT-scale consumer assistant: hundreds of millions of weekly users, streaming chat, multiple model tiers.
questions.answer: Separate the control plane (auth, session routing, conversation storage, safety) from the GPU inference data plane, streaming tokens to clients over SSE from serving pools that use continuous batching, paged and prefix KV-cache, and tensor/pipeline parallelism for the largest tier. Route requests across model tiers so easy prompts hit smaller, cheaper models and hard ones hit the flagship, with admission control and fair queueing that optimizes time-to-first-token. Split prefill (compute-bound) from decode (bandwidth-bound) onto suitable hardware, deploy capacity regionally, and autoscale on queue depth and GPU utilization with graceful degradation under overload. Persist conversation state durably with eventual consistency so threads resume anywhere. The dominant tradeoffs are batch size (throughput versus latency), tier routing (cost versus quality), and context length (capability versus memory and cost).

questions.question: Design and build a webhook delivery system that reliably delivers events to customer-registered URLs.
questions.answer: Accept events into a durable queue, then have delivery workers POST to each customer's registered URL with the payload, a signature (HMAC) for authenticity, and an idempotency key so consumers can dedupe. Retry failed deliveries with exponential backoff and jitter up to a bounded window, and move exhausted events to a dead-letter queue with a replay API and a dashboard; apply per-endpoint concurrency and rate limits plus a circuit breaker so one slow consumer cannot block others. Guarantee at-least-once delivery (consumers must be idempotent) and preserve per-subscription ordering only if required, since strict ordering limits parallelism. Validate endpoints on registration, enforce timeouts, and prevent SSRF by restricting target hosts. Tradeoffs are ordering versus throughput, retry aggressiveness versus overwhelming consumers, and exactly-once (impractical) versus at-least-once with idempotency.

questions.question: Design a system to schedule jobs in a distributed environment.
questions.answer: Store jobs and schedules in a durable store, with a scheduler that computes due times (including cron and delays) and enqueues ready jobs onto partitioned work queues consumed by a pool of stateless workers. Use leader election or sharded ownership so each job is dispatched once, leases with heartbeats so a crashed worker's job is reclaimed, and idempotency keys plus at-least-once semantics so retries are safe. Track job state (pending, running, succeeded, failed) with retries, backoff, timeouts, and a dead-letter path, and support priorities, dependencies (DAGs), and fairness across tenants. Scale by sharding the schedule space and horizontally adding workers, keeping the hot set of near-due jobs in a time-ordered structure. Tradeoffs are exactly-once (hard) versus at-least-once with idempotency, scheduling precision versus overhead of frequent polling, and strong leader consistency versus availability.

questions.question: Design an in-memory database. / Design Slack.
questions.answer: For an in-memory database, keep data in hash maps and auxiliary structures (skip lists or sorted sets for ranges) behind a single-threaded or sharded event loop for predictable concurrency, and provide durability via append-only logging and periodic snapshots, with replication to followers for availability and read scaling. Enforce memory limits with eviction policies (LRU/LFU) and TTLs, and partition keys by consistent hashing to scale horizontally, accepting that cross-shard transactions are costly. For Slack, the core is real-time messaging: clients hold persistent WebSocket connections to gateway servers that fan out messages via a pub/sub bus to channel subscribers, messages persist to a sharded datastore (by channel or workspace), and presence, unread counts, and search run as separate services. Tradeoffs in both cases are consistency versus availability and latency, durability guarantees versus write throughput, and fan-out-on-write versus fan-out-on-read for message delivery.

questions.question: A customer says “the model got worse” after you upgraded model versions in their deployment. How do you verify and respond?
questions.answer: First reproduce and quantify rather than trust the impression: pull representative requests from before and after the upgrade and compare outputs on the same inputs, checking whether behavior genuinely changed and on which dimensions. Run both model versions through the eval suite and the customer's own key use cases, segmenting by slice so a regression in one workflow is not hidden by aggregate stability. Often the model is not globally worse but behaves differently in tone, verbosity, formatting, or edge-case handling, or the surrounding prompts and parsing assumed the old model's quirks. Communicate findings transparently, offer a quick mitigation such as prompt adjustments or temporarily pinning the prior version, and if a real regression exists, roll back and feed the failing cases into the gate. Close the loop by adding those cases to the regression suite so the same issue is caught next time.

questions.question: An enterprise customer reports that responses from your deployed system have gotten slow. Walk me through the diagnosis.
questions.answer: Start by confirming and scoping the slowdown with metrics: look at latency percentiles over time, not averages, and determine whether it is end-to-end or a specific stage, which tenants and request types are affected, and when it began. Use traces to break latency into retrieval, prompt assembly, model inference, tool calls, and network, since the regression usually localizes to one span. Common causes include longer prompts or outputs raising token counts, retrieval returning more or larger chunks, a model or provider change, increased load and queuing, retries from errors, or a downstream dependency degrading. Correlate the onset with recent deploys, config changes, traffic growth, and provider status. Mitigate the hot path, for example by trimming context, caching, parallelizing tool calls, or adjusting capacity, then verify the percentile recovers and add an alert.

questions.question: How do you approach GenAI safety in consumer products?
questions.answer: Start from the specific harms a consumer product can cause, such as exposure of minors to unsafe content, self-harm and crisis situations, harassment, misinformation, and privacy leakage, and build policies around those before touching the model. Combine aligned model training with layered runtime guardrails: input and output moderation classifiers, refusal and safe-completion behavior, escalation paths for crisis topics, and age-appropriate experiences. Invest heavily in evaluation and red-teaming across languages and demographics, measure safety metrics alongside quality, and roll out gradually with monitoring for emerging abuse patterns. Give users transparency, reporting mechanisms, and control, and keep a fast feedback loop from incidents back into policy, training, and filters. Safety is continuous operational work, tuned to the actual user population and their vulnerabilities.

questions.question: How would you design safeguards for an AI system that can take actions on behalf of a user?
questions.answer: Apply least privilege and explicit scoping so the agent can only perform the specific actions the user authorized, and nothing broader. Classify actions by impact and reversibility, allowing low-risk reversible actions autonomously while requiring explicit user confirmation for high-impact or irreversible ones like payments, deletions, or external messages. Treat all external content the agent reads as untrusted to prevent injection from redirecting its behavior, enforce allowlists on destinations and spending limits, and keep a complete audit log with the ability to review and undo. Add monitoring for anomalous action patterns, a kill switch, and clear surfacing to the user of what the agent is about to do and why. The guiding principles are least privilege, human-in-the-loop for consequential actions, and bounded blast radius.

questions.question: An enterprise customer says: “We want AI to automate our claims processing.” You're the engineer in the room. What do the first two weeks look like?
questions.answer: Week one is discovery: I sit with the claims adjusters, map the real end-to-end workflow, pull a representative sample of actual claims including the messy edge cases, and quantify current volume, cost, and error rates so we have a baseline. I separate what's genuinely automatable from what needs a human in the loop, and I resist the urge to boil the ocean by picking one high-volume, well-structured claim type as the first target. Week two I build a thin prototype against that slice, usually extraction plus a decision step with confidence thresholds that route uncertain cases to a human, and I define the success metrics and guardrails with their compliance and risk people. I'd deliver a scoped pilot plan with clear accuracy targets, a review mechanism, and an honest view of what won't be automated. The deliverable is agreement on scope and metrics, not a finished system.

questions.question: Do you have experience working with APIs? Are you used to working with C-suite executives?
questions.answer: Yes on both. I've built and consumed REST and increasingly LLM and streaming APIs, handling auth, rate limits, retries, idempotency, pagination, and versioning, and designing contracts that downstream teams can depend on. With executives I focus on outcomes, cost, risk, and timelines rather than implementation detail, give a clear recommendation with the tradeoffs, and translate technical constraints into business terms. I'm comfortable pushing back when a request won't deliver what they actually want, as long as I bring an alternative. The combination matters in a forward-deployed role because you often have to design the integration and sell the approach in the same meeting.

questions.question: What is your favourite product and why?
questions.answer: Choose a product you genuinely use and analyze it like a builder: name the core user problem it solves and why its solution is better than alternatives. Discuss specific design or engineering decisions you admire, the tradeoffs involved, and even one thing you would improve to show critical thinking. Connect your reasoning to user needs and measurable value rather than surface-level features. What good looks like is demonstrating product sense, curiosity, and the ability to reason about why something works, not just that you like it.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you made a mistake.
questions.answer: Pick a real, meaningful mistake with actual consequences, not a humblebrag, and describe it with STAR focusing on accountability. Explain what went wrong, your role in it, and resist the urge to shift blame. Emphasize how you noticed it, owned it to the relevant people, and the concrete actions you took to fix it. Close with the specific lesson and the change in habit or process you adopted, since interviewers are evaluating self-awareness and growth more than the error itself.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had a conflict with someone. How did you resolve it and what did you learn?
questions.answer: Choose a professional conflict rooted in a substantive disagreement, not a personality clash, and present it fairly from both sides. Use STAR to describe how you sought to understand the other person's perspective, communicated your own, and worked toward a resolution focused on the shared goal. Emphasize listening, empathy, and finding common ground rather than winning. End with the outcome and what you learned about collaboration or communication, which demonstrates maturity and emotional intelligence.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had conflicting priorities with stakeholders and how you secured alignment.
questions.answer: Frame this around stakeholder management: describe the competing priorities, who wanted what, and why the tension was legitimate rather than trivial. Explain how you clarified goals, surfaced tradeoffs with data, and facilitated a shared understanding of constraints and impact. Emphasize how you aligned people through transparent communication and by anchoring on the common objective rather than imposing your view. Close with the agreed outcome and the result, showing you can drive alignment without authority while keeping relationships intact.

questions.question: What is the project you are most proud of?
questions.answer: Select a project with real impact where your contribution was significant, and make clear specifically what you did versus the team. Use STAR to convey the challenge, your role, the key decisions, and the measurable outcome, and explain why it matters to you personally. Highlight the hardest part and how you overcame it to show depth rather than just pride. What good looks like is authentic enthusiasm paired with concrete evidence of ownership, skill, and impact.

questions.question: You are receiving an unbounded stream of event IDs. Return the k most frequent IDs seen so far, at any point, with bounded memory.
questions.answer: Because the stream is unbounded and memory is bounded, exact top-k is impossible, so use the Space-Saving (or Misra-Gries/Count-Min) sketch with a fixed number of counters. Keep a map of at most m monitored ids with counts; on each event, increment if present, otherwise if there is room add it, else evict the minimum-count entry and reuse its slot, assigning the new id that count plus one. At any query, return the k highest-count entries. This gives approximate frequencies with a bounded overcount error related to 1/m, uses O(m) memory independent of stream length, and O(1) amortized per event with a min-structure or a Stream-Summary bucket list for the eviction.

questions.question: Closest key: given a dictionary with letter keys and lists of letters as values, find the closest key.
questions.answer: Interpret closeness as graph/alphabet distance and model the dictionary as adjacency where each key points to its value letters. If closeness means fewest hops, run BFS from the query key over the value lists to find the nearest reachable key; if it means smallest alphabetic distance, compute abs(ord(key) - ord(target)) over candidate keys and take the minimum. Clarify the metric first since it changes the algorithm entirely. Edge cases are the key not existing, ties (define a deterministic tiebreak like lexicographic), self-references, and disconnected keys with no reachable target; BFS is O(V+E), the direct distance scan is O(number of keys).

questions.question: Write a function to compute root-mean-square error given y_pred and y_true lists.
questions.answer: Compute the element-wise differences between predictions and truths, square them, take their mean, then the square root: sqrt(mean((y_pred[i]-y_true[i])^2)). With NumPy this is np.sqrt(np.mean((pred-true)**2)); in pure Python sum the squared errors, divide by n, and sqrt. Validate that the two lists are equal length and non-empty to avoid a divide-by-zero, and consider casting to float. It is O(n) time and O(1) extra space, and RMSE is in the same units as the target, penalizing large errors more than MAE.

questions.question: Parse bigrams: extract two-word phrases from strings for NLP feature engineering.
questions.answer: Split each string into tokens (lowercasing and stripping punctuation as needed), then slide a window of size two over the token list emitting consecutive pairs (tokens[i], tokens[i+1]) for i from 0 to len-2. Join each pair into a phrase or keep it as a tuple feature, and typically count frequencies in a dict for feature engineering. Edge cases are strings with zero or one token (no bigrams), handling sentence boundaries so you do not form bigrams across sentences, and consistent normalization so 'New York' and 'new york' map together. It is O(n) in token count.

questions.question: Define the bias-variance trade-off and discuss the relationship between the two.
questions.answer: The bias-variance trade-off decomposes expected generalization error into bias squared, variance, and irreducible noise. Bias is systematic error from an overly rigid model that underfits, while variance is error from excessive sensitivity to the particular training sample, which overfits. The two typically move in opposite directions as model capacity changes: increasing complexity lowers bias but raises variance, so minimizing total error means finding the capacity where their sum is smallest. Techniques like regularization, ensembling, and more data shift this balance, with more data especially helping to reduce variance.

questions.question: What are the assumptions of linear regression?
questions.answer: Linear regression assumes a linear relationship between predictors and the expected response, and independence of the error terms. It assumes homoscedasticity (constant error variance), normally distributed errors for valid inference and confidence intervals, and little or no multicollinearity among predictors. It also assumes the predictors are measured without substantial error and that the model is correctly specified with no important omitted variables. Violations affect either coefficient estimates (e.g., omitted-variable bias) or the validity of standard errors and tests (e.g., heteroscedasticity).

questions.question: Distinguish regularization from validation: when is each the right tool?
questions.answer: Regularization controls model complexity during training by adding a penalty (such as L1 or L2) or using dropout and early stopping to reduce variance and prevent overfitting. Validation is an evaluation procedure, like a held-out set or k-fold cross-validation, used to estimate generalization performance and select hyperparameters, including the regularization strength itself. Use regularization when the model is overfitting and you want to constrain it; use validation whenever you need an unbiased estimate of performance or must choose among models or hyperparameters. They are complementary: validation tells you how much and which kind of regularization to apply.

questions.question: Derive the gradient of cross-entropy loss with softmax inputs, and explain why we fuse them numerically.
questions.answer: With softmax outputs p_i = exp(z_i)/sum_j exp(z_j) and one-hot target y, the cross-entropy loss is L = -sum_i y_i log p_i. Its gradient with respect to the logits is strikingly simple: dL/dz_i = p_i - y_i, the difference between predicted probabilities and the true distribution. We fuse softmax and cross-entropy numerically because computing them separately risks overflow in exp and the loss of precision from log of a tiny number; the combined form uses the log-sum-exp trick (subtracting the max logit) for stability. This also yields the clean p - y gradient directly, avoiding division by potentially tiny probabilities.

questions.question: Explain the SVD and give two places it shows up in modern deep learning.
questions.answer: The singular value decomposition factorizes any matrix A as U Sigma V^T, where U and V are orthogonal and Sigma is diagonal with nonnegative singular values ordered by magnitude. It gives the best low-rank approximation of a matrix (Eckart-Young) and reveals its rank, range, and null space. In deep learning it underlies low-rank adaptation methods like LoRA, which inject trainable low-rank factors into weight matrices for efficient fine-tuning, and it appears in weight compression and spectral analysis of layers. It also shows up in PCA and in initialization and conditioning analyses where singular values describe how a layer stretches activations.

questions.question: On average, how many fair coin flips until you see two heads in a row? Walk me through it.
questions.answer: Let E be the expected number of flips to get two heads in a row. Define states by the current streak: from the start (no useful streak) and from one-head. From start, with probability 1/2 we flip tails and restart, and with probability 1/2 we get a head and move to the one-head state. From one-head, with probability 1/2 we get the second head and finish, else we flip tails and restart. Solving the equations E = 1 + (1/2)E + (1/2)E1 and E1 = 1 + (1/2)(0) + (1/2)E gives E = 6 flips.

questions.question: When would you choose Q-learning over policy gradients, and vice versa?
questions.answer: Choose Q-learning (value-based) when the action space is discrete and modest, you want off-policy learning from a replay buffer for sample efficiency, and a greedy policy over learned values suffices. Choose policy gradients when actions are continuous or high-dimensional, you need a stochastic policy, or you want to optimize the policy directly and handle large/continuous action spaces where argmax over Q is intractable. Policy gradients handle non-differentiable or structured action spaces and give convergence to a (local) optimum but suffer high variance and poorer sample efficiency. Actor-critic methods combine both, using a learned value baseline to reduce policy-gradient variance.

questions.question: You have a binary loan-approval classifier and limited access to feature weights. How do you explain a rejection?
questions.answer: With only black-box or limited access, use model-agnostic local explanation methods such as LIME or SHAP that perturb the applicant's features and fit a local surrogate to attribute the decision to specific inputs like debt-to-income ratio or credit history. Compute counterfactual explanations that state the minimal feature changes that would flip the rejection, which are actionable and align with adverse-action requirements. Report the top contributing features with their direction and magnitude, and validate the explanation's fidelity against the model's actual behavior. Be careful about correlated and proxy features so the explanation is both faithful and compliant.

questions.question: Your pretraining loss suddenly diverges at step 300k of a long run. Diagnose and fix it.
questions.answer: First treat it as either data, numerics, or hardware. Inspect the exact batches around step 300k for corrupted, duplicated, or anomalous samples, and check whether a learning-rate schedule change, a resumed checkpoint, or a new data shard coincided with the divergence. Look at gradient and activation norms, logit magnitudes, and optimizer state for overflow, especially in low precision, and check for a silent hardware or communication fault producing NaNs on one rank. The practical fix is to roll back to the last healthy checkpoint, skip or clean the offending data, lower the learning rate or tighten gradient clipping, raise Adam epsilon or add z-loss and query-key normalization to bound logits, and resume; keep the diverged run's logs to confirm the root cause.

questions.question: Design the training setup for a model that doesn't fit on one accelerator, say 70B parameters on a pod.
questions.answer: A 70B model cannot fit one accelerator, so combine parallelism dimensions: tensor parallelism to split each layer's matrices within a node over fast interconnect, pipeline parallelism to place layer stages across nodes with micro-batching to limit the bubble, and data parallelism with optimizer-state sharding (ZeRO or FSDP) across the remaining devices. Use bf16 or mixed precision with activation checkpointing to cut memory, and size tensor-parallel groups to stay within high-bandwidth NVLink domains while pipeline and data parallel cross slower links. Add sequence or context parallelism if long contexts make activations the bottleneck, and tune micro-batch count and gradient accumulation for throughput. Include frequent sharded checkpointing and overlap of communication with compute to keep utilization high on the pod.

questions.question: Design the serving system for a multimodal assistant (text + image in, streaming text out) at hundreds of millions of users.
questions.answer: Accept mixed text and image inputs, encode images with a vision encoder into embeddings that are projected into the language model's token space, prepend them to the text tokens, and stream generated text back over SSE. Separate an image-preprocessing and encoder tier (often batched, cacheable by image hash) from the LLM decode tier, and serve both on GPU pools with continuous batching, paged KV-cache, and prefix caching for shared prompts. Since image tokens inflate context length and prefill cost, cap resolution, cache encoded images, and route by request complexity across model tiers. Deploy regionally, autoscale on utilization, and run input/output safety classifiers on both modalities. The dominant tradeoffs are image fidelity versus token count and prefill latency, batch size versus time-to-first-token, and cost versus quality from tiered routing.

questions.question: Design a personalised recommendation system for rental listings using demographics, property metadata, amenities, price, reviews and location.
questions.answer: Combine a candidate-retrieval stage that filters listings by hard constraints (location radius, price range, dates, must-have amenities) with a personalized ranking model that scores the shortlist. Represent users with demographics and interaction history, and listings with metadata, amenities, price, images, review embeddings, and geo features, then train a ranker (gradient-boosted trees or a neural net) on booking and engagement labels, optimizing a multi-objective of click, inquiry, and booking. Handle cold start with content features and location popularity, and incorporate review text via embeddings and sentiment. Serve from a feature store with precomputed listing vectors and an ANN index, keeping latency low by caching candidates. Tradeoffs are personalization versus fairness and diversity of exposure for hosts, freshness of availability and price versus caching, and offline ranking metrics versus online booking-rate experiments.

questions.question: Design a classifier that predicts the optimal moment to insert a commercial break in a video.
questions.answer: Frame it as a sequence-labeling or scoring problem over video timeline positions, where the model predicts for each candidate boundary the probability it is a good ad-break moment. Features include scene-change detection, shot boundaries, audio energy and silence, speech/dialogue gaps, semantic scene segmentation, and narrative or emotional arc signals, plus content-type priors; a temporal model (CNN/transformer over frame and audio embeddings) scores positions. Label training data from editorially chosen break points and user signals like low abandonment after a break, and constrain predictions with business rules (minimum spacing, no mid-sentence, target break count). Evaluate offline against held-out editorial labels and online by completion rate and ad-tolerance metrics. Tradeoffs are maximizing ad inventory versus viewer experience and churn, and precision of natural boundaries versus meeting required ad load.

questions.question: How would you improve product search results, focusing on the fraction of relevant documents retrieved (recall)?
questions.answer: To improve recall you must surface more of the truly relevant items, so start by adding a dense retrieval path alongside lexical BM25 and fuse them, since embeddings capture semantic matches that keyword search misses. Expand queries with synonyms, spelling correction, stemming, and learned query rewriting, and relax overly strict filters that silently drop relevant results. Mine hard negatives and use click and purchase logs to train the retriever, and widen the candidate set (larger top-k) feeding the reranker so recall is recovered even if early stages are imperfect. Measure recall@k against a labeled or judged relevance set and watch that precision does not collapse. The central tradeoff is that boosting recall usually lowers precision and raises cost, so compensate with a strong reranking stage that restores precision over the larger candidate pool.

questions.question: Justify using a neural network for a given problem: what do you need to know about the network, dataset, timeline and business context?
questions.answer: Before choosing a neural network, establish whether the problem has enough signal and data: dataset size and label quality, feature richness, and whether the input is high-dimensional or unstructured (images, text, audio, sequences) where deep models excel versus tabular data where gradient-boosted trees often win. Check the performance bar and whether a simple baseline already meets it, since a linear or tree model may be cheaper, interpretable, and sufficient. Weigh the timeline and operational cost: training infrastructure, inference latency and serving cost, maintenance, and the need for explainability or regulatory transparency. Consider the business context, cost of errors, and whether labeled data can be sustained for retraining. Justify a neural network only when nonlinearity and representation learning on unstructured or large data clearly beat simpler alternatives on the metric that matters, net of complexity and cost.

questions.question: Build the evaluation harness for a new frontier model release. What does it need to do?
questions.answer: A frontier-release harness must run a broad, versioned battery covering core capabilities, reasoning, coding, long-context, multilingual, instruction-following, and tool use, plus safety, refusal, and robustness suites, all reproducibly with pinned prompts, decoding parameters, and scoring code. It needs decontamination checks and private held-out sets so scores are trustworthy, and it should support both exact-match and LLM-as-judge scoring with calibrated human agreement. Automate comparison against prior models and competitors with per-slice breakdowns, confidence intervals, and regression flags so you see not just averages but where the new model wins or loses. Include adversarial, long-horizon, and real-usage replay evaluations because static benchmarks miss product-relevant behavior, and capture cost and latency alongside quality. Finally, make runs auditable and rerunnable so results can be reproduced and extended as new risks emerge.

questions.question: Do 1 million Seattle ride trips suffice to build an accurate ETA prediction model? How would you decide?
questions.answer: It depends on coverage, not raw count: a million trips is plenty of data volume, but ETA accuracy hinges on whether those trips represent the conditions you must predict across time of day, day of week, weather, seasonality, road segments, and rare events. Decide by plotting a learning curve of error versus training-set size to see whether accuracy has plateaued, which tells you if more data would even help. Then check error by slice to find under-covered regimes such as rush hour, construction, or specific neighborhoods where sparse data yields high error. Validate with a time-based holdout to catch drift, and compare against a reasonable baseline to judge whether the achieved error meets the product requirement. If the plateau is reached and slice errors meet targets, it suffices; otherwise collect more targeted data rather than just more volume.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a researcher or tech lead about priorities, and what happened.
questions.answer: Describe a specific disagreement about priorities where you held a well-reasoned position, and present the other person's view respectfully. Explain how you backed your case with data, user impact, or risk analysis and engaged in genuine dialogue rather than defending ego. Show that you could commit and support the decision if overruled, and be honest about the outcome including cases where you were persuaded. The goal is to demonstrate that you can challenge thoughtfully, influence through reasoning, and stay collaborative regardless of who prevailed.

questions.question: Given an array nums of n integers where n > 1, return an output array (product of array except self).
questions.answer: Avoid division by computing prefix and suffix products. First pass left to right fills output[i] with the product of all elements before i; second pass right to left multiplies output[i] by a running product of all elements after i. The result at each index is the product of everything except itself, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space beyond the output array. This naturally handles zeros, which a divide-the-total approach cannot do correctly; the only subtlety is initializing the running products to 1 and the array having at least two elements as guaranteed.

questions.question: Find the minimum window in S which will contain all the characters in T.
questions.answer: Use a sliding window over S with two pointers and a frequency map of the characters needed from T plus a counter of how many required characters are currently satisfied. Expand the right pointer, decrementing needs as characters are covered; once all of T is covered, contract the left pointer to shrink the window while still valid, recording the smallest valid window seen. Continue until the right pointer reaches the end, then return the recorded minimum substring (or empty if none). This is O(|S| + |T|) time and O(unique chars) space; edge cases include duplicate characters in T (the map counts multiplicities), T longer than S, and no valid window.

questions.question: Serialize and deserialize a binary tree.
questions.answer: Serialize with a preorder DFS, writing each node's value and a sentinel like '#' for null children, producing an unambiguous string. Deserialize by consuming that token stream in the same preorder: read a token, if it is the sentinel return null, otherwise create a node and recursively build its left then right subtrees. The null markers are what make the structure recoverable without needing a second traversal. Both operations are O(n) time and O(n) space for the string and recursion stack; BFS/level-order with sentinels works equally well, and you must agree on a delimiter that cannot collide with node values.

questions.question: Convert a binary tree to a circular doubly linked list.
questions.answer: Do an in-order traversal to visit nodes in sorted order, linking each visited node to its predecessor via left/right pointers that now act as prev/next. Track the head (first node) and the previously visited node; on each visit set prev.right = current and current.left = prev. After the traversal, close the ring by linking head.left to the last node and last.right to head. This reuses the tree's two pointers as the doubly linked list pointers, runs in O(n) time with O(h) recursion/stack space, and must handle the empty tree and a single node (which links to itself).

questions.question: Alien dictionary: determine character ordering from a sorted word list.
questions.answer: Build a directed graph where an edge u to v means character u precedes v, derived by comparing each adjacent pair of words and finding their first differing character. Then topologically sort the graph (Kahn's algorithm with in-degree counts, or DFS) to produce a valid character ordering. Two critical edge cases: a cycle means the ordering is invalid so return empty, and the prefix case where a longer word precedes its own prefix (like 'abc' before 'ab') is also invalid input. Complexity is O(total characters) to build plus O(V+E) to sort; characters never compared remain unconstrained and can appear in any relative order.

questions.question: K closest points to origin; top-k frequent elements; minimum number of conference rooms.
questions.answer: K closest points to origin: compute squared distances and use a size-k max-heap (or quickselect for O(n) average) to keep the k smallest, giving O(n log k). Top-k frequent elements: count frequencies in a hash map, then push into a min-heap of size k or bucket-sort by frequency for O(n). Minimum conference rooms: sort start and end times, sweep with two pointers incrementing a counter on a start and decrementing on an end, tracking the max concurrent, equivalently a min-heap of end times; O(n log n). All three share the pattern of a heap to maintain a bounded best-set or a sweep over sorted events.

questions.question: Regular expression matching with '.' and '\*'.
questions.answer: Use dynamic programming where dp[i][j] is whether the first i characters of the string match the first j of the pattern. A '.' matches any single character; a '*' means zero or more of the preceding pattern element, so dp[i][j] is true either by taking zero occurrences (dp[i][j-2]) or, if the current char matches the element before '*', by consuming one char (dp[i-1][j]). Initialize dp[0][0] true and handle patterns like 'a*b*' matching empty via the zero-occurrence transition in the first row. It is O(m*n) time and space, reducible to O(n) space; the tricky part is the '*' lookback to the preceding element.

questions.question: Two-part warm-up: given a stream of user actions, return the k most engaged-with items. Then: why might your heap solution be the wrong choice in production?
questions.answer: Count engagement per item in a hash map in one pass, then extract the k highest either with a size-k min-heap for O(n log k) or bucket sort by count for O(n). The heap retains the current best k, evicting the smallest when a higher-count item arrives. In production the heap may be wrong because the action log is an unbounded, possibly distributed stream where you cannot hold every item's exact count in memory, counts drift over time so you want windowing or decay, and a single machine becomes a bottleneck. The right answer is an approximate streaming sketch (Space-Saving or Count-Min with a heap of monitored keys) with bounded memory, merged across shards.

questions.question: Your ads CTR model shows a 2% offline AUC gain, but the online A/B is revenue-neutral with worse calibration. What is going on, and what do you do?
questions.answer: An offline AUC gain that does not convert online usually signals a mismatch between the offline objective and the live system. AUC only measures ranking order, so it can improve while calibration (the absolute probability estimates that feed the auction/bidding or expected-revenue computation) degrades, and revenue depends on calibrated probabilities, not just ordering. Likely causes include training/serving skew, distribution shift from feedback loops and position bias, an offline metric that ignores the business objective, or overfitting to historical logged data. I would add calibration metrics (log loss, ECE, reliability plots), recalibrate (e.g., isotonic or Platt scaling), align offline evaluation with the online decision, and verify the A/B instrumentation and segment-level effects.

questions.question: Explain the architectural choices in a Llama-class model: why grouped-query attention, RoPE and SwiGLU instead of the vanilla 2017 Transformer?
questions.answer: The vanilla 2017 Transformer used multi-head attention, sinusoidal absolute positions, post-LayerNorm, and ReLU/GELU MLPs; a Llama-class model swaps each for a more efficient or higher-quality choice. Grouped-query attention shares KV heads to shrink the KV cache and speed decoding with minimal quality loss; RoPE gives relative positional awareness that extrapolates better and supports context extension; SwiGLU gated MLPs improve quality per parameter; and pre-RMSNorm stabilizes deep training more cheaply than post-LayerNorm. These changes target inference cost (KV cache), long-context behavior (RoPE), and training stability and quality (RMSNorm, SwiGLU). The result is a model that trains more stably and serves faster at the same or better quality.

questions.question: What breaks when you scale LLM training from 8 GPUs to thousands, and how do modern stacks deal with it?
questions.answer: At thousands of GPUs, a single device can no longer hold the model or activations, so you combine data, tensor, pipeline, and sometimes expert parallelism, each adding communication that can dominate if not overlapped with compute. Collective operations (all-reduce, all-to-all for MoE) strain interconnect bandwidth, and pipeline parallelism introduces bubbles that need careful microbatch scheduling. Memory pressure is handled with sharded optimizer states (ZeRO/FSDP), activation checkpointing, and mixed precision, while stragglers, network hiccups, and hardware failures force frequent checkpointing and elastic restarts. Numerical stability (loss spikes, fp8/bf16 scaling) and reproducibility also get harder, so stacks add gradient clipping, careful initialization, and monitoring.

questions.question: You need to serve a Llama-class 70B+ model to hundreds of millions of assistant users. What does the serving stack look like and where does the money go?
questions.answer: The stack is a global, stateless API front end with token-based auth and rate limiting, feeding regional serving clusters each running a high-throughput engine with continuous batching, PagedAttention, and prefix caching. The 70B+ model is quantized (FP8/INT8) and sharded with tensor parallelism within nodes, likely with disaggregated prefill/decode and autoscaling tied to demand across many GPUs. Most of the money goes to GPU compute: the fleet of accelerators and their power and datacenter cost dominate, driven by how efficiently you keep them batched and how large and precise the model is. Secondary costs are long-context KV-cache memory, cross-node interconnect, networking, and redundancy for availability, so the main cost levers are model size/quantization, batch efficiency, caching, and accelerator economics.

questions.question: You're dropped into an unfamiliar multi-file codebase with a failing behaviour and an LLM assistant available. Walk me through how you'd fix it.
questions.answer: First I reproduce the failure deterministically and capture the exact error, stack trace, or wrong output, since a reliable repro is the foundation. I use the assistant to orient quickly, asking it to map the relevant modules and trace the data flow from the failing behavior back toward its source, while I verify its claims against the actual code rather than trusting them. Then I localize by reading the implicated code and adding targeted logging or a failing test that pins the bug, form a hypothesis, and make the smallest change that fixes the root cause. Finally I run the test suite to confirm the fix and check for regressions, and I keep the assistant's role to acceleration and explanation while I own the verification.

questions.question: Walk me through a post-training recipe to turn a pretrained base model into a personalised assistant.
questions.answer: Begin with supervised fine-tuning on high-quality instruction-response pairs covering the assistant's desired tasks, tone, and formats, teaching it to follow instructions and adopt the persona. Then apply preference optimization, DPO or RLHF, on comparisons that encode helpfulness, harmlessness, and style to sharpen behavior and reduce undesired outputs. For personalization, add user- or domain-specific adapters or system prompts, mix in a small amount of persona and safety data, and incorporate retrieval for up-to-date or private knowledge rather than baking it into weights. Throughout, hold out general and safety evaluations to guard against forgetting and regression, and iterate on data quality, which dominates final quality.

questions.question: Design the recommendation system for Instagram Reels.
questions.answer: Use the standard two-stage recommender: candidate generation retrieves a few thousand Reels from billions using multiple sources (two-tower embedding retrieval over user and video vectors, followed/engaged authors, trending, and exploration) via ANN, then a heavy multi-task ranking model scores candidates for probabilities of watch-time, like, share, follow, and skip, combined into a single value with tuned weights. Features span user history, video content embeddings, author, freshness, and context, served from a low-latency feature store with precomputed video embeddings. Address cold start for new videos and users with content signals and exploration, and counter feedback loops and filter bubbles with diversity and exploration terms. Scale with sharded ANN indexes, caching, and GPU-batched ranking within tens of milliseconds. Tradeoffs are engagement optimization versus long-term satisfaction and integrity, exploration versus exploitation, and ranking model size versus latency.

questions.question: Design a personalised news-feed ranking system / the “next post” logic for Facebook's feed.
questions.answer: Retrieve candidate posts from the user's network and follows plus recommended sources, then rank them with a multi-task model predicting the probabilities of meaningful actions (comment, like, share, dwell, hide) and combine these into a value score with weights tuned to long-term engagement and integrity. Features include the viewer's affinity to the author, content type and embeddings, recency, and past interactions, served from a feature store; apply pass-level logic to inject diversity, demote borderline content, and cap per-author dominance. The next-post decision balances predicted value with freshness, diversity, and policy constraints rather than raw predicted engagement alone. Evaluate with online A/B tests on retention and satisfaction, not just clicks, since proxy metrics can be gamed. Tradeoffs are short-term engagement versus long-term health, personalization versus echo chambers, and model complexity versus the sub-100-ms ranking budget.

questions.question: Design a recommendation system for Facebook Ads, and an evaluation framework for ads ranking.
questions.answer: Ads ranking maximizes expected value to the platform while respecting advertiser bids and user experience, so rank by effective-value that combines predicted click or conversion probability (pCTR/pCVR) with the bid, typically in a generalized second-price or value-based auction. Candidate ads are retrieved by targeting and budget constraints, then scored by calibrated CTR and CVR models (features: user, ad creative, advertiser, context), with calibration critical because the probabilities feed the auction directly. The evaluation framework needs offline metrics (AUC, log loss, calibration error), counterfactual or replay estimation for auction changes, and online A/B tests measuring revenue, advertiser ROI, and user experience guardrails like ad load and negative feedback. Tradeoffs are platform revenue versus user experience and advertiser outcomes, calibration accuracy versus discrimination, and exploration of new ads versus exploiting proven ones; budget pacing and delivery fairness must also be modeled.

questions.question: Design the ML components behind an Instagram Story feature.
questions.answer: Stories need several ML components: a ranking model that orders which friends' and followed accounts' stories appear first based on affinity, recency, and predicted engagement; content understanding (classification, object and scene detection, OCR, face grouping) to power effects, stickers, and safety; and recommendations for discovery of public stories. Rank story trays with a lightweight model over affinity and freshness features served at request time, and run heavier media understanding asynchronously at upload for tagging, moderation, and ad suitability. Handle ephemerality with TTL-based storage and ensure moderation runs before wide exposure. Evaluate with tap-forward/backward, completion, and reply rates online, plus classifier precision/recall offline. Tradeoffs are freshness versus personalization in tray ordering, latency of on-upload processing versus thoroughness, and privacy of face and content analysis versus feature richness.

questions.question: Design an end-to-end classification pipeline for Marketplace listings.
questions.answer: Build a multi-stage pipeline that classifies listings by category and attributes and flags policy violations, taking seller-provided text and images as input. Preprocess and extract features (text embeddings from title and description, image embeddings, price, seller signals), then run a hierarchical classifier for category and a multi-label model for attributes, plus a separate integrity classifier for prohibited or fraudulent items. Train on labeled listings and human-reviewed samples, handle the long tail of categories with embeddings and hierarchy, and route low-confidence or high-risk predictions to human review whose labels feed retraining. Serve at scale with batched inference at listing-creation time, caching image embeddings, and monitor drift as new product types appear. Tradeoffs are precision versus recall for integrity (false positives block legitimate sellers), the human-review rate you can afford, and model complexity versus the latency acceptable during listing creation.

questions.question: Design a language translation model / service.
questions.answer: Serve translation with a sequence-to-sequence transformer (encoder-decoder) trained on large parallel corpora, optionally a single multilingual model covering many language pairs with shared representations to help low-resource languages. The service tokenizes with subword units, runs batched GPU inference with beam search or sampling, and post-processes for casing, punctuation, and placeholders; a language-detection step picks the source if unspecified. For scale and latency, use continuous batching, quantization or distillation for cheaper tiers, caching of common segments, and streaming for long documents. Improve quality with domain adaptation, back-translation for data augmentation, and glossary or terminology constraints for enterprise use. Evaluate with BLEU/COMET offline and human adequacy/fluency judgments, since automatic metrics are imperfect. Tradeoffs are a single multilingual model (parameter sharing, simpler ops, some per-pair quality loss) versus specialized models, and translation quality versus latency and serving cost.

questions.question: How would you build the evaluation system for a Meta AI assistant before and after each model release?
questions.answer: Build a standing, versioned offline suite spanning the assistant's core intents, reasoning, safety, multilingual, and tool use, with both automated scoring and a calibrated LLM-as-judge plus a human-rated gold slice, and refresh it with real, decontaminated usage patterns. Before a release, run the candidate against this suite and the prior production model, comparing per-slice with confidence intervals and hard safety gates, and route borderline or high-risk cases to human raters. Gate the ship on no significant regression on key slices and acceptable cost and latency, then roll out behind a canary or A/B. After release, monitor live quality through sampled automated evals, user feedback, engagement and escalation signals, and alert on regressions tied to the new version. Feed every discovered failure back into the offline suite so coverage grows with each release.

questions.question: Design the harmful-content detection system for Facebook and Instagram uploads.
questions.answer: Build a multi-stage pipeline that scores uploads across policy categories like nudity and sexual content, violence, hate, self-harm, and CSAM, using specialized models per modality for images, video, audio, and text plus OCR for text in images. Run cheap high-recall filters at upload to block the clearest violations immediately, including hash-matching against known-bad databases for CSAM and other previously-seen content, then route uncertain cases through heavier classifiers and into human review queues prioritized by severity and reach. Combine content signals with behavioral and virality signals so fast-spreading borderline content gets reviewed before it causes wide harm, and feed reviewer decisions back as training labels. Support appeals, maintain per-category precision and recall targets, localize for language and cultural context, and handle CSAM through mandated reporting and strict access controls. The system must balance latency, scale, reviewer wellbeing, and the asymmetric cost of missing severe harms.

questions.question: How do modern multimodal models get image and video understanding into an LLM, and what changes for video specifically?
questions.answer: Modern multimodal LLMs pass images through a pretrained vision encoder and then bridge into the language model via a lightweight projector or resampler that maps visual patches into the token embedding space, or via gated cross-attention layers; the LLM is then trained or fine-tuned on interleaved image-text data to align the modalities. For video the key change is handling the temporal axis under a token budget: you sample frames, merge or pool tokens spatially and temporally, and add temporal position information so the model knows frame order and can reason about motion and events. Long videos push you to hierarchical encoding, keyframe selection, or retrieval rather than dense per-frame tokens, and audio or captions are often fused as extra streams. The reasoning target also shifts to temporal grounding and long-horizon understanding rather than static description.

questions.question: Give me an example of a project where you used data and machine learning. What obstacles did you hit?
questions.answer: Choose a concrete project and set it up with the business or research goal, the data you used, and the modeling approach. Focus the story on the obstacles you hit, such as data quality, labeling, leakage, drift, or evaluation ambiguity, and walk through how you diagnosed and addressed each. Show your problem-solving process and the tradeoffs you made under real constraints rather than a clean textbook narrative. Finish with the measurable outcome and what you would improve, demonstrating both technical depth and pragmatism.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you drove a significant result through ambiguity, and a time you were wrong.
questions.answer: Treat this as two linked stories and prepare both deliberately. For driving results through ambiguity, use STAR to show how you defined the problem, made assumptions explicit, and made progress despite unclear requirements, ending with quantified impact. For being wrong, pick a genuine misjudgement, own it without deflection, and describe how you corrected course and what you changed afterward. What good looks like is balancing confident initiative with authentic humility, showing you can act decisively yet update on evidence.

questions.question: Tell me about maintaining a production ML pipeline. Why Meta?
questions.answer: For the pipeline part, describe operating a production system over time: monitoring, retraining, handling drift and failures, and the reliability practices that kept it healthy, with specifics on scale and tradeoffs. Emphasize ownership, on-call or incident handling, and how you balanced stability with iteration. For the company-fit part, give specific, researched reasons tied to the team's scale, products, and problems you want to work on rather than generic praise. What good looks like is concrete operational maturity combined with a sincere, well-informed motivation.

questions.question: Build an in-memory key-value store with SET/GET/DELETE, then add transactions with BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK, including nested transactions.
questions.answer: Back the store with a dict and a stack of transaction frames, each frame recording the pending writes/deletes for that nesting level. SET/GET/DELETE read through the frames top-down then the base; BEGIN pushes a new frame; COMMIT merges the top frame into the one below (or the base if outermost); ROLLBACK pops and discards the top frame. Use a tombstone sentinel in a frame to represent a delete that shadows a committed value. Nested transactions fall out naturally because frames stack; COMMIT only finalizes to base when the stack empties. Edge cases are COMMIT/ROLLBACK with no active transaction and ensuring reads honor tombstones; operations are near O(1) except merge which is O(frame size).

questions.question: Write an iterator class that lazily flattens an arbitrarily nested list of lists/integers: no generators, explicit state.
questions.answer: Hold an explicit stack of iterators (or of (list, index) positions), initialized with an iterator over the top-level list. hasNext advances by peeking the top iterator: if its next element is an integer, cache it and return true; if it is a nested list, push an iterator over that list and recurse; if an iterator is exhausted, pop it and continue, returning false only when the stack empties. next returns the cached integer (calling hasNext first if needed). This replaces recursion with an explicit stack so state persists across calls without generators. Amortized cost is O(1) per element over the whole traversal; edge cases are empty sublists and deeply nested structures handled by stack depth.

questions.question: Here is a scheduler class from a small LLM inference engine. One method, \_admit_requests, is a stub: no spec, no docstring, no tests. Walk me through your first thirty minutes.
questions.answer: In the first thirty minutes I read the surrounding scheduler to infer the implicit contract: what calls _admit_requests, what state it reads (waiting queue, running set, KV/memory budget, max batch size), and what it must return or mutate. I trace one request's lifecycle end to end and inspect the data structures to reverse-engineer the admission policy the rest of the code assumes, noting invariants like not exceeding memory or batch limits. I write characterization tests that pin current observable behavior and a few scenarios (empty queue, over-budget, exactly-at-limit) before changing anything. Only then do I draft a minimal spec and a first implementation, confirming assumptions with a teammate or by instrumenting logs rather than guessing.

questions.question: Estimate the KV-cache memory to serve a 70B-class model at 128k context. What do you do when it doesn't fit?
questions.answer: KV-cache size per token is roughly 2 (K and V) times number of layers times hidden-per-KV-head times bytes; for a 70B model with grouped-query attention this is often around 0.125-0.3 MB per token in FP16. At 128k context that is on the order of 20-40 GB for a single sequence, so even a handful of concurrent long-context requests can exceed a GPU's memory. When it does not fit I quantize the KV cache to FP8 or INT4 (halving or quartering it), exploit GQA/MQA to shrink per-token size, and use PagedAttention to eliminate fragmentation. Further options are sliding-window or sparse/compressed attention to bound the cache, offloading cold blocks to CPU or NVME, limiting max context or concurrency, and sharding the cache across GPUs with sequence parallelism.

questions.question: Design a rate limiter for an LLM API where cost scales with tokens, not requests.
questions.answer: Since cost tracks tokens, I meter both input and output tokens rather than request counts and enforce limits on token budgets. I would use a token-bucket or leaky-bucket algorithm per API key where the bucket is denominated in tokens, refilling at a sustained tokens-per-second rate with a burst capacity. Because output length is unknown in advance, I reserve an estimated maximum at admission and reconcile the actual count when the stream finishes, refunding or charging the difference. I enforce limits in a fast shared store (for example Redis) for distributed consistency, apply separate limits for input versus output and for concurrency, and return clear rate-limit headers so clients can back off gracefully.

questions.question: You're training on tens of thousands of GPUs and hardware fails constantly. How do you keep goodput high?
questions.answer: At tens of thousands of GPUs, goodput (fraction of time doing useful work) is dominated by failures and stragglers, so the strategy is fast detection and cheap recovery. Use frequent asynchronous and in-memory or sharded checkpointing so a restart loses minutes not hours, and keep hot spares plus automated health checks that detect dead or slow nodes and reconfigure the job. Make restarts fast with elastic training that can drop a failed replica and continue, and monitor per-rank step times to find and eject stragglers before they stall collectives. Overlap communication with computation, isolate flaky hardware proactively, and track goodput as a first-class metric so you can target the biggest losses.

questions.question: Loss spikes mid-run on a large pretraining job. Walk me through your debugging process.
questions.answer: Correlate the spike with concrete events: a specific data shard, a schedule or hyperparameter change, a resumed checkpoint, or a particular rank or hardware unit. Examine gradient norms, activation and logit magnitudes, loss on individual micro-batches, and optimizer moments to see whether it is an outlier batch, numerical overflow in low precision, or exploding attention logits. Reproduce by replaying the suspect batches, and distinguish a transient spike that self-recovers from true divergence. Fixes include skipping or cleaning bad data, tightening gradient clipping, lowering the learning rate, adding z-loss or query-key layernorm to bound logits, and if needed rolling back to a healthy checkpoint with adjusted settings.

questions.question: Design a deduplication pipeline for a web-scale pretraining corpus. It has to run as a streaming process.
questions.answer: Stream documents through a staged pipeline that first does cheap exact-dup removal via content hashing, then near-duplicate detection using MinHash signatures with locality-sensitive hashing to bucket similar documents without all-pairs comparison. Keep the LSH band index and seen-hash set in a sharded, memory-bounded store so each incoming document is checked and either added or dropped in a single pass, enabling true streaming. Apply both document-level and substring or paragraph-level dedup to catch boilerplate, and shard by hash bucket across workers so the index scales horizontally. Tune Jaccard thresholds and shingle size to balance recall of duplicates against false positives, and keep provenance and counts for auditing and tuning.

questions.question: Design the serving stack for a consumer chatbot with real-time search over a social-media firehose.
questions.answer: Combine a conversational LLM with a real-time retrieval tier over the social firehose: ingest the stream into a near-real-time index (inverted plus embeddings) with aggressive time-decay and freshness windows, so queries about recent events retrieve the latest posts. The serving path routes a user turn to query planning, fetches fresh candidates with recency-biased ranking and credibility signals, and passes them to the LLM to synthesize a grounded, cited answer, streaming tokens back. Keep the firehose indexing pipeline decoupled and horizontally scaled with immutable segments and short merge intervals for seconds-to-minutes freshness. Serve the LLM on GPU pools with batching and prefix caching, and cache retrieval for trending queries. Tradeoffs are freshness versus index cost and ranking stability, retrieval recall versus noise and misinformation from unvetted posts, and latency of live retrieval within the chat response budget.

questions.question: You have four hours to build and demo a working AI-powered product. How do you spend them?
questions.answer: Describe a clear prioritization plan: spend the first stretch scoping the smallest valuable slice and deciding what to cut, then build a thin end-to-end path before polishing. Emphasize leveraging existing APIs, models, and frameworks to maximize working functionality within the time, and reserving buffer to ensure the demo actually runs. Mention de-risking the hardest unknown early and defining what a credible demo must prove. What good looks like is pragmatic scoping, bias toward a working product over perfection, and clear reasoning about tradeoffs under time pressure.

questions.question: Pair-programming: build a service that takes a user question, enriches it with data from a third-party API, and answers via a chat-model API. How do you structure it?
questions.answer: Structure it as three decoupled layers behind a thin orchestrator: an input/parse layer that validates and normalizes the question, an enrichment layer that calls the third-party API (with timeout, retry, and caching), and an answer layer that builds the prompt from the question plus enrichment and calls the chat model. The orchestrator wires them and owns error handling so a failed enrichment degrades gracefully rather than crashing. Keep the external clients behind interfaces so they are mockable and swappable, make calls async where I/O-bound, and separate prompt construction into its own module for testing. Cross-cutting concerns are timeouts, retries with backoff, input validation against injection, and observability (logging latency and failures at each hop).

questions.question: Mistral 7B shipped with grouped-query attention and sliding-window attention. What does each buy you, and what does each cost?
questions.answer: Grouped-query attention reduces the KV cache by sharing key/value heads across query-head groups, cutting the dominant inference memory and bandwidth cost with almost no quality loss. Sliding-window attention limits each token to attend only to a fixed window of recent tokens, making attention cost linear in sequence length and bounding the cache, while stacked layers still propagate information beyond one window indirectly. What GQA costs is a little representational capacity in K/V; what sliding-window costs is direct long-range attention, so distant tokens are reached only through multiple layers, which can weaken precise long-distance recall. Together they make a small model cheap to serve on long inputs at a modest quality trade-off.

questions.question: Explain how a Mixtral-style sparse mixture-of-experts model works. Why does a ~47B-parameter model run at roughly the cost of a ~13B one?
questions.answer: A Mixtral-style model replaces each dense MLP with a set of experts (e.g., eight) and a router that selects the top two per token, so only two experts run for any given token. Total parameters count all experts (~47B), but per-token compute only touches the active ones plus shared attention, roughly matching a ~13B dense model's FLOPs. The catch is memory: all experts must be resident, so you pay the full parameter footprint even though compute stays low, and routing adds load-balancing and communication overhead. The payoff is much greater capacity and quality at near-constant inference cost per token.

questions.question: Estimate the KV-cache memory for serving Mistral 7B, and design the rolling-buffer cache that sliding-window attention enables.
questions.answer: Mistral 7B has 32 layers and uses grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads of dimension 128, so per token the KV cache is 2 * 32 * 8 * 128 * 2 bytes ≈ 1 MB in FP16, meaning a 32k-token context is about 32 GB per sequence if stored fully. Sliding-window attention with a window of W (e.g., 4096) means a token only attends to the last W tokens, so you never need to store more than W tokens of KV per sequence. I design the cache as a fixed-size rolling (ring) buffer of W slots per layer: as new tokens arrive, they overwrite the oldest slots modulo W, with the attention kernel indexing the buffer circularly. This bounds KV memory to about W tokens (~4 MB per sequence for W=4096) regardless of total sequence length, trading unlimited history for a constant-memory, constant-cost decode step.

questions.question: You need to quantize a model for a customer's hardware. How do you choose a scheme, and how do you prove quality hasn't regressed?
questions.answer: I start from the hardware's supported formats and kernels (does it accelerate INT8, FP8, INT4?) and the quality budget, then pick the lightest scheme that meets it, typically weight-only INT8/INT4 with group-wise scales for memory-bound decode, or FP8 weights+activations where supported. I choose a method matched to the target: AWQ or GPTQ for low-bit weights, SmoothQuant for INT8 activations, and reserve quantization-aware training for aggressive 2-4 bit targets. To prove quality I evaluate the quantized model against the FP16 baseline on a representative suite: task benchmarks, perplexity, and crucially the customer's real workload and distribution, reporting deltas with confidence intervals. I also check tail behavior and worst-case prompts, and only ship if the regression is within an agreed threshold.

questions.question: How does function calling actually work with an LLM, and how do you make it reliable enough for production agents?
questions.answer: The model is given tool definitions as schemas in its context, and when it judges a tool is needed it emits a structured call with a name and JSON arguments; your runtime parses that, validates it, executes the real function, and feeds the result back for the model to continue. The model only proposes calls, so your orchestration layer owns execution, security, and correctness. To make it production-reliable, enforce strict schema validation and reject or repair malformed calls, return errors as structured observations with bounded self-correction, add timeouts, retries with backoff, and idempotency for safe reexecution. Bound total steps and cost, gate irreversible actions behind approval, scope tool permissions tightly, and log full traces with an evaluation suite so you can catch regressions.

questions.question: After fine-tuning on a customer's task, target accuracy is up but the model got worse at everything else. What happened and what do you do?
questions.answer: This is catastrophic forgetting: optimizing hard on the narrow customer task shifted weights away from the general capabilities, trading breadth for the target metric. Confirm it with a broad held-out evaluation suite so you can quantify the regression, not just the target gain. Remedies are to reduce training intensity (lower learning rate, fewer epochs, early stopping), mix in general or replay data alongside the task data, or switch to LoRA so base weights stay frozen. You can also regularize toward the base model or merge the fine-tuned and base weights, then re-evaluate both target and general metrics to find the right balance.

questions.question: Design an on-prem deployment of an open-weight model for a European bank that cannot send data to any external API.
questions.answer: Deploy an open-weight model entirely inside the bank's network on their GPUs, with the model, tokenizer, and all inference software packaged for offline installation and no outbound calls. Build the serving stack (batched GPU inference, autoscaling within the on-prem cluster), RAG indexes, and vector stores on internal infrastructure, integrating with the bank's identity provider and data sources behind the firewall. Since there is no external API, you own capacity planning, upgrades, monitoring, and security hardening, and you provide model updates as signed artifacts imported through their controlled process. Enforce data residency, audit logging, and encryption to satisfy regulators, and size GPUs for peak internal load since you cannot burst to a cloud. Tradeoffs are open-model quality and the operational burden of self-hosting versus a managed API, fixed capacity versus elastic scaling, and slower update cadence versus full data control and compliance.

questions.question: Design a token-based rate limiter for a multi-tenant LLM API. Implement the core, then tell me what changes when it's distributed.
questions.answer: Implement per-tenant token buckets: a map from tenant id to a bucket holding current tokens and last-refill time, refilling lazily at the tenant's rate up to its burst capacity, and admitting a request only if a token (or enough tokens for the request's cost) is available. Charging by token cost rather than per-request fits LLM usage where requests vary in size. When distributed, the bucket state must be shared and updated atomically across nodes, so move it to Redis with a Lua script (or compare-and-swap) to do the refill-and-decrement in one atomic step, preventing two nodes from both spending the last token. You then must handle clock skew, the store becoming a hot/single point of failure, and the latency of a network hop per check, often mitigated with local token leasing.
