questions.question: Our flagship is a sparse MoE with ~10x more total than active parameters. Why is that architecture a good fit for private enterprise deployment, and where does it hurt?
questions.answer: A sparse MoE with roughly ten times more total than active parameters stores a large pool of knowledge and specialization while only activating a slice per token, so you get strong quality at the inference compute of a much smaller dense model. For private enterprise deployment that is attractive because latency and throughput are governed by active parameters, and the broad capacity helps across diverse internal domains without many separate fine-tunes. Where it hurts is memory: all experts must be loaded, so GPU footprint and cost scale with total parameters, making single-box or constrained on-prem deployment hard. Routing also complicates batching, load balancing, and quantization, and small-batch enterprise traffic can underutilize experts and hurt efficiency.

questions.question: You have an embedding model and a reranker. Why sell both? Design the two-stage retrieval pipeline and tell me when the reranker earns its latency.
questions.answer: You sell both because they do different jobs: the embedding model is a cheap, precomputable first stage that scans millions of documents to recall a broad candidate set, while the reranker is an expensive, high-precision second stage that reorders a small candidate set using full query-document interaction. The pipeline embeds and indexes all documents offline, retrieves the top 50 to 200 by vector (and optionally keyword) similarity at query time, then runs a cross-encoder reranker over just those to pick the final top few for the generator. The embedder optimizes recall at scale; the reranker optimizes precision at the top where it actually matters for the LLM's limited context. The reranker earns its latency when first-stage recall is high but ordering is noisy, when the context budget is tight so top-k precision drives answer quality, and when the accuracy gain outweighs the added per-pair inference cost; for easy queries or very loose latency-free budgets it may not.

questions.question: An enterprise wants semantic search over ~100M documents but is balking at vector-index cost. Walk me through embedding compression options and the maths.
questions.answer: At 100M documents the dominant cost is RAM for the vectors, so the maths starts with dimensions times bytes times count: 100M vectors at 768 dims in float32 is 100e6 * 768 * 4 bytes, about 307 GB, plus index overhead. The first lever is dimensionality reduction, for example Matryoshka embeddings or PCA truncating 768 to 256 dims, cutting memory roughly 3x. The second is quantization: scalar quantization to int8 gives a 4x cut with little recall loss, and product quantization compresses each vector to a handful of codebook bytes for 10 to 30x reduction at some recall cost; binary quantization is the most aggressive at 32x with a reranking rescore step to recover accuracy. The third is architectural, using IVF-PQ or disk-based indexes so only centroids and compressed codes stay in RAM, so I would combine dimension truncation plus PQ and a rerank-on-full-precision pass to land under tens of GB while holding recall within target.

questions.question: How would you evaluate multilingual retrieval quality when employees query in French and Korean over mostly-English documents?
questions.answer: I evaluate on queries in the actual languages employees use (French and Korean) against the mostly-English corpus, building a labeled set of query-to-relevant-document pairs that reflect real cross-lingual needs rather than only same-language retrieval. I measure recall@k, MRR, and nDCG per language and per query type so I can see whether French or Korean queries underperform English ones and whether the multilingual embedding model actually aligns the cross-lingual vector space. I include transliteration, code-switching, and domain-term cases, and I check that the reranker and any translation step preserve relevance. Because judgments require bilingual annotators, I complement human labels with careful LLM-as-judge grounded in the retrieved documents, and I track whether answer quality, not just retrieval, holds up end to end in each language.

questions.question: A customer 10x'd their indexed documents and reports answer quality “got noticeably worse.” Drive the investigation.
questions.answer: More documents mean the relevant evidence is now a smaller fraction of a larger, denser space, so I would first separate retrieval from generation: measure whether recall@k and the rank of known-good documents degraded after the scale-up. Common culprits are near-duplicate and contradictory documents crowding the top-k, embedding-space saturation where many chunks look similar, fixed k now returning more distractors, and index parameters (efSearch/nprobe) left untuned for the larger corpus hurting approximate recall. I would check for stale or duplicate content, add or tune a reranker to restore top-k precision, revisit chunking and metadata filtering to narrow the search, and verify the index was rebuilt with appropriate parameters. Then I confirm the fix on a held-out labeled set so I am treating the real regression, not a symptom.

questions.question: Design an agent that automates an enterprise workflow, say, drafting RFP responses from internal documents and a CRM. What does “enter-prise-grade” add?
questions.answer: The core loop retrieves relevant internal documents and CRM records, grounds a draft RFP response in them with citations back to sources, and lets a reviewer edit before anything is sent. I would use retrieval over a governed document store plus structured CRM queries as tools, a drafting step constrained to the firm's template, and a verification pass that checks every claim is supported by a retrieved source. Enterprise-grade adds the non-model concerns: access control so the agent only sees documents the requesting user is entitled to, audit logging of every retrieval and generation, data residency and PII handling, versioning and approval workflows, and SLAs with monitoring. It also means evaluation against real RFPs, graceful degradation, human sign-off on outbound content, and integration with existing identity and permission systems so authorization is enforced in infrastructure rather than in the prompt.

questions.question: A bank wants the whole stack (model, RAG, agents) deployed air-gapped on their own GPUs. What actually changes versus your SaaS?
questions.answer: Air-gapped deployment shifts you from a managed, elastic, continuously updated service to a fixed, customer-operated appliance. You can no longer autoscale into cloud capacity, so GPUs must be sized for peak and the bank owns hardware, power, and failure handling; updates become signed offline artifacts shipped and imported through their change-control rather than continuous rollout. Telemetry, centralized logging, and remote debugging disappear, so you need on-prem observability and support tooling that works without phoning home, plus license enforcement that functions offline. RAG and agent tools must integrate only with internal systems and secrets, and every dependency must be vendored for offline install. Security, compliance, data residency, and audit become the customer's and your shared responsibility inside their boundary. The tradeoffs are full data control and compliance versus loss of elasticity, slower updates, higher operational cost, and no live telemetry to improve the system.

questions.question: An enterprise customer wants to deploy your RAG system but has no labelled data. How do you evaluate it before and after launch?
questions.answer: With no labels, first create an evaluation foundation: assemble representative questions from the customer's documents and expected-use interviews, and have a subject expert or your team label a small gold set to anchor metrics. Evaluate retrieval and generation separately, measuring retrieval recall and relevance on the gold questions and answer faithfulness, relevance, and completeness via an LLM-as-judge calibrated against the gold labels. Before launch, run this suite plus adversarial and out-of-scope questions, and set thresholds and a human spot-check on a sample. After launch, instrument faithfulness and citation checks on sampled live traffic, capture user feedback, thumbs, and escalations, and monitor retrieval quality and drift. Continuously grow the eval set from real queries so coverage improves and regressions are caught early.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you owned an ambiguous problem end-to-end without much direction.
questions.answer: Pick an open-ended problem where direction was genuinely lacking, and show how you created structure: clarifying the goal, breaking it down, and making defensible assumptions. Walk through how you prioritized, made decisions with incomplete information, and sought input where useful without waiting to be told what to do. Emphasize the bias to action balanced with checkpoints to validate you were solving the right problem. Close with the outcome and lesson, demonstrating self-direction, judgment, and comfort with ambiguity.

questions.question: Walk me through DeepSeekMoE. How is it different from a standard top-2 MoE like Mixtral?
questions.answer: DeepSeekMoE refines standard MoE with fine-grained experts, splitting the feed-forward into many smaller experts so routing can compose more specialized combinations for the same active parameter budget. It also dedicates a few shared experts that every token always uses, capturing common knowledge so the routed experts can specialize rather than redundantly learning general patterns. Compared to a top-2 Mixtral design, this increases expert count and specialization and reduces redundancy, improving capacity efficiency. The combination of fine granularity plus shared experts is the key architectural difference.

questions.question: DeepSeek-V3 uses auxiliary-loss-free load balancing. What was wrong with the auxiliary loss, and how does the bias trick work?
questions.answer: A load-balancing auxiliary loss pushes tokens to spread across experts, but it fights the main language-modeling objective, introducing gradient interference that can hurt quality and require careful weighting. DeepSeek-V3 drops this extra loss and instead adds a per-expert bias term to the routing scores used only for the top-k selection, not for the combination weights. After each step the bias is nudged down for overloaded experts and up for underused ones, steering future tokens toward balance without contaminating the training gradient. This keeps utilization even while leaving the model's learning objective clean.

questions.question: What is multi-token prediction (MTP) and why train with it?
questions.answer: Multi-token prediction trains the model to predict several future tokens at each position, using additional lightweight prediction heads or modules rather than only the immediate next token. This denser training signal improves sample efficiency and encourages representations that plan ahead, often yielding better quality. At inference the extra heads can also be reused for speculative-style decoding, proposing multiple tokens to verify in parallel and reducing latency. It is a training-time technique whose benefits persist even if you decode one token at a time.

questions.question: Implement top-k MoE routing with a shared expert in PyTorch, and point out the efficiency and correctness traps.
questions.answer: Compute per-token router logits with a linear layer, take the top-k experts with their softmax-normalized gating weights, always add a shared expert's output, and sum the weighted expert outputs. For efficiency do not loop per token; instead sort or group tokens by expert and run each expert on its batched slice (or scatter/gather), so you avoid running inactive experts and keep GEMMs dense. Correctness traps include renormalizing the gate weights over the selected top-k (not the full set), applying gates after the expert computation, handling empty-expert batches without NaNs, and keeping the shared expert out of the top-k routing while still adding it. Watch dtype and capacity: dropped-token capacity limits must be handled explicitly, and gradients must flow through the gate weights for the router to learn.

questions.question: Sketch how you would serve a 671B-parameter MoE model with low latency under GPU-memory constraints.
questions.answer: A 671B MoE model has huge total parameters but activates only a few experts per token, so the strategy is to exploit sparsity: shard experts across many GPUs with expert parallelism while keeping the attention and shared layers replicated or tensor-parallel. Quantize weights to FP8/INT8 to fit the enormous parameter count into aggregate HBM, and use a fast interconnect since every token triggers an all-to-all to route to its experts. For low latency I minimize the routing hop count, co-locate frequently co-activated experts, balance load to avoid hot experts, and overlap the all-to-all communication with compute. Disaggregated prefill/decode and prefix caching help, and I size the fleet so the active-parameter working set stays bandwidth-efficient per decode step.

questions.question: R1-Zero was trained with RL and essentially no SFT first. What did that show, and why did full R1 add SFT back?
questions.answer: R1-Zero showed that pure RL with verifiable rewards on a strong base model can induce sophisticated reasoning behaviors, including longer chains of thought and self-verification, without any supervised reasoning demonstrations, demonstrating that reasoning can emerge from reward alone. However its outputs suffered from poor readability, language mixing, and formatting problems because nothing shaped the style. Full R1 added a cold-start SFT phase on curated reasoning data before and alongside RL to fix readability and alignment and to give the RL a better starting point. The lesson is that RL supplies the reasoning capability while SFT supplies human-preferred presentation and stability.

questions.question: FP8 training at 671B scale is hard. What actually breaks in low precision, and how do you make it stable?
questions.answer: In FP8 the tiny dynamic range and few mantissa bits make large activations, attention logits, and gradient values overflow or round to zero, and accumulation error compounds over many steps, causing divergence. Weight update signal can also be lost when small gradients underflow. Stabilizing it requires fine-grained per-tile or per-block scaling rather than a single tensor scale, keeping sensitive accumulations and certain layers (embeddings, norms, the optimizer master weights, often attention softmax) in higher precision, and using delayed or dynamic loss scaling. Careful handling of outlier channels, high-precision accumulation in matmuls, and monitoring of overflow counts keep a 671B-scale FP8 run numerically stable.

questions.question: How do you build a training dataset without triggering model collapse when much of your data is synthetic?
questions.answer: Model collapse happens when training repeatedly on model-generated data narrows diversity and amplifies the model's own errors, so the distribution degrades over generations. Prevent it by anchoring on a substantial core of real human data and treating synthetic data as an augmentation, not a replacement. Aggressively filter and verify synthetic samples, preferring data with external validation such as passing unit tests, matching ground-truth answers, or human or strong-judge acceptance, and deduplicate to preserve diversity. Mix sources, cap the synthetic fraction, and continuously monitor diversity and downstream metrics so you catch distributional drift early.

questions.question: DualPipe overlaps computation and communication in training. Why is that overlap the whole game at this scale, and what is the trade-off?
questions.answer: At extreme scale, cross-device communication for expert routing, gradients, and activations can stall the accelerators, so if compute waits on communication, utilization collapses and the training cost explodes. DualPipe schedules forward and backward micro-batches so that communication of one chunk is hidden behind computation of another, keeping the pipeline bubble near zero and the devices busy. That overlap is the whole game because at this scale communication volume is enormous and bandwidth is the binding constraint, so hiding it directly determines throughput and effective FLOPs. The trade-off is substantial complexity and higher memory from holding more in-flight micro-batches and duplicated buffers, plus a schedule that is harder to implement and tune.

questions.question: DeepSeek claims frontier-class results at a fraction of the usual training cost. If an interviewer asks “how is that even possible,” what is your structured answer?
questions.answer: Give a structured, mechanisms-based answer rather than speculation: separate the possible levers into data quality and curation, architecture and sparsity choices like mixture-of-experts, training efficiency techniques, and hardware and systems optimizations. Note that reported cost figures often exclude research, failed runs, and infrastructure, so headline numbers deserve scrutiny. Acknowledge uncertainty and distinguish what is plausible from what is unverified, showing you reason from first principles about where efficiency gains realistically come from. What good looks like is a calm, organized breakdown that demonstrates technical depth and healthy skepticism without dismissiveness.

questions.question: Kimi's headline feature is very long context. When you push from 8K to hundreds of thousands of tokens, what actually breaks first, and why?
questions.answer: The first thing to break is usually positional generalization: RoPE angles beyond the trained range are out of distribution, so attention degrades unless you interpolate or use YaRN. Close behind is memory, since the KV cache grows linearly with length and quickly exhausts GPU memory and bandwidth, making attention memory-bound. Attention compute also scales quadratically, so prefill latency explodes without sparse, windowed, or chunked attention and optimized kernels. Finally, quality softens through lost-in-the-middle effects and a scarcity of genuinely long training documents, so the model may technically ingest the tokens yet reason over them poorly.

questions.question: Kimi K2 uses Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). Explain what it does and how it compares to GQA for KV-cache reduction.
questions.answer: Multi-head Latent Attention projects keys and values into a shared low-rank latent vector that is cached, then up-projects per head during attention, so the cache stores a small latent instead of full per-head K and V. This can cut KV-cache size more aggressively than GQA while retaining more head-specific expressiveness, because GQA simply shares a few KV heads across query groups and loses some capacity. MLA typically also decouples the RoPE-carrying dimensions so positional information is preserved despite compression. The net is comparable or better cache reduction than GQA with less quality sacrifice, at the cost of extra projection compute and implementation complexity.

questions.question: Kimi K2 is a 1T-parameter MoE with ~32B active per token and hundreds of experts. Explain the routing and the systems cost of training it.
questions.answer: Each token's router selects a small top-k from hundreds of experts (plus shared experts), so only ~32B of the 1T parameters activate, keeping per-token FLOPs modest while total capacity is enormous. The systems cost is dominated by expert parallelism: experts are sharded across many devices, so every layer needs all-to-all communication to dispatch tokens to their experts and gather results, which stresses interconnect bandwidth and must be overlapped with compute. You also must hold all 1T parameters in aggregate memory, keep experts load-balanced to avoid stragglers and dropped tokens, and combine expert parallelism with data, tensor, and pipeline parallelism plus heavy checkpointing. Communication, load imbalance, and memory, not raw arithmetic, are the binding constraints.

questions.question: How do you take a model trained at 8K–32K and make it work at 128K or more?
questions.answer: Start from a model trained at 8K-32K and extend positional encodings with RoPE interpolation or YaRN so angles stay in the learned range, then continue training (long-context fine-tuning) on a modest amount of genuinely long documents to adapt the model. On the systems side, enable memory- and IO-efficient attention (FlashAttention), possibly sliding-window or sparse/chunked attention, and KV-cache reductions like GQA/MLA and quantization to make the longer cache affordable. Validate with targeted long-context evaluations (needle-in-a-haystack, multi-document reasoning) to confirm the model actually uses the added range rather than just accepting it. The attraction is that post-hoc extension is far cheaper than pre-training long from scratch.

questions.question: Walk me through why you would disaggregate prefill and decode onto separate machines, as Mooncake does. What does that buy you and what does it cost?
questions.answer: Prefill is compute-bound and bursty while decode is long-running and memory-bandwidth-bound, so co-locating them means a big prefill stalls ongoing decodes and neither phase runs at its ideal batch size. Disaggregating onto separate machines lets you scale and batch each phase independently, run prefill on compute-optimized nodes and decode on bandwidth-optimized nodes, and protect decode tail latency from prefill spikes. It also enables a global KV-cache store so prefix reuse and cache pooling span the whole fleet, improving hit rates. The cost is transferring the KV cache from prefill to decode over the network, which adds latency and bandwidth pressure plus scheduling complexity, so it pays off mainly at large scale with long prompts and high load.

questions.question: A chat assistant re-sends a long conversation history on every turn. How do you avoid recomputing all of it, and what are the pitfalls?
questions.answer: Reuse the KV cache across turns via prefix caching: because the conversation history is a shared prefix, its KV state is kept so each new turn only prefills the newly appended tokens instead of the whole history. In practice you persist the per-session KV cache (in GPU memory, or offloaded to CPU/remote store) keyed by the conversation prefix and resume decoding from it. Pitfalls include cache eviction under memory pressure forcing a full recompute, exact-match sensitivity so any edit to earlier messages or a changed system prompt invalidates the prefix, and sticky routing requirements so the session lands on the node holding its cache. You also must bound total KV growth for very long dialogues, using summarization, truncation, or sliding windows, and handle correctness if sampling or tool outputs alter history.

questions.question: For a long-context assistant, when is a 1M-token context window the right tool, and when should you use retrieval instead?
questions.answer: A 1M-token window is the right tool when the task needs holistic reasoning over a bounded, coherent body of text that fits, such as analyzing one long contract, codebase, or conversation where cross-references and global structure matter and missing any part breaks the answer. Retrieval is better when the knowledge base is large or unbounded, changes frequently, needs access control, or when only a small relevant slice is needed per query, because stuffing everything is costly, slower, and dilutes attention with irrelevant tokens. Long context also degrades with lost-in-the-middle effects and pays latency and dollars proportional to tokens on every request. In practice I use long context for deep single-document reasoning and retrieval for scale, freshness, and cost, and often combine them by retrieving a focused subset into a large window.

questions.question: Training a trillion-parameter model, attention logits can blow up and destabilise the run. What is going on, and how does something like MuonClip address it?
questions.answer: When unbounded query-key dot products grow, attention logits can become extremely large, saturating the softmax and producing huge or NaN gradients that destabilize a trillion-parameter run. The underlying issue is that nothing constrains the scale of the query and key projections as training proceeds. MuonClip addresses this by combining the Muon optimizer with a clipping mechanism that rescales the query and key weight matrices to cap the maximum attention logit, bounding the softmax inputs directly at the source rather than patching symptoms. This keeps logits in a safe range so the run stays stable without sacrificing the optimizer's efficiency.

questions.question: Kimi K1.5 scaled RL for reasoning without a process reward model or tree search. Why deliberately keep the RL recipe that simple?
questions.answer: Kimi K1.5 kept the RL recipe simple, using plain policy optimization with verifiable outcome rewards instead of a process reward model or tree search, because those add components that are expensive, brittle, and prone to reward hacking. Process reward models require costly step-level labels and can be gamed, while search inflates inference and training cost and complicates the pipeline. A simple outcome-based signal with long context lets the model learn its own reasoning strategies and scales cleanly with compute and data. The bet is that capability comes mainly from scaling RL on good verifiable signals, not from elaborate search or reward machinery.

questions.question: Kimi K2 targets agentic and coding tasks. How would you evaluate whether an agentic model is actually good, beyond a single benchmark number?
questions.answer: A single number hides how an agentic model fails, so evaluate across many realistic, verifiable tasks measuring end-to-end success, not just a leaderboard figure. Look at trajectory quality, correct tool selection and arguments, error recovery, efficiency in steps and cost, and robustness to perturbed instructions and environments. Include long-horizon and multi-tool tasks, and test generalization on held-out tasks created after training to rule out contamination and overfitting to the benchmark harness. Examine failure modes such as loops, hallucinated calls, giving up, or taking unsafe irreversible actions, and measure consistency across repeated runs since agents are stochastic. Combine programmatic success checks with human or judge review of trajectories, and validate on your actual target workflows rather than only public suites.

questions.question: GLM's original pre-training objective is autoregressive blank infilling. How does it differ from BERT and GPT, and why did the team argue it unifies understanding and generation?
questions.answer: GLM's autoregressive blank infilling masks spans of text and trains the model to regenerate them autoregressively, with the unmasked context visible bidirectionally and the mask filled left-to-right. This differs from BERT, which predicts independent masked tokens with a bidirectional encoder (good for understanding, weak at generation), and from GPT, which is purely left-to-right (good at generation, lacking bidirectional context). Because blank infilling conditions on full surrounding context yet generates sequentially, the team argued it captures both bidirectional understanding and autoregressive generation in one objective. Varying span lengths lets it span short cloze-style tasks and long free-form generation under the same framework.

questions.question: GLM-4.5 is an MoE with 355B total but 32B active parameters. Explain the economics: what does that split buy you and what does it cost?
questions.answer: The 355B total gives the model a large reservoir of capacity and specialized knowledge, but routing activates only ~32B per token, so inference compute and latency track the small active set rather than the full size. Economically you get quality closer to a very large dense model at the serving cost of a ~32B one, improving throughput per FLOP. The cost is memory and infrastructure: all 355B parameters must be resident across devices, requiring expert parallelism and all-to-all communication, plus load balancing to keep experts busy. Small-batch or on-prem deployments may underutilize experts and still pay the full memory bill.

questions.question: Implement a top-k MoE router in PyTorch. Then contrast auxiliary-loss load balancing with a loss-free approach.
questions.answer: A top-k router is a linear layer producing per-expert logits; take the top-k, softmax over just those to get gating weights, dispatch each token's hidden state to its selected experts, and combine their outputs by the gate weights. Auxiliary-loss balancing adds a term that penalizes uneven expert usage (for example the product of mean routing probability and dispatch fraction per expert), pushing tokens to spread out, but it competes with the main loss and needs tuning. A loss-free approach instead maintains a per-expert bias added to the routing scores for selection only, adjusted up or down based on recent load, so balance is enforced without injecting a competing gradient into the model. The loss-free method keeps the training objective clean and tends to be more stable.

questions.question: What is Multi-Token Prediction (MTP), why add an MTP layer, and how does it help at inference time?
questions.answer: Multi-Token Prediction trains the model with extra heads that predict more than just the next token at each position, densifying the learning signal and encouraging look-ahead representations. Adding an MTP layer or module gives a cheap auxiliary objective during training that improves sample efficiency and downstream quality. At inference those heads can propose multiple candidate future tokens that the main model verifies in parallel, enabling speculative-style decoding that lowers latency. Even if you decode one token at a time, the representations learned under MTP tend to be better.

questions.question: GLM has been bilingual Chinese/English since GLM-130B. What changes in tokenization, data and evaluation when a model must serve both languages well?
questions.answer: Serving two languages well starts with tokenization: the vocabulary must cover Chinese characters efficiently so Chinese text does not fragment into many tokens and inflate cost, while keeping English fertility low, which usually means a larger balanced byte-level BPE vocabulary. Data must be curated and balanced across both languages (and code), with attention to script-specific normalization and avoiding one language dominating and degrading the other. Evaluation needs native benchmarks in each language rather than translated proxies, since translation masks fluency and cultural-knowledge gaps. The through-line is balance and parity, in vocabulary, corpus mix, and measurement, so neither language is a second-class citizen.

questions.question: AutoGLM and CogAgent operate real GUIs from screenshots over tens of steps. Design the agent: perception, action space, and error recovery for a 50-step task.
questions.answer: Perception converts each screenshot into a structured representation by detecting interactive elements and their positions, ideally fusing visual grounding with any available accessibility or DOM tree to get reliable element targets rather than raw pixels alone. The action space is a small set of primitives, click, type, scroll, drag, key press, and wait, each parameterized by a target element or coordinate, which keeps the model's decisions discrete and verifiable. For a long task I maintain a plan with subgoals and a running memory of what has been done, re-grounding against the original goal each step to prevent drift. Error recovery relies on verifying expected post-conditions after each action, detecting when the screen did not change as expected, retrying or trying alternatives, backtracking on dead ends, and escalating to a human when stuck, all under a step and time budget.

questions.question: GLM-4.5 is a hybrid reasoning model with a thinking mode and a direct-response mode. How do you build one model that does both, and what are the training and serving implications?
questions.answer: You build a hybrid model by training on data that contains both long chain-of-thought traces and direct concise answers, gated by a control signal such as a system flag or special token so the model learns to produce or suppress a thinking segment on demand. Post-training mixes both modes in SFT and RL so neither capability is lost, and the reward or preference data reinforces correct mode selection. In training the challenge is balancing the two distributions so thinking mode stays strong without making direct mode verbose, and keeping evaluation for both. In serving you expose a mode switch, budget tokens and latency differently per mode, and may route or set a thinking budget since thinking mode costs far more tokens and time.

questions.question: Why does long-horizon agentic RL need a disaggregated, asynchronous design (as in the slime framework) rather than colocated-synchronous?
questions.answer: Long-horizon agentic RL spends most wall-clock time in environment rollouts of highly variable length, so a colocated-synchronous design forces fast generation and slow policy updates to block on each other, leaving accelerators idle and letting the slowest trajectory gate every step. A disaggregated, asynchronous design separates rollout workers from the trainer, letting many environments run continuously and stream completed trajectories into a buffer the learner consumes at its own pace. This decouples generation throughput from training throughput, hides the long-tail latency of variable episodes, and keeps both sides busy. The cost is managing off-policy staleness between the sampling policy and the learner, which the framework handles with versioning and correction.

questions.question: GLM-4.5's post-training trains expert models per domain then unifies with self-distillation. Walk through why you would train specialists and then merge them.
questions.answer: Training per-domain specialists first lets each model use domain-optimal data, reward signals, and hyperparameters without the interference you get when conflicting objectives share one training run, so each reaches a higher ceiling on its domain. You then unify them into a single model via self-distillation, generating high-quality outputs from each expert and training the unified model to reproduce them across all domains. This gives one deployable model that approaches the combined specialists' quality while avoiding the capacity contention and negative transfer of training everything jointly from the start. It also modularizes the pipeline, so you can improve or replace one specialist without redoing the whole post-training.

questions.question: Design AutoGLM end to end: a cloud service letting users delegate multi-step phone tasks (“order my usual coffee”) to an autonomous agent. Architecture and failure modes.
questions.answer: Architect AutoGLM as a cloud planner driving device-side execution: an LLM-based planner decomposes a high-level goal into steps, maintains task state and memory, and issues actions to an executor that controls the phone via UI automation or app APIs, perceiving screen state through accessibility trees and vision. Ground each action in the current observed screen, verify effects before proceeding, and gate irreversible or sensitive steps (payments, sharing) behind confirmation and policy checks, with user-scoped credentials never exposed to the model. Persist session state so long tasks survive interruptions, and provide clear handback to the user on ambiguity. Failure modes include UI drift breaking selectors, misgrounded actions on the wrong element, partial completion leaving inconsistent state, infinite loops, auth and CAPTCHA walls, and acting on stale screens; mitigate with verification after each step, timeouts, retries with replanning, idempotency, and human confirmation for risky actions.

questions.question: How would you evaluate an agentic coding model on SWE-bench and τ-bench style benchmarks without fooling yourself?
questions.answer: Use the official sandboxed harnesses with fixed environment states and programmatic verification, run each task multiple times to report pass rate with variance rather than a single lucky run, and distinguish pass@1 from pass@k honestly. Decontaminate: confirm the model was not trained on the benchmark issues or their solutions, and test on newer or held-out instances created after the training cutoff. Audit the harness itself for leakage such as hints in the environment, overly permissive test oracles, or tasks solvable by pattern-matching rather than reasoning, and inspect passing trajectories to ensure the agent solved the real problem. Report cost, step count, and failure modes alongside pass rate, and avoid tuning prompts on the test set. Finally, correlate benchmark gains with performance on your own private, representative tasks to ensure the numbers transfer.

questions.question: Qwen2.5-Coder trains with repository-level fill-in-the-middle using tokens like <|fim_prefix|>, <|fim_suffix|>, <|repo_name|>. Write the function that formats a repo-level FIM example, and explain why repo-level beats file-level.
questions.answer: Format the example by concatenating the repository context and the split file: emit the repo-name token followed by the repository identifier, optionally the file path and relevant cross-file context, then the FIM-encoded target file as prefix-token + code-before + suffix-token + code-after + middle-token + code-to-predict. The model learns to predict the middle given both surrounding context and the broader repo. Repo-level beats file-level because real completions depend on symbols, imports, and types defined in other files; giving the model sibling-file context lets it resolve cross-file references and match project conventions, whereas file-level FIM is blind to anything outside the current file and hallucinates APIs that actually live elsewhere in the repo.

questions.question: Qwen uses byte-level BPE with a ~151K vocabulary, augmented for multilingual coverage and with digits split into single characters. Why those choices, and what are the trade-offs?
questions.answer: Byte-level BPE guarantees every input is representable (no unknown tokens) since it falls back to raw bytes, and a large ~151K vocabulary lowers token fertility across many languages, reducing cost and context usage for multilingual and code text. Splitting digits into single characters makes numeric representation uniform and consistent, which helps arithmetic and reduces odd number-specific token artifacts. The trade-offs are a larger embedding and output matrix (more parameters and memory), and that single-digit numbers use more tokens, slightly lengthening numeric sequences. Overall it favors broad coverage and consistency at some cost in vocabulary size and number token count.

questions.question: Qwen3 unifies a thinking mode and a non-thinking mode in one model with a caller-settable thinking budget. How would you train that, and how would you serve it?
questions.answer: Train a single model on data that includes both long chain-of-thought traces and direct answers, marking each mode so the model learns to switch, then teach it to respect a budget by varying the allowed thinking length during fine-tuning and optionally reinforcing shorter-but-correct reasoning. The thinking budget can be exposed as a control token or a stop condition on the reasoning segment, and preference optimization can reward staying within budget while preserving accuracy. At serving time, parse the request's budget, let the model emit reasoning up to that many tokens (truncating or forcing the answer when the budget is hit), and strip or hide the thinking span from the final response. This gives callers a latency/quality dial in one deployed model instead of two.

questions.question: Qwen ships both dense and MoE models (30B with ~3B active; 235B with ~22B active). When would you pick the 30B-A3B MoE over a 32B dense?
questions.answer: Pick the 30B-A3B MoE when inference speed and throughput matter most, since it only activates ~3B parameters per token and decodes much faster and cheaper than a 32B dense model at comparable quality on many tasks. It shines when you have enough GPU memory to hold all experts and want high tokens-per-second for serving many requests. Choose the 32B dense model when memory is tight (dense needs far less than holding all experts), when you need the most consistent quality on hard reasoning, or when batching is small and MoE experts would be underutilized. The decision is essentially trading memory footprint and routing complexity for lower active-compute latency.

questions.question: Qwen2.5 extends context to 128K (and ~1M for Turbo) using YaRN plus Dual Chunk Attention, mostly training-free. Explain how, and why post-hoc extension is attractive.
questions.answer: YaRN rescales RoPE frequencies so positions beyond the training length map back into the learned range (interpolating low frequencies while preserving high-frequency local detail), extending context largely without retraining. Dual Chunk Attention splits the long sequence into chunks and composes intra-chunk and inter-chunk attention with remapped relative positions, so the model handles distances far beyond what it saw in training. Combining them reaches 128K (and ~1M for Turbo) with little or no additional training. Post-hoc extension is attractive because pre-training natively at such lengths is enormously expensive in compute and long-document data, so cheap adaptation that reuses the base model is far more practical.

questions.question: Qwen3 uses strong-to-weak distillation, bootstrapping smaller models from flagship ones. How does that work and why is it cheaper?
questions.answer: Strong-to-weak distillation uses the flagship model as a teacher to generate training targets, and the smaller student is trained to match the teacher's output distribution and reasoning traces instead of learning from scratch or from expensive RL. It is cheaper because generating teacher outputs and doing supervised distillation costs far less compute than running full RL and extensive search for each small model, and the teacher's already-refined behavior transfers directly. The student inherits reasoning and formatting without rediscovering them, so you get many sizes from one flagship investment. The main cost is one high-quality teacher plus inference to produce the distillation corpus.

questions.question: Qwen's reasoning models train with RL using verifiable rewards on maths and code. Why is that preferred over PPO with a learned reward model for these domains?
questions.answer: On math and code the answer is objectively checkable, so a verifier gives an exact, unhackable reward (correct answer, passing tests) that a learned reward model only approximates. PPO with a learned reward model inherits that model's errors and blind spots, invites reward hacking, and needs costly preference labeling and reward-model training. Verifiable rewards are cheap to scale across large generated problem sets, provide a clean signal for long reasoning chains, and keep the policy honest because partial-credit gaming is hard when correctness is binary. You only fall back to learned rewards where correctness is not programmatically checkable.

questions.question: Qwen ships open weights that top public leaderboards. As the release engineer, how do you make sure the benchmark numbers are trustworthy and not contaminated?
questions.answer: As release engineer, treat trustworthiness as a provenance problem: run decontamination checks measuring n-gram and embedding overlap between the training corpus and each public benchmark, and probe for memorization by comparing original versus perturbed test items. Reproduce the numbers with a pinned, public harness and standard prompts so results are independently verifiable, and avoid any prompt or hyperparameter tuning on the test sets. Supplement public leaderboards with private held-out and freshly created post-cutoff evaluations, since a gap between public and private scores signals overfitting. Report variance across runs, per-slice breakdowns, and the exact evaluation configuration so reviewers can audit. Document data sources and decontamination steps publicly so the community can trust and reproduce the claims.

questions.question: Qwen2.5-VL uses a native dynamic-resolution ViT with window attention and multimodal RoPE. Why native resolution instead of fixed tiling, and what does MRoPE encode?
questions.answer: Native dynamic resolution feeds the image at its true aspect ratio and size (padded to patch multiples) instead of forcing it into fixed square tiles, which avoids distortion, wasted padding, and the loss of fine detail or global layout that tiling causes, and it lets token count scale with image content so small images stay cheap and large ones keep detail. Window attention keeps this efficient by restricting most attention to local windows rather than all patches, making high-resolution inputs tractable. Multimodal RoPE (MRoPE) decomposes rotary position encoding into separate temporal, height, and width components so a token's position carries 2D spatial coordinates and, for video, a time index. This lets the model reason about where things are in the frame and when they occur across frames, generalizing better to varying resolutions and video lengths than a flattened 1D position.

questions.question: Alibaba open-sources Qwen under Apache 2.0 while running a commercial cloud business. Walk me through the strategy, and tell me about an ambiguous technical decision you owned end to end.
questions.answer: For the strategy, explain the logic of open-sourcing a strong model to drive ecosystem adoption, developer goodwill, and standardization while monetizing through the cloud platform that runs it at scale, plus talent and feedback benefits. Discuss the tradeoffs and competitive dynamics rather than treating it as purely altruistic. Then pivot to a STAR story about an ambiguous technical decision you owned, emphasizing how you framed options, weighed tradeoffs, decided under uncertainty, and the outcome. What good looks like is commercial and strategic reasoning paired with concrete evidence of independent technical ownership.

questions.question: Write code to measure a tokenizer's fertility across languages, and explain what you would do with the result.
questions.answer: Fertility is the average number of subword tokens the tokenizer emits per word (or per some linguistic unit). Measure it by running the tokenizer over a comparable corpus in each language, counting total tokens divided by total whitespace/linguistically defined words, ideally on parallel text so languages are directly comparable. Higher fertility means a language is encoded less efficiently, consuming more of the context window and more compute per unit of meaning, which signals under-representation in training and vocabulary. With the result I would rebalance vocabulary training data toward high-fertility languages, consider vocabulary expansion or a more multilingual tokenizer, and account for the cost disparity in pricing and context-budget decisions.

questions.question: Why is tokenization the first bottleneck for Indian-language LLMs, and how does a low-fertility tokenizer change the economics?
questions.answer: Indian-language scripts are underrepresented in typical tokenizer training, so a default BPE fragments them into many bytes or subwords, giving high fertility (many tokens per word) that inflates cost, latency, and context consumption and leaves less room for actual content. Because pricing and compute scale with tokens, a user writing Hindi or Tamil can pay several times more than an English user for the same information, and long inputs hit context limits sooner. A low-fertility tokenizer, trained with strong coverage of these scripts (including proper handling of conjuncts and combining characters), packs more characters per token, cutting cost and latency and effectively lengthening usable context. It also tends to improve quality, since the model sees more coherent units rather than scattered byte fragments.

questions.question: How do you deploy a capable assistant on cost-sensitive or on-device hardware without a datacentre GPU? Walk through the efficiency toolkit.
questions.answer: The toolkit starts with picking a small, capable base model (a few billion parameters) and distilling a larger teacher into it. Then aggressively quantize to 4-bit (or lower) weights with group-wise scales, often with quantization-aware training to recover quality, which shrinks both memory and bandwidth. Use efficient architectures (GQA/MQA, sliding-window or sparse attention) to cut KV cache, and apply pruning or sparsity where supported. On-device you exploit the NPU/GPU with a tuned runtime, keep context short, use prompt caching for repeated prefixes, and offload or stream to a server only for hard queries via a small-first routing strategy, trading some capability for dramatically lower cost and latency.

questions.question: Design cross-lingual RAG: the knowledge base is in English and Hindi, but users ask in Tamil, Telugu or transliterated Hinglish.
questions.answer: I decouple the language of the query from the language of the index by using a strong multilingual embedding model that maps Tamil, Telugu, English, Hindi, and transliterated Hinglish into a shared vector space, so cross-lingual matches work without per-pair translation. To handle transliteration and code-switching I normalize and, where helpful, transliterate or translate queries into the index languages as an additional retrieval path, fusing results so I do not depend on a single representation. I generate the answer in the user's query language while keeping citations to the English or Hindi source spans, and I use a multilingual reranker to sharpen top-k precision. I evaluate with native-speaker-labeled query sets per language, including Hinglish, to confirm recall and faithfulness hold across all the input forms.

questions.question: Sarvam-M ships hybrid think/non-think modes and was post-trained with SFT then RLVR. How would you build that, and why RLVR over vanilla RLHF?
questions.answer: Build it by first collecting SFT data spanning both a thinking mode with explicit reasoning and a non-think mode with direct answers, gated by a control token, to teach instruction following and mode switching. Then apply RLVR, optimizing against automatic verifiers on tasks like math, code, and other checkable outputs to sharpen reasoning and correctness. RLVR is preferred over vanilla RLHF here because the verifiable signal is exact and resistant to reward hacking, avoids the expense and noise of collecting human preferences and training a reward model, and scales to large problem sets. You still keep some preference or safety data for open-ended helpfulness and tone where no verifier exists.

questions.question: A regional government wants an assistant in a low-resource language with only a few thousand sentences of clean text. How do you adapt a model to it?
questions.answer: With only a few thousand clean sentences, start from a strong multilingual base model that already shares script or linguistic features and avoid training from scratch. Use parameter-efficient fine-tuning like LoRA to adapt without overfitting or forgetting, and augment the tiny corpus with back-translation, cross-lingual transfer, and carefully filtered web or synthetic data, ideally validated by native speakers. Extend or adapt the tokenizer if the language is poorly segmented, and leverage cross-lingual alignment so the model transfers capabilities from high-resource languages. Evaluate with native-speaker review and held-out tests, and consider retrieval for factual content so you do not rely on scarce data to encode knowledge.

questions.question: Design a real-time voice agent for a citizen helpline in Hindi and three regional languages, targeting sub-250 ms perceived latency over a phone line.
questions.answer: Build a streaming voice pipeline minimizing perceived latency: stream audio from the phone line to streaming ASR with partial hypotheses and voice-activity and endpoint detection, feed stabilized text to an LLM (or intent/dialog model) that supports multilingual Hindi and the regional languages, and synthesize the reply with streaming TTS so audio starts before the full response is ready. Run language identification and code-switch handling, since callers mix languages, and keep models warm and colocated to cut network hops. Achieve sub-250 ms perceived latency by overlapping stages (barge-in support, early endpointing, incremental TTS), small fast models or distilled LLMs for the turn, and response caching for common intents, while a slower path handles complex queries with a filler utterance. Tradeoffs are ASR accuracy versus endpointing speed, LLM quality versus latency (favoring small models or tool-backed retrieval), and TTS naturalness versus first-audio delay; degrade gracefully to IVR or human on low confidence.

questions.question: How would you evaluate an Indic LLM properly? Why is running translated English benchmarks not enough?
questions.answer: Translated English benchmarks are insufficient because translation strips culturally and linguistically specific phenomena: code-mixing, script and transliteration variation, honorifics, dialects, and locally grounded knowledge that native speakers actually use. They also inherit translation errors and test a translated distribution rather than genuine native usage, often rewarding English-centric reasoning. Evaluate an Indic LLM on natively authored tasks across the relevant languages and scripts, covering generation, comprehension, reasoning, and culturally specific knowledge, with native-speaker human evaluation and calibrated judges. Include code-switched and romanized inputs, measure per-language and per-script performance since quality varies widely across low-resource languages, and test fairness and safety in-language. Build the gold sets with native annotators and check for contamination, because many multilingual benchmarks leak into training data.

questions.question: Build a Voice Activity Detector from scratch. How do you make it robust for phone-quality Indian-language audio?
questions.answer: Start with framing the audio into short windows (20-30 ms), extract features such as log-energy, zero-crossing rate, and spectral features or log-mel, and classify speech versus non-speech; a small neural net (a few conv or GRU layers) trained on labeled speech/noise generally beats pure energy thresholds. Add hangover and minimum-duration smoothing so brief pauses do not chop words and brief noises do not trigger false starts. For phone-quality Indian-language audio, train on in-domain data: 8 kHz narrowband telephony, with diverse languages, accents, codecs, and realistic noise (traffic, crosstalk, music on hold), and augment with the actual codecs and SNRs you expect. Tune operating thresholds for the recall-latency tradeoff the application needs, calibrate per channel, and evaluate with frame-level and onset-latency metrics on held-out phone recordings.

questions.question: Whisper transcribes Hinglish poorly, often forcing output into one language or hallucinating. Why, and how would you build an ASR that handles code-mixed speech?
questions.answer: Whisper is trained with a single language token per utterance and on predominantly monolingual data, so it tends to lock to one language and either translate or hallucinate when the speech switches scripts and languages mid-sentence, and Hinglish is underrepresented in its training distribution. To handle code-mixed speech, build on data that genuinely contains Hinglish with correct mixed-script transcripts, and use a tokenizer and output vocabulary that cover both Devanagari and romanized Hindi plus English without forcing a language choice. Fine-tune or train a multilingual model without a hard language-identification bottleneck, or make language a soft per-token decision, and add contextual biasing for domain terms and names. Evaluate on a dedicated code-switch test set with transliteration-aware scoring so you measure real mixed-language accuracy rather than aggregate WER that hides it.

questions.question: Bulbul-style TTS has to speak code-mixed, mixed-script text naturally. What are the hard parts of text normalization and prosody for Indian-language TTS?
questions.answer: The hard parts start with text normalization over mixed scripts: the same utterance may contain Devanagari, romanized Hindi, and English, with numbers, dates, currency, abbreviations, and English loanwords that each need language-aware expansion and correct grapheme-to-phoneme conversion, including deciding which pronunciation system applies to a given word. Transliteration ambiguity means romanized Hindi can map to several pronunciations, and schwa deletion in Indic languages must be modeled correctly or words sound wrong. Prosody is hard because phrase breaks, stress, and intonation differ between the embedded languages, and code-mixed sentences need smooth switching of pronunciation and rhythm without jarring seams. You address this with a robust normalization and G2P front end, language and script tagging at the token level, training data with natural code-mixed speech, and prosody modeling conditioned on language identity so the voice stays natural across the switch.

questions.question: A state agency wants to move a paper-and-call-centre welfare-scheme service onto a multilingual assistant, on-prem for data residency. How do you scope and ship it?
questions.answer: I'd start by sitting with caseworkers and citizens to map the actual journeys, the eligibility rules, and the documents involved, and I'd confirm the exact data-residency and language requirements with their security and legal teams before any design. Because it must run on-prem, I'd plan for a self-hosted open model sized to their hardware, with retrieval over the authoritative policy documents so answers stay grounded and auditable rather than relying on the model's memory. For multilingual support I'd validate quality per language with native speakers and keep a human handoff for low-confidence or high-stakes cases like benefit denials. I'd ship a narrow pilot covering the highest-volume scheme first, with logging, an eval set built from real inquiries, and clear escalation paths, then expand once accuracy and trust are demonstrated. Throughout I'd treat accessibility and the call-center fallback as first-class, since this is a vulnerable population.

questions.question: Implement “top-k most frequent search queries” over a large query log, then tell me what breaks when the log becomes an unbounded stream across many machines.
questions.answer: On a bounded log, count frequencies in a hash map and extract the top-k with a size-k min-heap, O(n) to count and O(n log k) to select, or bucket sort for O(n). When the log becomes an unbounded multi-machine stream this breaks because you cannot store a counter per distinct query in memory, no single machine sees all events, and exact counts drift over time. The fix is approximate, distributed sketches: each shard maintains a mergeable structure like Count-Min Sketch plus a heap of candidate heavy hitters, or Space-Saving counters, and a coordinator merges the sketches to estimate global top-k. You accept bounded error for bounded memory, add windowing or decay for recency, and partition by key hash to reduce merge overhead.

questions.question: Low-level design: sketch the classes and interfaces for the tool-calling layer of an agent host, where tools can come from native code, an OpenAPI spec, or an MCP server.
questions.answer: Define a common Tool interface exposing a name, a JSON-schema describing parameters, and an invoke(args) method returning a structured result, so the agent host treats all tools uniformly. Provide adapter classes implementing that interface for each source: a NativeTool wrapping a local function, an OpenAPITool that reads a spec and maps operations to invocations against an HTTP client, and an MCPTool that proxies calls to an MCP server over its transport. A ToolRegistry discovers and holds tools and surfaces their schemas to the model; a Dispatcher validates arguments against the schema, routes to the right adapter, and normalizes errors and timeouts. This isolates transport and discovery differences behind the adapter boundary, so adding a new source is a new adapter, not changes to the agent loop.

questions.question: A Copilot chat feature has a p95 budget of 3 seconds to first useful content. Where does the time go, and how do you cut it?
questions.answer: The time splits into client and network overhead, request queueing, prefill of the prompt, and then streaming the first useful token. Under a 3-second p95 budget the usual culprits are long prompts (large prefill), queueing during load spikes, cold starts, and retrieval or pre-processing steps on the critical path. To cut it I would shrink and cache the prompt (prefix/prompt caching for fixed system context), use chunked prefill so first token streams sooner, reduce retrieval latency and do it in parallel, and keep warm capacity with headroom to avoid queueing. I would also stream partial content as soon as available and route to a faster/smaller model or quantized variant to shorten prefill and decode.

questions.question: Estimate the annual serving cost of adding an LLM summary feature for 100 million weekly active users, and how you'd cut it by 10x.
questions.answer: Estimate per-summary token cost: suppose each summary processes ~2k input tokens and emits ~200 output tokens, and each of 100M WAUs triggers it a few times a week, giving on the order of hundreds of billions of input and tens of billions of output tokens per year. Multiply by the per-token serving cost (driven by GPU-seconds, model size, and batch efficiency) to get an annual figure that lands in the millions of dollars range depending on model and utilization. To cut it 10x I would use a smaller distilled model for summarization, quantize weights and KV cache, batch aggressively for throughput, and cache or deduplicate summaries for unchanged content. Shortening prompts, truncating inputs, and routing only non-trivial items to the model compound with committed-use or better accelerator pricing to reach an order of magnitude.

questions.question: Design a Copilot feature that answers questions over a user's work email, documents and meetings, without ever leaking content the user can't access.
questions.answer: Make permission enforcement the backbone: index the user's email, documents, and meetings with their source ACLs, and at query time retrieve only content the authenticated user can access, filtering the vector and lexical search by their identity and group memberships before any content reaches the model. The Copilot resolves the query, retrieves permitted snippets, and an LLM generates a grounded answer citing only sources the user could already open, with defense-in-depth defaulting to deny and never caching cross-user content. Keep ACLs synced incrementally so revoked access takes effect immediately, and isolate tenants and users so no prompt or cache can leak another's data. Log access for audit, and run output checks to avoid echoing restricted content pulled into context. Tradeoffs are index-time versus query-time permission enforcement (freshness versus speed), retrieval recall versus strict least-privilege, and latency of permission expansion versus answer speed.

questions.question: Design an agent that can take actions in a spreadsheet (“insert a pivot table of Q3 sales by region”): orchestration, tools and failure handling.
questions.answer: Orchestrate with an LLM planner that interprets the request against the live spreadsheet state (sheet names, ranges, headers, data types) and emits a sequence of typed tool calls against a spreadsheet API rather than free-form text, so actions like create-pivot-table have validated parameters (source range, rows, columns, aggregation). Ground the plan by first reading the relevant structure, confirm the target range and interpretation when ambiguous, and apply operations transactionally so a failed step can roll back without corrupting the workbook. Validate each action's result (did the pivot produce expected shape), and handle failures with retries, replanning, or surfacing a clear error to the user. Keep operations idempotent and preview destructive changes before committing. Tradeoffs are autonomy versus confirmation for irreversible edits, the expressiveness of the tool schema versus safety and validability, and latency of read-plan-verify loops versus responsiveness.

questions.question: How would you evaluate a meeting-summarisation feature before shipping it to a hundred million users?
questions.answer: Define summary quality concretely before measuring: factual faithfulness to the meeting, coverage of key decisions and action items, conciseness, and absence of hallucinated or sensitive content. Build an offline eval with representative meeting transcripts and reference summaries or rubric-based human ratings, and use an LLM-as-judge for faithfulness and coverage calibrated against the human labels, segmenting by meeting type, length, language, and audio quality. Run adversarial cases such as overlapping speakers, jargon, and off-topic chatter, and gate on faithfulness and safety thresholds since a confident wrong summary erodes trust at scale. Before shipping to that many users, canary to a small fraction and A/B test on engagement, edits, and explicit feedback while watching cost and latency. After launch, sample live outputs for automated faithfulness checks and user feedback, and feed regressions back into the suite.

questions.question: Your Copilot summarises incoming email. An attacker emails a target user with hidden instructions addressed to the model. Walk me through the attack and your defence.
questions.answer: The attacker hides instructions in the email body, often in white text, tiny fonts, HTML comments, or metadata, so a human skims past them but the summarizer ingests them as part of its context; those instructions might tell the model to exfiltrate prior email content, insert a phishing link into the summary, or alter the summary to mislead the user. This is classic indirect prompt injection, and the danger is amplified if the Copilot also has send or search capabilities. Defenses: strip or normalize hidden content and render the email as plain visible text, clearly delimit the untrusted email so the model treats it as data to be summarized rather than commands to follow, and run an injection-detection classifier over inbound content. Constrain the Copilot's capabilities so a summarization task cannot trigger sends or data access, scan the generated summary for injected links or leaked data, and surface provenance so users can tell summary from instruction. Assume some injections slip through and limit what a compromised summarization step can actually do.

questions.question: A shipped Copilot feature that summarises job applicants for recruiters is accused of working worse for some groups. How do you establish whether that's true, and what do you do about it?
questions.answer: First establish whether the claim is real by defining the groups and an appropriate metric, then auditing on representative data: slice recruiter-facing quality and the model's assessments by applicant group, measuring error rates, score distributions, and downstream selection differences with confidence intervals and significance tests, not anecdotes. Check for the usual root causes, unrepresentative training data, labels that encode historical bias, features that proxy for protected attributes, and resume artifacts correlated with demographics such as names, schools, or language. If a real disparity exists, remediate through data improvement, debiasing, feature review, threshold calibration, or restricting the feature's scope, and re-evaluate to confirm the gap closed without new harms. Be transparent with affected users, document the findings and mitigations, and add ongoing fairness monitoring since recruiting is high-stakes and legally sensitive. If the audit cannot be done reliably or the harm is serious, consider pausing the feature until it can be fixed.

questions.question: Tell me about a time a technical decision you championed turned out to be wrong. What happened, and what did you change afterward?
questions.answer: Choose a decision you actively advocated for, which raises the stakes and shows conviction, and explain why it looked right initially. Describe honestly how and when it proved wrong, the impact, and how you responded once the evidence was clear. Emphasize owning it publicly rather than quietly, and the concrete process or mindset change you made afterward. What good looks like is intellectual honesty, accountability for a position you championed, and demonstrable learning rather than defensiveness.

questions.question: Find the top-K most frequent items in a high-volume event stream with bounded memory.
questions.answer: Use a streaming heavy-hitters sketch with memory proportional to k rather than the number of distinct keys. Space-Saving keeps m counters (m a small multiple of k): increment a key if monitored, otherwise evict the current minimum and reassign its count+1 to the new key, then report the k highest counters. Count-Min Sketch with a companion heap of candidates is an alternative, trading a tunable overestimate for fixed memory. Both give O(1) amortized per event and O(m) space independent of stream length, returning approximate top-k; for recency you add a sliding window or exponential decay, and across machines you merge per-shard sketches at a coordinator.

questions.question: Divide two integers without using multiplication, division or modulo. Find the number of connected components in a graph. Check balanced parentheses.
questions.answer: Divide without multiply/divide/modulo by subtracting shifted copies of the divisor: repeatedly double the divisor (left shift) to find the largest multiple fitting into the remaining dividend, subtract it, and accumulate the corresponding power of two into the quotient, handling sign and the INT_MIN overflow edge case; this is O(log n). Connected components: run DFS/BFS or union-find over the graph, counting how many traversals (or distinct roots) are needed to cover all nodes, O(V+E). Balanced parentheses: push opening brackets on a stack and on each closing bracket check it matches the top, returning false on mismatch or leftover, O(n) time and space.

questions.question: What is the closed-form solution of linear regression, and when do you use gradient descent instead?
questions.answer: The closed-form (normal equation) solution is w = (X^T X)^{-1} X^T y, which minimizes squared error analytically. It is exact and requires no tuning but costs roughly O(n d^2 + d^3) due to forming and inverting the d-by-d matrix, and it breaks down when X^T X is singular or ill-conditioned. Use gradient descent (or stochastic/mini-batch variants) when d is large, when data does not fit in memory or arrives in streams, or when the problem is non-linear/regularized without a convenient closed form. Gradient descent scales better per iteration and integrates naturally with online learning and complex loss functions.

questions.question: What are the differences between L1 and L2 regularization in logistic regression?
questions.answer: Both add a penalty on the coefficients to the logistic (log-loss) objective to reduce overfitting. L1 (lasso) penalizes the sum of absolute coefficients, producing sparse solutions that zero out irrelevant features and performing implicit feature selection, which is valuable in high-dimensional logistic models. L2 (ridge) penalizes squared coefficients, shrinking them smoothly toward zero and handling correlated predictors better while keeping all features. L1 is non-differentiable at zero (requiring subgradient or coordinate methods), whereas L2 keeps the objective smooth and strictly convex for a unique solution; elastic net blends both.

questions.question: Write the loss function for logistic regression and prove it has a global minimum.
questions.answer: For labels y in {0,1} and predicted probability p = sigmoid(w^T x), the loss is the negative log-likelihood L(w) = -sum_i [y_i log p_i + (1 - y_i) log(1 - p_i)]. This is convex in w: the Hessian is X^T S X where S is diagonal with entries p_i(1 - p_i) >= 0, making it positive semidefinite, so L is convex. A convex function has no non-global local minima, so any stationary point is a global minimum. The minimum is unique (strictly convex) when the data is not perfectly separable and the design matrix has full rank; with separable data the optimum drifts to infinity, which regularization fixes.

questions.question: How is KL divergence loss different from cross-entropy loss? And from contrastive loss?
questions.answer: Cross-entropy H(P,Q) = -sum P log Q equals the entropy of P plus KL(P||Q); when the target P is fixed (as with one-hot or fixed soft labels), minimizing cross-entropy and minimizing KL divergence are equivalent up to the constant entropy term. KL is the pure divergence between two distributions and is commonly used for matching soft distributions, such as in knowledge distillation or variational inference. Contrastive loss is fundamentally different: rather than matching a target distribution, it operates on pairs or batches in an embedding space, pulling positive pairs together and pushing negatives apart (e.g., InfoNCE) to learn representations. It optimizes relative distances/similarities instead of per-example probability matching.

questions.question: How do bagging and boosting differ? What is the computational difference between XGBoost and Random Forest?
questions.answer: Bagging trains many models in parallel on bootstrap resamples and averages them to reduce variance, with Random Forest adding random feature subsampling per split; the trees are independent so training parallelizes trivially. Boosting trains models sequentially, each correcting the residual errors of the ensemble so far, which reduces bias (and some variance) but is inherently sequential across rounds. XGBoost is a gradient-boosted tree method that builds trees one after another using second-order gradients, so successive trees depend on prior ones, though it parallelizes split-finding within each tree. Random Forest can train all trees fully in parallel, making it faster to fit and less prone to overfitting from over-boosting, while XGBoost usually achieves higher accuracy with careful tuning and regularization.

questions.question: Explain the bias-variance trade-off, cross-validation, and the curse of dimensionality.
questions.answer: The bias-variance trade-off splits generalization error into bias (underfitting from overly simple models) and variance (overfitting from overly complex ones), minimized at intermediate capacity. Cross-validation estimates generalization by partitioning data into k folds, training on k-1 and validating on the held-out fold rotated k times, giving a lower-variance performance estimate and a principled way to tune hyperparameters. The curse of dimensionality is the phenomenon that as feature count grows, data becomes sparse, distances concentrate, and the volume to cover grows exponentially, so models need exponentially more data and are prone to high variance. High dimensionality therefore worsens variance, which is why dimensionality reduction and regularization matter.

questions.question: How do GRU cells work, and how do they address the vanishing gradient problem? How does a BiLSTM work?
questions.answer: A GRU uses two gates: an update gate that interpolates between the previous hidden state and a candidate state, and a reset gate that controls how much past state feeds the candidate. By letting the hidden state be carried forward additively through the update gate (near-identity when the gate is open), gradients can flow across many time steps without the multiplicative shrinkage that causes vanishing gradients in vanilla RNNs. It is a lighter alternative to the LSTM with fewer parameters and no separate cell state. A BiLSTM runs two LSTMs, one left-to-right and one right-to-left, and concatenates their hidden states so each position has context from both past and future, which helps tasks where the full sequence is available.

questions.question: What is Attention in machine learning models? What happens in a neural network if you remove all the hidden layers?
questions.answer: Attention is a mechanism that computes a weighted combination of value vectors, where the weights come from the compatibility between a query and a set of keys, letting the model focus on the most relevant parts of the input regardless of distance. It enables modeling long-range dependencies and, in transformers, parallel computation over the whole sequence. If you remove all hidden layers from a neural network you are left with a direct mapping from inputs to outputs, i.e., a linear model (logistic regression for a sigmoid/softmax output), which can only represent linear decision boundaries and cannot capture nonlinear interactions.

questions.question: Discuss precision, recall and F1: when would you prioritise one over the others?
questions.answer: Precision is the fraction of positive predictions that are correct (TP/(TP+FP)), recall is the fraction of actual positives recovered (TP/(TP+FN)), and F1 is their harmonic mean, balancing the two. Prioritize precision when false positives are costly, such as flagging something for an expensive or intrusive action (e.g., spam filtering where blocking real mail is bad). Prioritize recall when missing a positive is costly, such as disease screening or fraud/safety detection where false negatives are dangerous. Use F1 (or a weighted F-beta) when you need a single balanced number and have class imbalance, choosing beta to reflect the relative cost of the two error types.

questions.question: How do you handle data imbalance, collinearity, feature selection and regularization?
questions.answer: For imbalance, use class weights, resampling (SMOTE/undersampling), and appropriate metrics plus threshold tuning. For collinearity, detect it with correlation matrices or variance inflation factors and address it by dropping or combining redundant features, using PCA, or applying L2 regularization, which stabilizes coefficients under correlation. For feature selection, use filter methods (mutual information, correlation), wrapper methods (recursive feature elimination), or embedded methods such as L1 regularization and tree-based importances. Regularization (L1 for sparsity/selection, L2 for shrinkage, or elastic net) controls complexity to prevent overfitting, and all choices should be validated inside cross-validation to avoid leakage.
