questions.question: Explain how you would design and evaluate an A/B test. What is a p-value and how do you interpret it here?
questions.answer: Define a single primary metric and a hypothesis, then compute the required sample size from the baseline rate, minimum detectable effect, and desired power (usually 80%) and significance level (usually 5%) before launching. Randomly assign units to control and treatment, check that randomization produced balanced groups, run for a pre-committed duration to capture weekly seasonality, and avoid peeking that inflates false positives. Analyze with an appropriate test (e.g., two-proportion z-test or t-test), and guard against multiple comparisons and novelty effects. The p-value is the probability of observing a difference at least as extreme as the one seen if the null hypothesis (no true effect) were true; a small p-value (below the threshold) suggests the observed lift is unlikely due to chance alone, but it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.

questions.question: What is Maximum Likelihood Estimation and how does it differ from Bayesian inference?
questions.answer: Maximum Likelihood Estimation picks the parameter values that maximize the likelihood of the observed data, typically by maximizing the log-likelihood, producing a single point estimate. Bayesian inference instead treats parameters as random variables with a prior distribution and computes a full posterior via Bayes' rule, combining prior and likelihood. MLE gives a point estimate with no inherent uncertainty quantification over parameters and can overfit with little data, whereas Bayesian inference yields a distribution that captures uncertainty and regularizes through the prior. MLE is a special case of MAP estimation with a flat (uninformative) prior, and the two converge as data grows and the prior washes out.

questions.question: Why did transformers displace RNNs for language modelling, and what exactly does the KV cache buy you at inference time?
questions.answer: Transformers displaced RNNs because self-attention processes all positions in parallel (RNNs are inherently sequential), models long-range dependencies directly without vanishing-gradient decay, and scales far better on modern hardware. This parallelism made training on massive corpora feasible, which is what unlocked large language models. At inference the KV cache stores past keys and values so generating each new token reuses prior computation instead of re-attending to the whole prefix, making per-step cost linear rather than quadratic in the generated length. In effect the KV cache restores RNN-like efficient incremental decoding while keeping the transformer's training-time advantages.

questions.question: A customer's Bedrock-hosted workload costs too much. Cut inference cost dramatically without unacceptable quality loss.
questions.answer: First profile where tokens and latency go, then pull the biggest levers: switch to a smaller or distilled model or route easy requests to it, since model size dominates cost. Shorten prompts and truncate context, enable prompt/prefix caching for repeated system prompts, and cap output length to cut generated tokens. Choose a cheaper quantized model variant or a more cost-effective instance type and improve batching and utilization where you control the deployment. Validate quality on the customer's real workload against the baseline after each change, shipping only reductions that stay within an agreed quality threshold, and quantify the cost-per-token savings at each step.

questions.question: Design an agent that operates a web browser to complete multi-step tasks. How do you make it reliable enough to ship?
questions.answer: I would build a ReAct-style loop over a browser automation backend, giving the agent a small action set, navigate, click, type, scroll, extract, built on robust element targeting via accessibility tree or DOM selectors rather than brittle coordinates. Reliability comes from verifying post-conditions after each action, that the page reached the expected state, with waits for loading, retries on transient failures, and backtracking when a step fails. I keep the goal and a plan pinned in context, extract page content as structured observations the model can reason over, and treat page text as untrusted to resist prompt injection. I bound steps and cost, gate consequential actions like purchases or submissions behind human approval, and run an offline suite of recorded tasks plus live tracing to catch regressions before shipping.

questions.question: Design a multi-tenant inference platform that serves many foundation models to thousands of customers (Bedrock-shaped).
questions.answer: Build a multi-tenant control plane that manages model registration, routing, quotas, and billing over a shared data plane of GPU pools, where each foundation model is served by an autoscaling deployment with continuous batching and the scheduler bin-packs models onto hardware. Route requests by model ID through an API gateway enforcing per-tenant authentication, rate limits, and isolation, metering token usage for billing, and keeping popular models warm while cold or rarely used ones scale to zero and load on demand. Guarantee tenant isolation at the network, data, and quota levels, and offer both shared and dedicated-capacity options. Scale with GPU-aware autoscaling, request queueing with fairness, and regional capacity. Tradeoffs are utilization from multi-tenant packing versus noisy-neighbor isolation, cold-start latency for infrequent models versus the cost of keeping them warm, and shared throughput versus guaranteed per-tenant performance.

questions.question: How would you design a recommendation system to suggest books to users? How would you model a warehouse inventory problem?
questions.answer: For books, use a two-stage recommender: candidate generation via collaborative filtering and two-tower embeddings over read/rated history plus content features (genre, author, description embeddings) retrieved by ANN, then ranking by predicted engagement with personalization and diversity, handling cold-start books with content signals and new users with onboarding and popularity. For warehouse inventory, model it as an optimization and forecasting problem: forecast demand per SKU and location with time-series or ML models capturing seasonality and promotions, then decide reorder quantities and safety stock via inventory policies (newsvendor or (s,S)) that balance holding cost against stockout cost under lead-time uncertainty. Serve recommendations from a feature store with low latency; run inventory optimization as periodic batch planning. Tradeoffs are recommendation personalization versus discovery and the recommender's engagement metric versus actual reads, and for inventory, service level versus carrying cost plus robustness to forecast error.

questions.question: How would you decide an LLM-powered assistant is ready to launch to millions of customers?
questions.answer: Readiness is a multi-dimensional bar, not a single metric: quality on a representative, decontaminated eval suite must clear thresholds on the slices that matter, and safety, refusal, and abuse testing must pass hard gates. Validate robustness to adversarial and out-of-distribution inputs, confirm latency, cost, and reliability meet SLOs at expected load, and ensure observability, feedback capture, and rollback are in place. Run a staged rollout, canary then A/B, so real-user quality and behavioral metrics confirm offline results before full exposure, and define rollback triggers in advance. Have monitoring and on-call coverage, a regression gate for future changes, and human review of a live sample during ramp. Launch when offline gates pass, the canary shows no regression on key and guardrail metrics, and operational and safety readiness are confirmed.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your team's technical direction. What did you do? (Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit)
questions.answer: Use STAR and show the backbone-plus-commit balance explicitly: name a direction you genuinely disagreed with and the reasoning and evidence you brought to challenge it. Describe raising the concern constructively and persistently through the right channels rather than going along silently. Then show that once a decision was made, you committed fully and supported it even if it was not your preference. What good looks like is demonstrating you can push hard on substance, disagree respectfully, and still execute as a team player regardless of the final call.

questions.question: Tell me about your most significant failure. What happened, and what did you change afterward?
questions.answer: Select a substantial, real failure with genuine consequences, signaling self-awareness rather than a safe non-answer. Use STAR to explain the situation, your specific role and decisions, and what actually went wrong without deflecting blame. Focus most of the answer on how you responded, what you learned, and the lasting changes you made to your habits or processes. What good looks like is owning a meaningful setback with honesty and showing clear evidence that you grew from it.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you saw an opportunity to do something bigger than the initial scope. (Think Big)
questions.answer: Describe a moment you recognized the real problem or opportunity was larger than the assigned task, and explain the insight that revealed it. Walk through how you made the case for the bigger vision, balanced ambition with feasibility, and either expanded scope responsibly or planted the seeds for it. Emphasize connecting the larger idea to meaningful impact rather than scope creep for its own sake. What good looks like is visionary thinking grounded in pragmatism and the initiative to drive it forward.

questions.question: You need to run a ~3B-parameter language model on a phone with tight memory and power budgets. What changes versus serving the same model in a datacenter?
questions.answer: On a phone you are bound by a few gigabytes of unified memory, limited bandwidth, no datacenter interconnect, and strict power and thermal limits, so batch size is essentially one and there is no throughput amortization. You must quantize aggressively (4-bit or lower weights, often with QAT) to fit the ~3B model in memory, use the NPU/GPU with a mobile runtime, and keep the KV cache tiny via GQA and short context. There is no continuous batching benefit, cold-start model loading matters, and sustained generation throttles due to heat, so you optimize single-stream latency and energy per token rather than aggregate throughput. Features like speculative decoding, memory mapping of weights, and prompt caching help, but you trade raw capability for the ability to run locally with privacy and no network dependence.

questions.question: Explain post-training quantization versus quantization-aware training. What breaks when you push weights to 2–4 bits, and how do you recover quality?
questions.answer: Post-training quantization (PTQ) converts an already-trained FP model to low precision using calibration data and scaling, which is cheap and fast but loses accuracy as bit-width drops. Quantization-aware training (QAT) simulates quantization during training or fine-tuning so the weights adapt to the rounding noise, recovering much more quality at low bit-widths at the cost of a training run. Pushing weights to 2-4 bits breaks down because the representable grid becomes coarse, outlier weights and activations dominate the error, and some layers (embeddings, attention outputs) are especially sensitive. You recover quality with group-wise or per-channel scales, outlier-aware methods (AWQ/GPTQ), keeping sensitive layers in higher precision, mixed-precision schemes, and QAT or light fine-tuning to let the network compensate.

questions.question: Estimate the KV-cache memory for a 3B on-device model at 4k context, and name the levers that shrink it.
questions.answer: A 3B model typically has around 26-32 layers; with GQA and modest KV-head dimensions the KV cache is roughly 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * bytes per token, on the order of 100-200 KB per token in FP16. At 4k context that is roughly 0.5-1 GB for a single sequence, significant on a phone with only a few GB total. Levers to shrink it: quantize the KV cache to INT8/INT4 (2-4x reduction), use GQA/MQA to cut KV heads, apply sliding-window attention to cap stored tokens, and limit context length. You can also offload or evict cold KV, use PagedAttention-style allocation to avoid waste, and compress or summarize history for long conversations.

questions.question: Time-to-first-token for your on-device feature is 1.8 s. Walk me through diagnosing and fixing it.
questions.answer: I decompose the 1.8s TTFT into model load / cold start, prompt tokenization, prefill compute, and any pre-processing before generation begins. On device the usual suspects are a large prompt driving long prefill on limited compute, weights not resident in memory (first-run load), the model running on CPU instead of the NPU/GPU, or thermal throttling. I measure each stage, then fix the dominant one: shorten or cache the prompt and system context, use prefix caching for the fixed preamble, preload and memory-map weights to remove cold start, and ensure the quantized model runs on the accelerator with the right runtime. Chunked prefill and streaming the first token sooner, plus a smaller model or lower precision, further cut the time to first useful content.

questions.question: Your on-device model must emit valid, schema-conforming tool calls. How do you guarantee validity rather than hope for it?
questions.answer: Do not rely on the model to emit valid JSON; constrain decoding so only schema-conforming tokens are permitted. The standard technique is constrained or grammar-based decoding, where the tool schema is compiled into a grammar or finite-state machine and the sampler masks out any token that would violate it, guaranteeing structurally valid output. For enum and type constraints this enforces allowed values directly, and it works well on-device because it needs no extra model calls. Pair it with a validation and repair pass as a backstop, and fine-tune or few-shot the model on the tool formats so the constrained output is also semantically sensible, not just syntactically valid.

questions.question: You have one on-device base model but a dozen features: summarization, rewriting, reply suggestions, tone adjustment. How do you specialise without shipping a dozen models?
questions.answer: Ship one shared base model and a set of small per-feature LoRA adapters that are swapped in at inference, so you store one set of weights plus tiny task adapters instead of a dozen full models. Each adapter is trained or distilled for its feature (summarization, rewriting, reply suggestions, tone), and the runtime loads the relevant adapter on demand with negligible added memory. This gives per-task quality close to separate fine-tunes while keeping the on-device footprint and update size minimal. Where capability overlaps, a shared instruction-tuned base with prompts or a multi-task adapter can cover several features, and adapters can be updated independently without reshipping the base.

questions.question: How would you improve an on-device model using signals from user devices without collecting user content?
questions.answer: Improve the model without collecting content by using privacy-preserving on-device signals: compute gradients or statistics locally and aggregate them with federated learning so only model updates, never raw user data, leave the device. Protect those updates with secure aggregation, so the server sees only the combined result, and add differential-privacy noise with clipping to bound any individual's contribution. Use coarse, non-identifying telemetry such as which suggestions were accepted to pick evaluation and training targets, and keep all personal text on the device. This yields population-level improvements with formal privacy guarantees and no content exfiltration.

questions.question: Design the routing layer that decides whether a user request is handled on-device, by a first-party server model, or by a third-party model.
questions.answer: Design a request router that scores each request on capability need, latency sensitivity, privacy, cost, and connectivity, then picks the cheapest tier that satisfies them: on-device for simple, private, offline-capable tasks; a first-party server model for heavier requests needing more capability; and a third-party model when it offers a needed capability, with explicit policy on what data may leave the device. Use a fast local classifier to make the routing decision with minimal overhead, fall back across tiers on failure or capacity limits, and cache decisions for repeated intents. Enforce privacy rules so sensitive content never routes off-device, and give the on-device path a timeout that escalates to server when it cannot answer confidently. Tradeoffs are on-device privacy and latency versus limited capability, server and third-party capability versus cost and data exposure, and routing accuracy versus the latency budget of the router itself.

questions.question: A user says “send Maya the photos from Saturday's hike.” Design the on-device path from that utterance to a structured app action with resolved parameters.
questions.answer: Run an on-device pipeline: intent classification recognizes a share-photos action, then entity and slot resolution maps "Maya" to a contact (disambiguating among matches), "Saturday's hike" to photos via the on-device photo index using date and location/semantic tags, and infers the target app and action. Assemble a structured action (recipient contact ID, resolved asset IDs, app intent) using local knowledge of contacts, calendar, and photo metadata, keeping all personal data on-device for privacy. Resolve ambiguity interactively (which Maya, which photos) and present a confirmation before sending, since messaging is an irreversible external action. Execute via the OS app-intent or deep-link API. Tradeoffs are on-device resolution accuracy and privacy versus the richer context a server could use, grounding reliability of fuzzy references like "Saturday's hike," and how aggressively to auto-resolve versus asking the user to confirm.

questions.question: You're shipping notification summarization to hundreds of millions of users in 30+ locales, and you cannot log user content. Design the evaluation and regression-detection story.
questions.answer: Without logging user content, build the evaluation on synthetic and opt-in proxy data: construct representative notification corpora across all locales with native speakers, plus adversarial and edge cases, and evaluate offline with faithfulness, conciseness, and safety metrics per locale. In production, rely on privacy-preserving signals that do not expose content, such as aggregated and differentially private metrics, on-device or ephemeral evaluation, user actions like dismiss, expand, or disable, and coarse quality counters computed locally and reported in aggregate. Detect regressions by comparing these aggregate distributions and action rates across model versions via canary and A/B, alerting on statistically significant shifts per locale. Pair this with a held-out human-rated synthetic set run on every release for a content-level quality gate. Because locales differ, segment every metric by language and never pool them into a single global average.

questions.question: Tell me about a time you had to make progress with incomplete information: you couldn't be told the full context of what you were building.
questions.answer: Describe how you made progress despite being unable to see the full picture: clarifying what you could know, defining clean interfaces and assumptions, and building modularly so the work remained correct regardless of hidden context. Emphasize trust, disciplined communication about what you needed versus what you did not, and validating your part through tests and contracts. Show comfort operating within constraints and asking targeted questions rather than demanding full disclosure. What good looks like is demonstrating sound engineering judgment, adaptability, and the ability to deliver reliably under deliberate ambiguity.

questions.question: Here's a CUDA kernel that's 10x slower than expected. Without running it, what are the usual suspects, and how do you confirm each?
questions.answer: Likely suspects are uncoalesced global memory access, so threads in a warp read scattered addresses; confirm with the profiler's memory throughput and transactions-per-request metrics. Warp divergence from branches that split threads in a warp; confirm by checking branch efficiency. Low occupancy from excessive registers or shared memory per thread limiting resident warps; confirm with the occupancy calculator and achieved-occupancy counter. Bank conflicts in shared memory, excessive atomics serializing, host-device transfer or kernel-launch overhead dominating, and failure to overlap compute with memory (memory-bound kernel); confirm each with Nsight Compute counters, a roofline analysis to see if you are memory- or compute-bound, and by toggling suspected factors to measure the delta.

questions.question: Implement the block manager for a paged KV cache: allocate, append, free, and copy-on-write prefix sharing.
questions.answer: Manage a pool of fixed-size physical blocks and a per-sequence block table mapping logical token positions to physical block ids, so a sequence's KV need not be contiguous. allocate pulls free blocks from a free list as the sequence grows; append writes new tokens into the last block, allocating another when it fills; free returns a sequence's blocks to the free list. For prefix sharing, multiple sequences point their block tables at the same physical blocks for a shared prompt prefix with a reference count; copy-on-write triggers when a sharer must write into a shared block, allocating a fresh block, copying the contents, and redirecting that sequence's table entry. This cuts fragmentation and memory for shared prefixes; edge cases are refcount bookkeeping, partial final blocks, and running out of free blocks (trigger preemption).

questions.question: A model runs fine in FP32 but produces garbage after conversion to FP16. Debug it.
questions.answer: FP16 has a far smaller dynamic range than FP32 (max around 65504 and tiny subnormals), so garbage usually means overflow to inf or underflow to zero somewhere. Add instrumentation to find the first layer whose activations become inf/nan or saturate, checking attention scores, large matmul accumulations, and exponentials in softmax. Common fixes: keep reductions and softmax/layernorm accumulations in FP32, use numerically stable formulations (subtract max before exp), scale or clamp activations, and ensure accumulation happens in FP32 even when storage is FP16. Confirm by comparing intermediate tensors against the FP32 reference layer by layer; if training, this is exactly what loss scaling addresses, and bf16 is an alternative with FP32-like range.

questions.question: Explain strategies to combat overfitting in tree-based classification models.
questions.answer: Limit tree depth, set a minimum number of samples per leaf or split, and prune (cost-complexity pruning) so individual trees cannot memorize noise. For ensembles, use bagging/Random Forests with feature and row subsampling to decorrelate trees, or gradient boosting with a small learning rate, shrinkage, early stopping on a validation set, and L1/L2 regularization on leaf weights. Reduce the number of features and use column subsampling per tree to curb overfitting on spurious splits. Always validate hyperparameters with cross-validation and monitor the gap between training and validation performance.

questions.question: Summarize the differences and benefits of the Adam optimizer compared with other methods for neural-network image classification.
questions.answer: Adam combines momentum (an exponential moving average of gradients) with per-parameter adaptive learning rates from a moving average of squared gradients, plus bias correction for the early steps. Compared to plain SGD it converges faster and is more robust to learning-rate choice and sparse or noisy gradients, which helps quick prototyping on image tasks. Compared to pure momentum or RMSProp, it merges the strengths of both, giving stable adaptive steps. However, for image classification well-tuned SGD with momentum and a learning-rate schedule often generalizes slightly better, so Adam (or AdamW, which decouples weight decay) is frequently used for fast convergence while SGD is used to squeeze out final accuracy.

questions.question: A network confuses pugs and pit bulls and some training labels are wrong. How do you modify the model and the data?
questions.answer: First treat the label noise: audit and clean the confused classes, use confident-learning or loss-based techniques to find likely mislabeled examples, and consider relabeling or applying noise-robust losses. On the model side, add targeted hard examples of pugs and pit bulls, use strong data augmentation, and possibly a higher-resolution or attention-based backbone that captures the fine-grained distinguishing features. Rebalance or reweight the two confusable classes and examine the confusion matrix and Grad-CAM to confirm the model attends to discriminative regions rather than background. Finally, re-evaluate on a carefully cleaned held-out set so noisy labels do not mask real progress.

questions.question: How do you evaluate a clustering model's effectiveness without pre-labelled groups?
questions.answer: Without labels, use internal validation indices: the silhouette coefficient (cohesion vs. separation), the Davies-Bouldin index (lower is better), and the Calinski-Harabasz ratio of between- to within-cluster dispersion. Assess stability by re-clustering on bootstrapped or perturbed subsets and measuring agreement (e.g., adjusted Rand index between runs). Use the elbow or gap statistic to judge the number of clusters, and visualize with PCA/t-SNE/UMAP to sanity-check separation. Ultimately tie evaluation to downstream utility or domain expert review, since internal metrics only measure geometric structure, not semantic correctness.

questions.question: You want to serve a 70B-parameter model on a single 80 GB GPU. Walk me through whether it fits and what single-stream tokens/sec you'd expect.
questions.answer: A 70B model in FP16 needs ~140 GB, which does not fit in 80 GB, so you must quantize: INT8 weights are ~70 GB and fit with limited room for KV cache, and INT4 weights are ~35 GB leaving comfortable KV-cache headroom. Single-stream decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so tokens per second is roughly HBM bandwidth divided by bytes read per token; on an 80 GB H100 (~3.35 TB/s) that is about 3350/70 ≈ 48 tok/s at INT8 and about 3350/35 ≈ 95 tok/s at INT4 as upper bounds. Real-world throughput is lower, typically 60-80 percent of the ceiling, due to KV reads, kernel overhead, and imperfect bandwidth use, so expect roughly 30-40 tok/s at INT8 and 55-75 tok/s at INT4. So it fits only quantized, and single-stream speed is set by bandwidth, not FLOPs.

questions.question: What does TensorRT / TensorRT-LLM actually do to a model to make it faster, and when will it not help?
questions.answer: TensorRT-LLM compiles the model into an optimized inference engine for a specific NVIDIA GPU: it fuses kernels (for example attention and layernorm), selects or generates high-performance kernels, applies quantization (FP8/INT8/INT4), uses efficient attention and paged KV, and plans memory and parallelism ahead of time. The result is lower latency and higher throughput than a generic eager-mode runtime, especially for stable, high-volume workloads. It will not help much when you are already memory-bandwidth-bound and the model is small, when the bottleneck is outside the model (queueing, network, retrieval), or when your workload changes shape constantly so the ahead-of-time build cannot be amortized. It also adds build complexity and reduced flexibility, and gives little benefit if your existing engine already fuses kernels and quantizes well.

questions.question: Design the parallelism strategy for serving a 405B-parameter dense model. TP, PP, EP: what goes where and why?
questions.answer: For a 405B dense model, weights alone are ~810 GB in FP16 (or ~405 GB in FP8), so you need many GPUs. I put tensor parallelism within a node (for example 8-way over NVLink) because it needs frequent all-reduces that demand the fastest interconnect. I use pipeline parallelism across nodes to span the layer depth, sized to keep pipeline bubbles small relative to microbatch count. There is no expert parallelism since the model is dense, so EP does not apply; instead I add data parallelism across replicas for throughput and use sequence parallelism to reduce activation/KV memory on long contexts. The guiding principle is to keep the communication-heavy TP on the fastest links inside a node, PP across slower cross-node links, and DP for scaling out.

questions.question: Design a podcast search engine with transcript indexing. / Design a recommendation algorithm for type-ahead search.
questions.answer: For podcast search, transcribe episodes with ASR, index the timestamped transcripts in a hybrid lexical-plus-dense store so queries match spoken content and return the exact moment, enriching with show metadata and speaker labels; rank by relevance plus recency and popularity, and handle transcription errors with fuzzy matching. For type-ahead, serve completions from a prefix structure (trie or FST) over a query log ranked by frequency, recency, and personalization, with a dense fallback for semantic suggestions, all within a few milliseconds so suggestions feel instant. Both benefit from caching hot prefixes and precomputed embeddings. Tradeoffs for podcast search are transcription cost and accuracy versus coverage and the storage of full transcripts; for type-ahead they are completion relevance and personalization versus the strict latency budget and the cold-start problem for rare or new prefixes.

questions.question: A customer's LLM chatbot on 8 GPUs is “too slow and too expensive.” You have one week with them. What do you do?
questions.answer: Day one I profile before changing anything: measure latency breakdown, tokens in and out, batch sizes, GPU utilization, and where the 8 GPUs are actually spending time, because 'slow and expensive' usually has one dominant cause. Common wins are moving to an optimized inference server with continuous batching and paged attention, right-sizing the model or quantizing it, and trimming bloated prompts and max-token settings that inflate cost silently. I'd check whether they even need all 8 GPUs at their real concurrency, since over-provisioning is common, and whether a smaller model plus retrieval meets quality. I'd validate quality on a held-out set after each change so we don't trade cost for correctness. By end of week I'd hand over measured throughput and cost-per-request improvements plus a short list of further optimizations.

questions.question: Describe a time you dealt with conflicting priorities or stakeholder feedback. What would your current manager say about you?
questions.answer: Handle the first part with a stakeholder-conflict STAR story: the competing priorities, how you surfaced tradeoffs with data, and how you aligned people on a shared goal and outcome. For the manager-perception part, give an honest, specific characterization backed by examples, mentioning genuine strengths and a real area you are improving. Keep it authentic rather than listing only flattering adjectives. What good looks like is demonstrated alignment skills plus credible self-awareness that an interviewer could imagine being confirmed by a reference.

questions.question: Implement non-maximum suppression. Then vectorise it.
questions.answer: Sort boxes by confidence score descending, then repeatedly take the highest-scoring remaining box, add it to the kept set, and remove any remaining box whose IoU with it exceeds the threshold, until none remain. The naive version is nested loops computing pairwise IoU, O(n^2) in the worst case. To vectorize, keep an array of candidate indices and, after selecting the top box, compute its IoU against all remaining boxes at once with array operations (vectorized intersection coordinates, areas, and union), then mask out those over the threshold in one step. Edge cases are empty input, zero-area boxes, and per-class NMS where you run it independently per class.

questions.question: Write an efficient ring buffer for high-rate sensor data with a fixed memory budget.
questions.answer: Preallocate a fixed-size array and maintain head and tail indices (or a count) that wrap modulo the capacity, so the buffer never grows and memory is bounded. Writes store at the tail and advance it; when full you either reject, block, or overwrite the oldest by also advancing head, which is the usual choice for high-rate sensor data where latest matters. Using a power-of-two capacity lets you wrap with a bitmask instead of modulo for speed. Edge cases are distinguishing full from empty (keep a count or leave one slot unused), and for concurrent single-producer/single-consumer use, atomic head/tail indices give a lock-free queue; all operations are O(1).

questions.question: How would you design the neural network architecture for multi-camera 3D object detection without lidar?
questions.answer: I would use multiple calibrated cameras feeding a shared backbone, then lift per-camera features into a common 3D or bird's-eye-view (BEV) representation using known camera intrinsics and extrinsics (e.g., lift-splat-shoot or a transformer that cross-attends image features into BEV queries). Fuse the multi-view features in BEV space so overlapping fields of view reinforce depth and resolve occlusion, and add temporal fusion across frames to recover depth and velocity that a single frame underconstrains. A detection head then predicts 3D boxes (center, dimensions, orientation, class) directly in the BEV/ego frame, trained with depth supervision or self-supervision to compensate for the lack of lidar depth. Key challenges are monocular depth ambiguity and precise calibration, so I would add depth priors, strong augmentation, and temporal consistency.

questions.question: How do you handle extreme class imbalance in rare-event detection (e.g. a child running into the road)?
questions.answer: Frame it with metrics that respect the cost asymmetry, such as recall at a very low false-negative rate and precision-recall curves, since missing the event is catastrophic. Use hard-negative mining, focal loss, and class or example reweighting so the rare positives dominate the gradient, and oversample or synthesize positives (including simulation and augmentation). Set the operating threshold to favor recall and add a secondary verification stage to control the resulting false alarms. Mine and label rare real-world positives aggressively, use temporal context, and validate on a realistically imbalanced, safety-focused test set rather than a balanced one.

questions.question: Explain how you would auto-label a fleet dataset and what quality controls you would put on it.
questions.answer: Auto-labeling runs a high-capacity offline model (often an ensemble, larger than the onboard model, with access to full-sequence and future frames) to generate pseudo-labels on unlabeled fleet logs, optionally refined by temporal smoothing and multi-sensor fusion. Quality controls include confidence thresholding to keep only high-certainty labels, consistency checks across time and sensors, and agreement between multiple models or model vs. human spot-checks. Route low-confidence or disagreement cases to human review (active learning), track label-quality metrics on an audited gold set, and monitor for systematic biases the auto-labeler introduces. Version the labels and continuously audit downstream model performance to catch degradation from noisy pseudo-labels.

questions.question: How would you detect and handle distribution shift between fleet data and your training set?
questions.answer: Detect shift by monitoring input-feature and prediction distributions over time using statistical tests (KS test, population stability index) and divergence measures, and by watching proxy metrics or delayed ground-truth performance. Train a domain classifier to distinguish training from fleet data; if it succeeds easily, the distributions differ, and its scores can quantify and localize the shift. To handle it, use importance reweighting or domain adaptation, retrain or fine-tune on freshly sampled and labeled fleet data (prioritizing shifted regions via active learning), and add targeted augmentation. Establish continuous monitoring with alerting and a retraining pipeline so the model tracks the evolving data distribution.

questions.question: The onboard compute budget is fixed. Walk me through quantizing and pruning a vision model without losing recall on small objects.
questions.answer: With a fixed onboard budget I quantize the detector, preferring per-channel INT8 (or QAT if PTQ loses recall) because activation outliers around small objects can hurt detection most. For pruning I use structured channel/filter pruning so the hardware actually speeds up, but prune conservatively in the backbone stages and feature-pyramid levels that carry high-resolution, small-object features. I fine-tune after each compression step with the deployment data, keeping input resolution high enough to preserve small objects since downscaling is the fastest way to lose them. I validate specifically on small-object recall (not just overall mAP), using size-stratified metrics and the hardest examples, and I keep sensitive layers in higher precision if recall regresses beyond the budget.

questions.question: Design the data engine: fleet triggers → upload → labelling → retraining → shadow-mode validation → release.
questions.answer: Build a closed-loop data engine: fleet triggers (disengagements, anomalies, rare-event detectors) flag interesting segments that are uploaded to cloud storage with metadata, then auto-labeling plus human annotation produces training labels, feeding a retraining pipeline that trains and evaluates new model versions. Validate candidates offline against regression suites, then in shadow mode where the new model runs alongside production without acting, comparing its outputs to the deployed model and ground truth, before a staged release (canary to wider rollout) with rollback. Mine for rare and high-value scenarios via embeddings-based similarity search over the archive rather than random sampling, and prioritize labeling budget on where the model is weak. Track dataset versioning and lineage for reproducibility. Tradeoffs are trigger selectivity versus upload and labeling cost, auto-label throughput versus quality, and shadow-validation confidence versus time-to-release.

questions.question: Disengagement rate is a weak proxy. How would you actually measure whether an autonomy release is safer than the last one?
questions.answer: Disengagement rate is weak because it conflates safety with driver behavior, policy conservatism, and operator judgment, and rare serious events make it statistically noisy. Measure safety directly through a layered approach: a validated simulator replaying real and synthetic scenarios to estimate collision and near-miss rates per mile, counterfactual analysis of what would have happened without intervention, and leading indicators such as hard braking, minimum time-to-collision, rule violations, and safety-margin distributions. Stratify by scenario cluster and operating conditions so a regression in one regime is not masked, and use statistical methods to bound rare-event risk given limited exposure. Compare the candidate release against the prior one on these metrics with confidence intervals, and require human review of any safety-critical events. Combine simulation, closed-course testing, and monitored on-road exposure rather than relying on a single proxy.

questions.question: How would you fuse camera, radar and IMU inputs into a single perception stack, and where would you fuse them?
questions.answer: Fuse at the level that matches each sensor's strengths: cameras give dense semantics and classification, radar gives robust range and velocity in bad weather, and IMU gives high-rate ego-motion for state estimation and de-skewing. A common design uses the IMU in a tight loop for pose and motion compensation, then fuses camera and radar either at feature level in a shared representation (for example projecting both into a common bird's-eye-view grid before a fusion network) for best accuracy, or at object level (independent detections combined by a tracker and Kalman/EKF filter) for modularity and interpretability. Mid/feature-level fusion captures complementary cues like radar velocity grounding camera detections, while late fusion is easier to validate and degrade gracefully. Calibrate and time-synchronize all streams carefully, and handle sensor dropout so the stack stays safe when one modality fails.

questions.question: Tell me about the most technically demanding thing you have shipped, and what you would do differently.
questions.answer: Pick your hardest shipped work and establish why it was demanding: scale, novelty, reliability constraints, or coordination complexity, with concrete specifics. Walk through the key technical decisions, the obstacles, and how you delivered it to production, quantifying the result. Then give a genuine, thoughtful reflection on what you would do differently, showing you learn rather than just succeed. What good looks like is deep technical substance paired with honest, specific hindsight rather than a token weakness.

questions.question: Implement a streaming top-k with a bounded-memory sketch; implement a sliding-window rate counter.
questions.answer: For streaming top-k use a bounded-memory sketch: Space-Saving with a fixed set of counters that evicts the minimum when a new key arrives, or Count-Min Sketch plus a heap of candidates, giving O(k) space and O(1) per event with approximate counts. For a sliding-window rate counter, keep per-bucket counts in a ring of time buckets (for example one bucket per second over the window) and sum the buckets for the current window, advancing and zeroing stale buckets as time moves; this is O(buckets) memory and O(1) amortized updates. Edge cases are bucket granularity trading accuracy for memory, clearing expired buckets lazily on access, and clock monotonicity.

questions.question: Your offline metric improved but the online A/B did not. Enumerate the reasons this happens and how you would tell them apart.
questions.answer: Possible causes include: the offline metric not aligning with the business objective; distribution shift or train/serve skew so offline data differs from live traffic; feedback loops and position bias in logged data; overfitting to the offline set or to the validation split; label leakage offline; and system effects online such as latency, caching, or the model changing user behavior. There are also statistical reasons: the A/B is underpowered, ran too short, or the offline gain was within noise. To distinguish them, check calibration and slice-level metrics, verify offline and online populations match, confirm feature parity between training and serving, audit for leakage and bias, and re-examine the A/B's power, duration, and metric definition. Running a counterfactual or logging-policy evaluation offline can bridge the gap.

questions.question: Explain position bias in ranking data and how you would debias training.
questions.answer: Position bias is the tendency of users to click higher-ranked items simply because they are more visible, so click logs conflate relevance with position and bias training toward whatever was shown on top. Left uncorrected, a model trained on clicks learns to reproduce the existing ranking rather than true relevance. Debiasing uses a propensity model: estimate the examination/click propensity for each position (e.g., via result randomization, intervention harvesting, or a position-based model) and apply inverse-propensity weighting to clicks so lower positions are upweighted. Alternatively, learn position effects jointly (a two-tower model with a position feature used at train time and fixed at inference) or use online exploration to collect less biased data.

questions.question: How do you design a feature store, and what causes training/serving skew?
questions.answer: A feature store centralizes feature definitions and serves them consistently to both training (offline/batch store, often a warehouse) and serving (online/low-latency store, often a key-value database), with a shared transformation layer so logic is written once. It handles feature registration, versioning, point-in-time correct joins for training labels, materialization pipelines, and freshness/TTL management. Training/serving skew arises when offline and online computations diverge: different code paths or libraries, time-travel errors that leak future data into training, stale or differently aggregated online features, and inconsistent handling of defaults or missing values. Prevent it by sharing transformation code, enforcing point-in-time correctness, logging served features for training, and monitoring distributions across the two paths.

questions.question: Design the ETA prediction system for a ride-hailing marketplace. What features, what model, how do you serve it in <100 ms?
questions.answer: Serve ETA with a learned model over road-graph and real-time features: segment-level speeds from live traffic, historical patterns by time-of-day and day-of-week, weather, request origin/destination and route, plus supply/demand context. A common design predicts travel time per route segment (or uses a graph neural network over the road network) and sums with learned corrections, trained on historical actual trip durations. To serve in under 100 ms, precompute and cache segment speed estimates updated continuously, keep features in a low-latency store, and run a lightweight model (gradient-boosted trees or a compact net) at request time, batching and caching route computations. Calibrate for bias since under- and over-estimates have asymmetric cost. Tradeoffs are freshness of live traffic versus feature-store update cost, model complexity (GNN accuracy) versus the latency budget, and point estimates versus predicting uncertainty for better decisions.

questions.question: Design a personalised feed ranking system with a two-stage candidate generation and ranking architecture.
questions.answer: Stage one generates candidates cheaply from a huge corpus using multiple retrieval sources, chiefly two-tower models producing user and item embeddings queried via ANN, plus heuristics like follows, trending, and recency, unioned to a few thousand items. Stage two ranks this shortlist with a heavy multi-task model scoring probabilities of the actions you care about (click, dwell, like, share) combined into a value, using rich cross features between user and item served from a feature store. This separation lets retrieval scale to billions while ranking spends compute only on candidates. Add a final policy pass for diversity, freshness, and integrity constraints, and evaluate with online A/B tests on retention. Tradeoffs are retrieval recall versus candidate-set size and cost, ranking model size versus the sub-100-ms budget, and engagement optimization versus long-term satisfaction and exploration.

questions.question: Design a content recommendation system for a streaming catalogue, including cold-start for new titles and new users.
questions.answer: Use two-stage retrieval and ranking over user-title interactions, with collaborative-filtering and two-tower embeddings for candidates and a ranking model predicting watch/completion. The crux is cold start: for new titles, rely on content features (genre, cast, synopsis and artwork embeddings, metadata) so they can be recommended before any interactions, and use exploration to gather early signal; for new users, use onboarding preferences, demographics, and popularity priors, then adapt quickly as behavior accrues. Blend content and collaborative signals (hybrid model) so coverage holds across the catalogue, and inject diversity and exploration to avoid over-concentrating on hits. Serve from precomputed embeddings and a feature store at low latency. Tradeoffs are exploration for cold items versus short-term engagement, content-based coverage versus collaborative accuracy for established titles, and freshness of embeddings versus recompute cost.

questions.question: Design “people you may know” / job-recommendation ranking at a professional network's scale.
questions.answer: For people-you-may-know, generate candidates from graph structure, chiefly friends-of-friends and shared attributes (company, school, groups), then rank with a model predicting connection acceptance using mutual-connection counts, profile similarity, and co-engagement features, at scale via precomputed second-degree neighborhoods and graph embeddings. For job recommendations, retrieve candidate jobs matching skills, title, and location via embeddings and filters, then rank by predicted apply/response probability using member-to-job affinity and recruiter signals. Both use a two-stage retrieve-then-rank design served from a feature store, with freshness so new connections and jobs surface quickly. Guard against over-recommending popular nodes and respect privacy constraints on what signals are usable. Tradeoffs are candidate recall from graph expansion versus the combinatorial cost of second-degree neighborhoods, precision of acceptance/apply prediction versus diversity, and personalization versus fairness across members and job posters.

questions.question: Design dynamic pricing / surge for a two-sided marketplace and describe the feedback loops that can go wrong.
questions.answer: Model price as a function of real-time supply and demand per geographic cell and time window: forecast demand and available supply, then set a multiplier that clears the market and improves reliability, bounded by caps and smoothed to avoid shocks. Serve it from streaming aggregates of open requests and available providers with a pricing model that maps imbalance to a multiplier, updated frequently per small geo-temporal unit. The dangerous feedback loops: high surge suppresses demand and attracts supply, which then collapses the multiplier and causes oscillation; providers may chase or game surge zones; and displayed prices influence the very behavior being predicted, so naive models trained on observational data learn biased elasticities. Mitigate with hysteresis, smoothing, caps, controlled experimentation to estimate true elasticity, and guardrails against runaway loops. Tradeoffs are market efficiency and reliability versus rider trust and fairness, and responsiveness versus price stability.

questions.question: Design a visual search system: user uploads an image, you return visually similar in-catalogue items.
questions.answer: Encode catalogue images with a vision embedding model (trained with metric learning so visually or semantically similar products sit close) and index the vectors in an ANN store; at query time embed the uploaded image the same way and retrieve nearest neighbors, optionally after detecting and cropping the main object. Rerank candidates with finer visual features and business signals (availability, popularity), and allow attribute filtering. Keep the index fresh as the catalogue changes with incremental updates, and precompute all catalogue embeddings offline so query-time cost is just one encode plus an ANN lookup, kept within tens of milliseconds by sharding and caching. Improve relevance with training data from click-throughs on visual results and hard negatives. Tradeoffs are embedding model size and accuracy versus encode latency, ANN recall versus speed and memory, and whole-image versus object-detection-first matching for cluttered user photos.

questions.question: Design a fraud-detection system with heavy class imbalance and an adversarial opponent.
questions.answer: Handle extreme class imbalance with a layered design: fast rules and an ML scorer (gradient-boosted trees or a neural net) on transaction, device, velocity, and graph features, trained with techniques for imbalance (class weighting, focal loss, careful resampling) and evaluated with precision-recall and cost-weighted metrics rather than accuracy. Because the opponent adapts, features and models must be retrained frequently, combined with anomaly detection and graph analysis to catch novel patterns the supervised model has not seen, and complemented by human investigators whose labels feed back. Serve in real time with a feature store and a decision policy that routes borderline cases to step-up verification rather than hard block, limiting false-positive friction for legitimate users. Maintain fast feedback from chargebacks and investigations. Tradeoffs are catching fraud (recall) versus blocking good users (precision and revenue), model freshness versus stability, and interpretability for investigators versus raw accuracy.

questions.question: Design an LLM-powered customer-support assistant on top of an existing help centre, with escalation to humans.
questions.answer: Ground the assistant in the existing help center via retrieval: index articles with hybrid lexical-plus-dense search, and on each user question retrieve relevant content so the LLM answers from source material with citations, reducing hallucination. Maintain conversation state, let the assistant perform safe lookups through typed tools, and define confidence and risk thresholds that escalate to a human agent with the full transcript and suggested answer when the question is out of scope, sensitive, or the user asks. Keep any state-changing action behind authorization and confirmation, and log interactions for quality review and retraining of retrieval and routing. Evaluate with offline answer-quality suites plus online deflection rate, escalation rate, and CSAT. Tradeoffs are deflection (automation) versus wrongly withholding a human, retrieval recall versus precision feeding the LLM, and answer latency versus thoroughness of grounding and verification.

questions.question: How do you monitor a deployed ranking model for drift, and what triggers a retrain?
questions.answer: Monitor the inputs, the predictions, and the outcomes separately: track feature distributions and prediction score distributions for covariate and prediction drift, and compare them against a training reference using divergence measures with alerting thresholds. When ground-truth labels arrive, even delayed, measure live ranking metrics such as NDCG, CTR, or conversion against expectations to catch concept drift where the input looks stable but the relationship changed. Watch business and guardrail metrics and segment by key populations so a regression in one slice is visible. Trigger a retrain on sustained metric degradation beyond a threshold, significant drift that correlates with performance loss, or on a scheduled cadence as data accumulates, rather than on transient noise. Validate any retrained model through the regression gate and a canary before full promotion to avoid shipping a worse model.

questions.question: Tell me about a model you shipped that made a measurable business difference, and one that did not.
questions.answer: Prepare both outcomes and treat them with equal honesty. For the successful model, use STAR and tie it to a concrete business metric, explaining how you connected the model to real value and measured it rigorously. For the one that did not move the needle, explain why, what you learned about problem selection, evaluation, or deployment, and how you responded. What good looks like is demonstrating that you judge models by business impact, not just offline metrics, and that you are candid about failures.

questions.question: Implement a thread-safe batching logger: many producer threads call log(msg); a background thread flushes batches of up to 100 messages every second or when full.
questions.answer: Producers call log(msg) which appends to a shared thread-safe queue (or a mutex-protected buffer) and signals a condition variable; the single background consumer waits on that condition. The consumer wakes when the buffer reaches 100 messages or a one-second timer elapses (whichever first), drains up to 100 messages under the lock into a local list, releases the lock, and flushes outside the critical section to minimize contention. Use a bounded queue to apply backpressure, flush remaining messages on shutdown via a sentinel/drain, and make the flush idempotent to retries. Key correctness points are not holding the lock during I/O, handling spurious wakeups, and ensuring the timer-based flush still fires when traffic is below 100 per second.

questions.question: You have a stream of billions of events and need the top-K most frequent keys with bounded memory. Exact is impossible: what do you do?
questions.answer: Exact counts over billions of distinct keys exceed memory, so switch to approximate heavy-hitter detection. Space-Saving maintains m counters (m a modest multiple of k): on each event increment if tracked, else evict the minimum-count entry and give the new key that minimum plus one, yielding the top-k with bounded overestimate error and O(m) memory. Count-Min Sketch plus a heap of candidate keys is the alternative, using hashing to estimate counts within an error bound. Across many machines, each shard keeps its own sketch and a coordinator merges them (both structures are mergeable), add windowing or decay for recency, and accept bounded error as the price of bounded memory.

questions.question: Given allowed IP ranges as CIDR blocks plus explicit deny ranges, implement is_allowed(ip) efficiently for millions of checks per second.
questions.answer: Precompute the allowed and deny CIDR blocks into a structure that answers longest-prefix match quickly, such as a binary radix/Patricia trie over IP bits, or sorted interval endpoints for binary search. Each IP is an integer; a lookup walks the trie by address bits to find the most specific matching rule and returns its allow/deny verdict, with deny taking precedence per the policy. Preprocessing is one-time; each check is O(32) for IPv4 (or O(128) IPv6) regardless of rule count, enabling millions of checks per second. Alternatively flatten all CIDRs into disjoint sorted intervals tagged allow/deny and binary-search the IP, O(log n); edge cases are overlapping ranges resolved by specificity, exact deny-over-allow precedence, and IPv4 vs IPv6.

questions.question: A Spark job joining a 2 TB fact table to a 50 GB dimension table has one straggler task running 100x longer than the rest. Diagnose and fix it.
questions.answer: The straggler almost certainly comes from data skew: one join key has a hugely disproportionate number of rows (often a null or default id) that all hash to one partition, so one task does most of the work. Confirm by inspecting partition sizes and the key distribution in the Spark UI. Fixes include a broadcast join since the 50 GB dimension may fit in memory with enough executor RAM, eliminating the shuffle entirely; if not, use salting, appending a random suffix to the hot key on both sides to spread it across partitions, or Spark's adaptive skew-join handling to split the skewed partition. Also filter nulls early and bump shuffle partitions so work distributes evenly.

questions.question: A Structured Streaming job reads Kafka and writes to a Delta table. The cluster is killed mid-batch and restarts. Does the customer get duplicate rows? Explain at the level of the checkpoint and the transaction log.
questions.answer: No, the customer does not get duplicates because Structured Streaming plus Delta provides exactly-once output through idempotent commits. The checkpoint durably records, per batch, the Kafka offset ranges that batch consumed; on restart the engine recomputes the same batch id from those offsets rather than re-reading arbitrary data. The Delta transaction log records each committed batch with its batch/version id, so if the batch had already committed before the kill, the restart's attempt to commit the same batch id is recognized and skipped, and if it had not committed, the recomputed batch commits atomically as a single log entry. The atomic log commit plus offset-tracking checkpoint together guarantee each input batch's writes appear exactly once.

questions.question: When would you fine-tune instead of using RAG or prompt engineering, and if you do, LoRA or full fine-tuning?
questions.answer: Fine-tune when you need a durable change in behavior, style, format, or a latency-sensitive compression of long prompts that prompting and retrieval cannot deliver reliably; use RAG when the gap is fresh or private knowledge, and prompt engineering first when the capability already exists. If you fine-tune, default to LoRA: it reaches near-full quality on most adaptation tasks with far less memory and cost, swappable per-task adapters, and lower forgetting risk. Choose full fine-tuning only when the domain shift is large, you have ample compute, and LoRA underperforms in evaluation. In practice these layer together: fine-tune for behavior, RAG for facts, prompting for final control.

questions.question: Take a working GenAI agent prototype to production for an enterprise. What's your checklist between demo and launch?
questions.answer: Between demo and launch, harden correctness and safety first: build a real eval suite over representative and adversarial tasks, add guardrails for prompt injection, data leakage, and unsafe or irreversible actions, and scope tool permissions to least privilege. Address reliability and operations with retries, timeouts, fallbacks, idempotency for side-effecting tools, rate limits, and load testing against SLOs for latency and cost. Add full observability, tracing, cost attribution, logging with redaction, feedback capture, and alerting, plus prompt and model versioning with a tested rollback path. Handle data governance, access controls, tenancy isolation, PII handling, and compliance for the enterprise context, and define a human-in-the-loop or escalation path for low-confidence or high-risk actions. Finally, stage the rollout with a canary and a regression gate so future changes cannot silently degrade the system.

questions.question: A customer insists on fine-tuning an open model on their support tickets because “we want our own model.” You think RAG solves it. What do you do?
questions.answer: I wouldn't argue abstractly; I'd propose a quick bake-off on their own tickets. First I'd dig into why they want their own model, since sometimes it's data control or latency rather than quality, which changes the answer. I'd stand up a RAG baseline over their resolved tickets and knowledge base in days and measure it against their real questions, because retrieval usually handles the 'answer from our documented knowledge' case that support tickets represent, and it updates instantly as policies change without a retraining cycle. If evals show RAG meets the bar, the data decides for them; if there's a genuine gap like consistent tone or a specialized format, I'd recommend fine-tuning for that narrow need, often on top of RAG rather than instead of it. The point is to let evidence on their data, not preference, drive the decision.

questions.question: An agent you shipped four months ago runs on a base model being deprecated in 60 days. How do you swap the model without regressing quality, and what had to be in place beforehand?
questions.answer: The swap is only safe because the eval harness was in place from day one: a representative suite of real tasks with automated scoring plus a sample for human review, so 'no regression' means something measurable. I'd run the new model through that suite side by side with the old one, look at aggregate scores and the specific cases that changed, and re-tune prompts since behavior shifts subtly between models. I'd roll it out behind a flag with a canary on a slice of traffic, monitor quality and cost in production, and keep the ability to revert instantly. What had to exist beforehand is that eval suite, prompt and model config decoupled from code so swapping is a config change, and production logging so I can compare real outputs. Without those you're flying blind and the 60 days becomes a scramble.

questions.question: Our compiler statically schedules every instruction and every chip-to-chip transfer. What does that compiler need to know that an NVCC-style compiler does not, and what breaks when it's wrong?
questions.answer: A statically scheduling compiler must know the exact timing and latency of every operation and every chip-to-chip transfer, the full memory layout and residency, and the deterministic interconnect topology and bandwidth, because it bakes a fixed schedule with no runtime arbitration. An NVCC-style compiler can rely on hardware to dynamically schedule warps, hide latency, and arbitrate memory and network at runtime, so it tolerates variable timing. When the static model is wrong, for example an op takes longer than assumed, a transfer is delayed, or contention appears, there is no dynamic fallback, so the schedule desynchronizes: buffers are read before writes complete, collectives deadlock or corrupt data, and correctness, not just performance, breaks.

questions.question: Design the IR and pass pipeline for a compiler targeting a spatial dataflow accelerator. Where does the memory-residency decision live, and why?
questions.answer: Use a multi-level IR: a high-level graph IR capturing tensor ops and dataflow dependencies, a mid-level IR after tiling/fusion that exposes loops and data movement, and a low-level IR mapping operations to spatial processing elements and routing. The pass pipeline runs graph canonicalization and fusion, then tiling and layout assignment, then placement and routing onto the spatial fabric, then scheduling of compute and communication, and finally lowering to hardware primitives. The memory-residency decision belongs at the mid-level tiling/scheduling pass, because that is where tile sizes, fusion boundaries, and the dataflow schedule are chosen and together determine what must stay resident in on-chip memory; deciding it earlier lacks the tiling information and deciding it later cannot change the schedule that created the pressure.

questions.question: Write the host-side runtime that feeds a deterministic accelerator across many chips. What is genuinely hard about it?
questions.answer: The host runtime loads the statically scheduled program onto every chip, sets up the input/output DMA buffers, launches execution in lockstep, and streams data in and out while respecting the fixed schedule. What is genuinely hard is maintaining global determinism and synchronization across many chips: feeding inputs so no chip stalls and breaks the schedule, overlapping host-device transfer with compute to keep the pipeline full, and coordinating collectives so all chips reach barriers together. You must also handle failure and recovery without nondeterminism, manage backpressure when the host cannot supply data fast enough, and ensure bit-exact reproducibility, all while the hardware offers no runtime scheduling to absorb timing variance.

questions.question: A model passes bit-exact against the functional simulator on one chip but produces wrong output at rack scale. How do you find it?
questions.answer: Since it is bit-exact on one chip, the bug is in the cross-chip dimension: inter-chip communication, collective ordering, or synchronization, not the per-chip math. I would first reproduce at the smallest rack scale that fails and bisect by number of chips to localize. Then I compare intermediate tensors at communication boundaries against the single-chip reference, checking collective results (all-reduce/all-gather) for ordering or partial-sum nondeterminism, buffer-reuse races where a transfer reads before a write completes, and off-by-one sharding or layout mismatches at chip boundaries. Logging per-chip checksums at each sync point pinpoints the first divergent step; common root causes are a mis-specified transfer latency in the static schedule, a reduction tree order mismatch, or a barrier that does not actually synchronize all chips.

questions.question: An LPU has no HBM at all, just on-die SRAM. Redo the decode roofline argument for that machine and tell me what changes.
questions.answer: On an SRAM-only machine the decode roofline changes because on-die SRAM bandwidth is orders of magnitude higher than HBM, so the memory-bandwidth wall that limits GPU decode largely disappears. Reading weights from SRAM is so fast that even at batch size 1 you can approach the compute-bound regime, so tokens per second is set by the chip's FLOPs and the deterministic dataflow rather than by weight-read bandwidth. The catch is capacity: SRAM per chip is tiny (hundreds of MB), so the model must be sharded across many chips, and the roofline becomes about inter-chip interconnect bandwidth and keeping the pipeline full. The upshot is very high single-stream token rates and lower benefit from large batching, at the cost of needing many chips and a tightly scheduled fabric to hold the weights.

questions.question: A 70B dense model at 8-bit weights, chips with ~230 MB of SRAM each. Walk me through the deployment and the unit economics.
questions.answer: A 70B model at 8-bit weights is ~70 GB, so with ~230 MB of SRAM per chip you need roughly 300+ chips just to hold the weights, plus overhead for KV and activations. You deploy by sharding the model across that fabric with tensor and pipeline parallelism matched to the static schedule, streaming tokens through a deterministic pipeline so each chip holds a fixed slice resident in SRAM. The unit economics are dominated by the large fixed fleet of chips and their power: cost per token is the amortized fleet cost divided by aggregate token throughput, so you need high sustained utilization to be competitive. Because batching gives less benefit than on GPUs (weights are already SRAM-resident), the model earns its keep through very low latency and high single-stream throughput rather than large-batch amortization, which changes how you price toward latency-sensitive workloads.

questions.question: On a GPU you batch to amortise weight reads. What is the batching calculus on an SRAM-only machine, and how should that change how we price?
questions.answer: On a GPU you batch to amortize the expensive HBM weight reads across many requests, which is why throughput rises steeply with batch size until you hit the compute wall. On an SRAM-only machine the weights already live in fast on-die memory, so there is no per-request weight-read cost to amortize; a single stream can nearly saturate the compute, and extra requests mainly add compute work rather than sharing a fixed read cost. That means batching yields diminishing returns and the machine is naturally good at low-latency single-stream serving. Pricing should therefore reflect per-token compute and the fixed fleet cost rather than assuming cheap large-batch throughput, so you can charge a premium for guaranteed low latency and determinism instead of relying on batch amortization to drive down unit cost.

questions.question: Determinism is the headline claim. What does it actually buy at p99, and why does it matter especially for agentic workloads?
questions.answer: Deterministic execution means the same input always produces the same output and the same timing, so there is no long tail from scheduling jitter, cache-state variance, or batch-composition effects; p99 collapses toward the median. That tight, predictable latency is valuable because you can set aggressive SLOs without huge headroom and avoid the worst-case stalls that dominate tail latency on dynamically scheduled GPUs. For agentic workloads it matters especially because they chain many model calls, and tail latencies multiply across steps, so even a small per-call variance compounds into large end-to-end unpredictability. Deterministic timing also makes reproducibility, debugging, and step-by-step orchestration far easier when an agent's behavior depends on prior outputs.

questions.question: How would you serve a large mixture-of-experts model on a statically scheduled fabric when expert selection is data-dependent?
questions.answer: The challenge is that a statically scheduled fabric wants a fixed dataflow, but MoE routing picks experts per token at runtime. One approach is to keep all experts resident across the fabric (expert parallelism) and route tokens via a deterministic all-to-all so the schedule is fixed even though which chip does useful work varies, accepting some wasted capacity. Alternatively, you cap and pad routing with a fixed capacity per expert (dropping or deferring overflow) so each step has a statically known shape, trading a little quality for schedulability. You can also batch tokens and perform the routing as a fixed gather/scatter over known expert slots, balance load to avoid hot experts, and overlap the routing communication with compute so the static pipeline stays full despite data-dependent selection.

questions.question: We pair LPX decode accelerators with NVIDIA GPUs doing prefill and attention. Design the serving path across those two machines.
questions.answer: Split inference across the two machines along the prefill/decode boundary: run compute-bound prefill and attention on the NVIDIA GPUs, which excel at the large matmuls of processing the prompt and producing the KV-cache, then transfer the KV-cache to the LPX decode accelerators that handle the memory-bandwidth-bound autoregressive token generation. This disaggregated design requires a fast interconnect to move the KV-cache without the transfer dominating latency, and a scheduler that pipelines prefill of new requests against ongoing decode so neither machine idles. Batch on each side independently (large prefill batches, continuous decode batching) and overlap communication with computation. Stream tokens from the decode side to the client. Tradeoffs are the KV-cache transfer cost and interconnect bandwidth versus the efficiency of specializing each phase, scheduling complexity versus utilization, and added latency from the handoff versus higher aggregate throughput and better cost-per-token.

questions.question: A prospective customer runs their workload on H100s. Talk me through when you would tell them not to move.
questions.answer: I'd tell them not to move when their H100 setup already meets their latency, throughput, and cost targets and the migration risk outweighs any marginal gain, because change has real cost in engineering time and regression risk. If they have sunk capital, a tuned stack, data-residency or compliance constraints that favor staying put, or workloads that are memory-bandwidth bound in ways the alternative doesn't improve, moving is often a lateral step at best. I'd also hold them if their bottleneck is actually software, prompt design, or batching rather than hardware, since new GPUs won't fix that. My advice follows a measured comparison on their real workload, not a spec sheet. The honest recommendation sometimes is to optimize what they have.

questions.question: Tell me about a performance optimisation you shipped. Give me the numbers, and tell me why I should believe them.
questions.answer: Describe the optimization with a clear before-and-after and specific numbers, but build credibility by explaining your measurement methodology. Detail how you established a baseline, controlled for confounders, measured in a representative environment, and validated the gain held in production rather than just a microbenchmark. Address variance, statistical confidence, and any caveats so the numbers are believable rather than cherry-picked. What good looks like is rigor and intellectual honesty about measurement, showing the interviewer you can be trusted with performance claims.

questions.question: Write the server-side handler for streaming token generation. Handle client disconnects correctly.
questions.answer: The handler sets a streaming response (SSE or chunked transfer) and runs the model's token generator in an async loop, writing each token to the client as it is produced and flushing so the browser renders incrementally. To handle disconnects, monitor the request's cancellation/disconnect signal (for example the ASGI disconnect event or a closed-connection check) and, when it fires, break the loop and cancel the underlying generation task so you stop spending GPU on a client that left. Use backpressure-aware writes so a slow client does not unbounded-buffer, release the KV cache and any slot on cleanup in a finally block, and send a terminal sentinel on normal completion. The key correctness points are prompt cancellation propagation, resource cleanup on every exit path, and not blocking the event loop.

questions.question: Design the scheduler for a continuous-batching inference engine.
questions.answer: The scheduler maintains a running batch plus waiting and (optionally) swapped queues, and at each decode iteration decides which requests to admit, continue, preempt, or evict. On admission it checks KV-cache capacity (in PagedAttention blocks), reserving blocks for new sequences and respecting a max batch size and token budget per step. It interleaves prefill and decode, using chunked prefill to bound per-iteration prefill work so ongoing decodes are not starved, and applies priority or fairness policies and per-request limits. When memory is exhausted it preempts or swaps the lowest-priority or newest sequences, and it emits finished sequences immediately so new requests can join on the next iteration, maximizing utilization while protecting tail latency.

questions.question: Explain speculative decoding. When does it help, when does it hurt, and why adapt the speculator to live traffic?
questions.answer: Speculative decoding uses a cheap draft model to guess several next tokens that the target model then verifies in one parallel pass, accepting the longest correct prefix so output quality is unchanged. It helps when decode is memory-bandwidth-bound at low batch size and the draft's acceptance rate is high, because you get multiple verified tokens per expensive weight read. It hurts when acceptance is low (wasted draft and verification work), when the draft model is too costly, or at high batch sizes where the target is already compute-bound and there is no spare bandwidth to exploit. You adapt the speculator to live traffic because acceptance depends on the actual prompt and output distribution, so continuously tuning the draft model or its speculation length keeps the acceptance rate high and avoids net slowdowns.

questions.question: Price a dedicated endpoint: estimate cost per million output tokens for a 70B model, and explain the throughput-latency trade.
