questions.question: Paired coding: write a chunker for a legal document that never splits a clause and carries enough context that a retrieved chunk is self-contained.
questions.answer: Segment the document along legal structure (clauses, sections, numbered sub-paragraphs) using the document's own delimiters so a chunk boundary never falls inside a clause. Greedily pack whole clauses into a chunk up to the token budget, and if a single clause exceeds the budget, keep it intact and allow it to be its own oversized chunk rather than splitting mid-clause. For self-containment, prepend carried context to each chunk: the section/clause heading path, a short summary of the parent, and defined-term references, plus a small overlap of the preceding clause so pronouns and cross-references resolve. Preserve original offsets and clause identifiers for citation; the key constraints are semantic-boundary-only splits, token-measured sizing, and enough injected context that a retrieved chunk stands alone.

questions.question: A lawyer asks about a 200-page credit agreement where the operative clause on page 140 depends on a defined term on page 8. How do you build retrieval that gets this right?
questions.answer: The core challenge is a long-range dependency: the operative clause on page 140 only means something via a defined term on page 8, so independent chunk retrieval fails. I chunk the agreement structure-aware along clauses and definitions, and I build a definitions index so every defined term is captured as its own retrievable unit with its location. At query or indexing time I resolve references: when a retrieved clause uses a defined term, I expand retrieval to pull that term's definition and any cross-referenced sections, effectively doing a dependency-following multi-hop retrieval, and I enrich each clause chunk with the definitions it depends on. Keeping metadata like clause numbers and defined-term links, and giving the generator both the clause and its resolved definitions with citations, is what gets the answer right; for truly interwoven questions I let an agentic loop fetch dependencies iteratively.

questions.question: When would you put a whole contract in the context window instead of retrieving over it? Defend the answer with numbers.
questions.answer: I put the whole contract in context when it is short enough that the token cost and latency are acceptable and when the question requires reasoning across many interdependent clauses where retrieval would miss cross-references. The maths: a 200-page agreement is roughly 100k to 150k tokens, which fits a long window but at, say, a few dollars per million input tokens costs on the order of tens of cents and adds seconds of latency per call, repeated on every query. For one-off deep analysis of a single bounded document that trade is worth it; for a 20-page contract at under 15k tokens it is clearly cheaper and more reliable than building an index. But across many documents or high query volume, those per-call token costs multiply fast, so retrieval wins economically, and the crossover is where repeated full-context spend exceeds the one-time cost of chunking plus cheap retrieval.

questions.question: Design an agent that takes a draft NDA and returns a redlined Word document reflecting the firm's playbook, not a chat response.
questions.answer: This is a document-editing agent, not a chatbot, so the output must be a redlined Word file with tracked changes, not prose. The pipeline parses the NDA into clauses, classifies each against the firm's playbook of standard positions and fallback language, and for each clause decides accept, edit, or insert, generating the specific revision and a short rationale comment. It then writes those as tracked changes and margin comments into the document format so a lawyer sees insertions, deletions, and reasoning exactly as if a colleague had marked it up. Grounding every edit in a cited playbook rule keeps it auditable, a human reviews before anything is finalized, and evaluation compares the agent's redlines against attorney-marked documents for precision and recall on expected changes.

questions.question: Present the architecture for a workflow reviewing 5,000 contracts against an 18-question diligence checklist, returning a review grid.
questions.answer: Model it as a batch document-analysis workflow: ingest 5,000 contracts, OCR and segment each into clauses, and for each of the 18 diligence questions retrieve the relevant clauses per contract and have an LLM answer with the finding plus a citation to the source span and a confidence. Fan the work out across contracts and questions in parallel through a queue, store results as a contract-by-question grid, and route low-confidence or high-risk answers to human reviewers whose corrections are recorded. Ground every answer in retrieved text to curb hallucination, and keep an audit trail of the exact clause supporting each cell. Scale with batched inference and caching of per-contract embeddings. Tradeoffs are per-question retrieval precision versus recall (missing a clause yields a wrong answer), LLM cost at 90k question-contract pairs versus accuracy, and the human-review rate needed to meet the reliability bar for legal diligence.

questions.question: A new frontier model is released and scores better on your benchmarks. What happens before it reaches customers?
questions.answer: A better benchmark score is necessary but not sufficient, so before reaching customers the model goes through a full evaluation and rollout pipeline. Verify the gains are real and not contaminated or benchmark-overfit by checking per-slice results, private held-out and post-cutoff sets, and behavior on your product's actual workflows, plus safety, robustness, and cost and latency. Run the regression gate against the current production baseline with confidence intervals so no key slice or guardrail regresses even if the average improves. If gates pass, stage a canary and A/B comparing live quality and behavioral metrics against the incumbent, with rollback triggers defined in advance. Only after the canary confirms no real-user regression does it ramp to full traffic, with monitoring and the ability to revert.

questions.question: Every assertion in a Harvey answer needs to link back to a specific passage. Design the grounding system, and tell me how you would measure the unsupported-claim rate.
questions.answer: Ground generation in retrieval so each assertion is produced from and linked to a specific source passage, then enforce at the claim level: decompose the answer into atomic assertions, align each to its cited span, and run an entailment check verifying the passage actually supports the assertion, with abstention or flagging when support is missing. Store span-level citations as structured metadata so every sentence maps to a locatable source, and block or rewrite assertions that fail verification before the answer reaches the user. Measure the unsupported-claim rate as the proportion of atomic assertions not entailed by their linked passage, calibrated against legal-expert annotations on a held-out sample, and track it as a release and monitoring metric. Given the legal domain, favor high precision and explicit abstention over confident but ungrounded claims, and add human review for high-stakes outputs. Faithful citation means verified entailment, not a plausible-looking reference.

questions.question: An agentic research query returns a memo citing a case that was overruled. Where does that get caught?
questions.answer: Ideally it is caught before generation by the retrieval and knowledge layer: citators and case-status metadata should mark the case as overruled or negative-treatment, and the retrieval system should either exclude it or surface the warning so the model never relies on it as good law. If it slips into drafting, a post-generation verification pass should check every cited authority's current status against a legal-status source and flag or strike any case with negative treatment, plus an entailment check that the cited case actually supports the proposition. A final human-in-the-loop review by the attorney is the backstop, since signing off on good law is their professional responsibility. The failure most often traces to stale or missing case-treatment data in the index, so the primary fix is keeping case-status metadata current and gating generation on it, with the verification pass and human review as defense in depth.

questions.question: Two partners at the same firm are on opposite sides of a deal. Design the data isolation for that, on top of normal multi-tenancy.
questions.answer: On top of standard tenant isolation, you need matter-level and ethical-wall isolation within a single firm so that the two partners and their teams cannot access each other's deal data. Model access control around matters and conflict walls: assign each deal and document to a matter, attach an ethical-wall policy that explicitly denies cross-access between the conflicted teams, and enforce it at every data path including retrieval, search indexes, embeddings, caches, and the agent's context so no shared index can leak one side's data to the other. Ensure retrieval is filtered by the requesting user's wall membership before anything reaches the model, keep per-matter encryption or logical separation, and audit all access for wall breaches. Make the walls configurable by the firm's conflicts team and fail closed, defaulting to deny when membership is ambiguous. The principle is that confidentiality walls are enforced in the data and authorization layer, never left to the model to respect.

questions.question: Estimate the cost and turnaround of running your diligence workflow over a 5,000-document data room, and tell me which lever you'd pull first.
questions.answer: Cost and turnaround are driven mostly by tokens and how many documents require the expensive deep pass, so I'd estimate from average pages per document, tokens per page, and the per-token model price, times 5,000, plus embedding and storage costs that are comparatively trivial. A rough run of that size is typically hours of wall-clock time with parallelism and a modest to moderate model spend, with the long tail being large or image-heavy documents. The first lever I'd pull is a cheap triage pass that classifies and filters documents so only the relevant ones get the costly full analysis, since in a data room a large fraction is boilerplate or irrelevant. That single step usually cuts both cost and time more than any model-level tuning. After that I'd batch aggressively and cache repeated clauses.

questions.question: A partner reports that Harvey missed a change-of-control clause in a contract it reviewed. Debug it.
questions.answer: I'd reproduce it first: re-run the exact contract and confirm the miss is consistent, then isolate where it broke. I'd check retrieval, whether the change-of-control clause text was even surfaced to the model, because if the clause used unusual wording or sat in a scanned or poorly-parsed section, the failure is in ingestion or retrieval, not reasoning. If the text was present and still missed, I'd examine the prompt and the clause taxonomy to see whether change-of-control was defined and asked for clearly, and test prompt and extraction fixes against that document. Then I'd add this contract and its clause to the regression eval set so the fix is verified and the miss can't silently return, and sweep for similar contracts that might share the flaw. Finally I'd report root cause and the mitigation honestly to the partner.

questions.question: Merge ranked results from N connector shards into a global top-k, applying a per-user permission filter. Do it efficiently.
questions.answer: Because each shard returns results already ranked, do a k-way merge rather than concatenate-and-sort. Seed a max-heap with the top candidate from each of the N shards; repeatedly pop the global best, apply the per-user permission filter, and if it passes add it to the output, then push the next item from the shard the popped result came from. Stop once you have collected k permitted results. This is O(m log N) where m is the number of items examined, far cheaper than sorting all results, and it streams shards lazily so you fetch only as deep as needed. Edge cases are applying the permission filter after popping so denied items do not consume output slots (fetch deeper to backfill), de-duplicating items appearing in multiple shards, and handling shards that exhaust early.

questions.question: Walk me through the latency budget of a query: query understanding → retrieval → rerank → LLM answer. Where do you spend and where do you cut?
questions.answer: Break the budget into query understanding (light, often a few ms to tens of ms), retrieval (embedding + vector search, tens to low hundreds of ms), reranking (a cross-encoder pass, can be large if applied to many candidates), and the LLM answer (prefill over retrieved context plus decode, usually the dominant cost). Most time and money go to the LLM, especially prefill over long retrieved context and the generated tokens, with rerank second if it scores many documents. To cut it I shrink and cache context, retrieve fewer but better passages, use a lightweight reranker or rerank a small candidate set, parallelize understanding and retrieval, and stream the answer with chunked prefill so first useful content appears early. I spend compute where it moves answer quality (good retrieval and the generator) and trim everywhere else, using a smaller or quantized model if quality allows.

questions.question: How would you chunk and embed heterogeneous enterprise content: Slack threads, Jira tickets, Google Docs, PDFs?
questions.answer: Heterogeneous content needs source-specific preprocessing before a shared embedding and index. Slack threads I chunk by conversation/thread with participants and timestamps preserved so context is not lost across short messages; Jira tickets I chunk by ticket, keeping fields like title, status, and comments as structured metadata; Google Docs and PDFs I parse layout-aware and chunk by section, handling tables and figures specially. I embed everything with one multilingual, general-purpose model into a common vector space but attach rich metadata (source type, author, timestamp, permissions, URL) so I can filter and cite, and I tune chunk sizes per source since a Slack message and a doc section have very different granularity. Recency and access control vary by source, so I normalize those signals and index them for filtering and ranking.

questions.question: Why is RAG the right architecture for an enterprise assistant instead of fine-tuning on the company's data? Where does RAG break?
questions.answer: RAG is the right default because it separates knowledge from the model: you can add, update, and delete documents without retraining, enforce per-user access control at query time, cite sources for auditability, and keep answers current as the corpus changes, all of which fine-tuning cannot do well since it bakes knowledge into weights and risks staleness and hallucination. Fine-tuning teaches style, format, or task behavior but is a poor way to inject frequently changing facts, and it offers no grounding or attribution. RAG breaks when questions need reasoning across many scattered documents or aggregation that single-pass retrieval misses, when retrieval recall is poor so the evidence never reaches the model, when content is contradictory or stale, and when the query is answerable only by computation over structured data rather than text lookup. In those cases you need multi-hop or agentic retrieval, better chunking and reranking, conflict handling, or a different architecture such as text-to-query over a database, often combined with light fine-tuning for behavior.

questions.question: Design an agent that takes actions in enterprise tools (file a Jira ticket, draft an email) on a user's behalf. How do you handle permissions and evaluate it?
questions.answer: Each tool, create Jira ticket or draft email, is a typed function, but actions execute under the user's own identity and permissions via delegated auth like OAuth, so the agent can never do more than the user is authorized to do. Enforce authorization in the downstream systems and an intermediary policy layer, not in the prompt, and keep writes to safe states where possible, drafting an email rather than sending it, so a human confirms consequential actions. Scope tokens narrowly, log every action with inputs and the initiating user for audit, and gate irreversible or external-facing steps behind explicit approval. Evaluate with an offline suite scoring tool-selection accuracy, argument correctness, and task success, plus online monitoring of intervention and error rates and sampled human review of real actions.

questions.question: Design agent orchestration across dozens of connected SaaS systems. Where is authorization enforced, and why can it not live in the model?
questions.answer: Authorization must be enforced at each connected system and at a central policy layer between the agent and those systems, never inside the model, because the model is non-deterministic, can be prompt-injected, and cannot be a trusted security boundary. The orchestrator calls each SaaS tool using the end user's delegated credentials with least-privilege scopes, and every request passes through a policy engine that checks the user's entitlements and the action's risk before it reaches the target system. The model only proposes actions; the infrastructure decides whether they are permitted, so a compromised or confused agent still cannot exceed the user's real permissions. This keeps a single auditable enforcement point, supports per-system access controls, and ensures permissions hold even if the prompt is manipulated.

questions.question: Design a connector framework that syncs content and permissions from 100+ SaaS apps into one index.
questions.answer: Build connectors per SaaS app that sync both content and its permission model into a unified index, normalizing each app's documents and ACLs into a common schema with a stable identity mapping so the same person across apps resolves to one principal. Use incremental sync via change APIs or webhooks where available and periodic full reconciliation otherwise, tracking deletions and permission changes so revoked access propagates quickly; default to deny on uncertainty. Store content embeddings plus lexical indexes and a parallel permissions store keyed per document, and enforce ACLs at query time by filtering to the caller's resolved groups. Make connectors resilient to rate limits, pagination, and schema drift, with per-connector isolation so one failing source does not stall others. Tradeoffs are freshness of permission sync versus API rate limits and cost, index-time versus query-time ACL enforcement, and the engineering burden of 100+ bespoke connectors versus a generic but weaker abstraction.

questions.question: Glean's ranking leans on a knowledge graph of people, content and activity. How would you build that graph, and how does it improve retrieval beyond embedding similarity?
questions.answer: Build the knowledge graph by extracting entities (people, documents, teams, projects) and edges from connector metadata and activity logs: authorship, sharing, edits, meetings, messages, and org structure, continuously updated as events stream in. This graph improves retrieval beyond embedding similarity by adding relational and social signals, boosting content authored or frequently accessed by people close to the searcher, recent and active documents, and items connected through shared projects, which semantic similarity alone cannot capture. At query time, fuse embedding relevance with graph-derived features (proximity to the user, document authority, recency of activity) in the ranker, effectively personalizing results by who you are and how you relate to the content. Tradeoffs are the cost and freshness of maintaining a large activity graph versus its ranking lift, personalization from social signals versus surfacing objectively authoritative content, and privacy, since activity edges must respect permissions and not leak who touched what.

questions.question: You have dozens of ranking signals and a brand-new tenant with zero interaction data. How do you rank, and how do you improve?
questions.answer: With no tenant interaction data, rank cold-start using signals that do not need history: content relevance (lexical plus dense similarity), document recency and authority from the knowledge graph (authorship, sharing, org proximity), and global priors learned across other tenants via a model that generalizes from transferable features rather than tenant-specific memorization. Combine the dozens of signals with a learned ranker trained on cross-tenant data or a sensible hand-tuned blend initially, and explore lightly to gather feedback. As the tenant accumulates clicks and engagement, blend in tenant-specific signals and retrain or fine-tune, shifting weight from priors to learned personalization, and use counterfactual logging to evaluate ranking changes safely. Tradeoffs are reliance on transferable global priors (robust but generic) versus tenant personalization (accurate once data exists), exploration to learn faster versus serving the best current ranking, and the risk of leaking cross-tenant signals that must be prevented.

questions.question: Design the evaluation framework for an enterprise AI assistant when you cannot look at customer data.
questions.answer: Without access to customer data, evaluate on representative synthetic and sanitized proxy datasets co-designed with the customer's domain experts, covering their key intents, documents, and adversarial cases across relevant languages. Use rubric-based scoring, calibrated LLM-as-judge, and a human-rated gold slice to measure faithfulness, relevance, completeness, and safety, and evaluate retrieval and generation separately. In production, rely on privacy-preserving signals that do not expose content, such as aggregated and differentially private metrics, on-device or in-tenant evaluation, and user actions like edits, retries, and escalations reported in aggregate. Gate releases on the offline synthetic suite and detect regressions by comparing these aggregate distributions across versions via canary and A/B. Let the customer run content-level evaluation inside their boundary and share only aggregate results so you never see raw data.

questions.question: Live coding: build the prompt for the next turn under a fixed token budget. The catch is our prefix cache.
questions.answer: Build the prompt by prioritizing components under the fixed token budget: reserve space for the required system prompt and the generation headroom, then fill the remainder with context ordered by importance (most recent turns and highest-relevance retrieved items first), trimming or dropping lower-priority content when the budget is exceeded. The prefix cache is the catch: keep the stable prefix (system prompt, static instructions, long shared context) byte-identical and at the front so it hits the cache, and never insert dynamic or per-turn content ahead of cacheable content, because any change to earlier tokens invalidates the cached prefix and forces full recompute. So the layout is cache-friendly-first: immutable shared prefix, then variable context, then the new turn, maximizing cache reuse while staying within budget. Count tokens with the real tokenizer and leave margin for the response.

questions.question: A conversation runs past the context window. What do you keep, and how do you decide?
questions.answer: Decide by relevance to the current goal, not recency alone: keep the system prompt and instructions, the most recent turns, and any content the user or task clearly still depends on, and drop or compress stale chatter. A practical strategy is to summarize older history into a compact running summary while retaining the last few verbatim turns and any pinned facts, or to re-retrieve the specific earlier details on demand rather than carrying everything. Preserve structural integrity (do not cut mid-message or orphan a tool call from its result) and keep tokens that affect correctness, like constraints, IDs, and decisions. In short, budget the window toward instructions, recent context, and task-critical facts, and summarize or externalize the rest.

questions.question: Our serving cost is dominated by KV cache, not weights. Get it down by an order of magnitude and tell me what you give up.
questions.answer: If KV cache dominates, attack the per-token KV footprint: quantize the KV cache to INT8 or INT4 (2-4x), and adopt GQA/MQA or distill to an architecture with far fewer KV heads, which can cut KV by a large factor. Add sliding-window or sparse/compressed attention to bound stored tokens, and cap or compress context length and conversation history via summarization. Use PagedAttention to remove fragmentation and offload cold KV blocks to CPU/NVMe, and share KV across requests with prefix caching. The tradeoffs you give up are some accuracy from KV quantization and sparse attention, loss of exact long-range recall from windowing and summarization, and extra latency or complexity from offloading, so you tune each lever to stay within an acceptable quality budget.

questions.question: Dialogues here average around 180 messages. Design the cache that sits between turns.
questions.answer: With ~180-message dialogues, the between-turn cache should persist each session's KV state so every new turn only prefills the latest message rather than the whole history. I would key the cache by the conversation prefix, keep hot sessions' KV in GPU memory with PagedAttention blocks, and tier colder sessions to CPU or a remote KV store, reloading on the next turn. To bound growth over 180 messages I apply a sliding window plus periodic summarization of older turns into a compact prefix, and quantize the KV cache to stretch capacity. I also need session-sticky routing so a turn lands on the node holding its cache (or a fast fetch if not), and careful invalidation when earlier messages or the system prompt change, since that breaks prefix reuse.

questions.question: You train natively in int8 rather than doing post-training quantization. Defend that.
questions.answer: Training natively in int8 is essentially quantization-aware training taken to the limit: the model learns weights and activations that are robust to int8 rounding, so there is no post-hoc accuracy cliff and no calibration guesswork. It avoids the outlier and distribution-shift problems that plague PTQ, giving better quality at int8 than converting an FP-trained model after the fact, and it guarantees the deployed numerics match what was trained. You also get memory and bandwidth savings during both training and inference, and the model is already in the target format so deployment is simpler and more predictable. The cost is a more complex, carefully engineered training pipeline and less flexibility to change precision later, but for a fixed int8 serving target it yields the best quality-per-bit.

questions.question: Estimate what one message costs us to serve, and tell me which lever moves it most.
questions.answer: Cost per message is the GPU time to prefill the input plus decode the output, times GPU cost per second: roughly (input_tokens / prefill_rate + output_tokens / decode_rate) * $/GPU-second, divided by effective batch sharing. For a typical message of a couple thousand input and a few hundred output tokens on a quantized mid-size model at good utilization, this lands in the fraction-of-a-cent range. The lever that moves it most is output token count combined with model size, because decode is the expensive per-token phase and scales directly with both; secondarily, batch utilization since idle GPU time inflates every message's cost. So I would focus on capping/shortening outputs, right-sizing (or quantizing) the model, and maximizing batching before anything else.

questions.question: Design discovery and search across millions of user-created characters.
questions.answer: Index millions of user-created characters into a hybrid search system: dense embeddings over character names, descriptions, personas, and tags for semantic matching, plus a lexical index for exact and rare-term queries, with structured filters (category, language, rating). For discovery, layer a recommendation stage, two-stage retrieval and ranking using popularity, engagement (chats, retention), freshness, and personalization from the user's history, with exploration so new characters surface despite no engagement. Handle the long tail and cold-start characters with content embeddings, and run safety and moderation classifiers so unsafe or policy-violating characters are filtered from discovery. Serve from sharded ANN indexes with caching and precomputed embeddings at low latency, keeping the index fresh as creators add characters. Tradeoffs are relevance and personalization versus diversity and exposure for new creators, engagement optimization versus safety and quality, and index freshness versus recompute cost at millions of items.

questions.question: Users complain that characters drift out of persona after a long session. Diagnose it.
questions.answer: Persona drift over long sessions usually traces to context management: as the conversation grows, the system prompt and persona definition get pushed out of the effective context window or diluted by accumulating history, so the model's conditioning weakens. Diagnose by reproducing long sessions and logging exactly what is in the context at each turn, checking whether the persona instructions are truncated, summarized away, or buried far from the latest turn. Measure persona consistency per turn index to confirm degradation correlates with session length and token count, and test whether reinforcing or re-injecting the persona restores it. Also check for conflicting instructions accumulated from the user, summarization that drops persona details, and the model's own tendency to regress to a generic voice. Fixes include periodically re-anchoring the persona, structured memory that preserves persona separately from transient history, and capping or summarizing history while protecting persona tokens.

questions.question: Engagement metrics and wellbeing metrics disagree. How do you build a system that resolves that?
questions.answer: When engagement and wellbeing disagree, the first step is to make the conflict explicit by defining and measuring both honestly rather than optimizing engagement alone, which can reward addictive or harmful patterns. Build wellbeing metrics from validated signals, user surveys, and expert-defined harm indicators, and treat them as guardrails that can veto engagement gains rather than as co-equal terms to be averaged away. Use a hierarchy where safety and wellbeing act as hard constraints and engagement is optimized only within them, and evaluate changes on both in every A/B test, blocking releases that lift engagement while degrading wellbeing. Investigate the mechanism behind the trade-off since not all engagement is harmful, and segment by vulnerable populations. Govern the thresholds through a cross-functional review rather than letting a single growth metric decide.

questions.question: Design the safety system for open-ended character chat.
questions.answer: Define policy clearly for an open-ended setting, covering self-harm and crisis, sexual content especially involving minors, harassment, violence, and illegal activity, while allowing the creative latitude that makes character chat valuable. Layer runtime guardrails: input classification, output moderation, and in-character safe behaviors so the model can stay in role while refusing or redirecting unsafe turns, with special high-sensitivity handling and resource escalation for self-harm and crisis signals. Enforce age-appropriate experiences and stricter rules for minors, because user-created characters and persistent personas create unique risks of boundary-pushing and attachment. Add conversation-level monitoring rather than only per-message checks, since harm often emerges across a long exchange, plus user reporting, rate limiting, and red-teaming against persona-based jailbreaks. Keep a tight feedback loop from incidents into policy, training, and filters, tuned to a potentially vulnerable user base.

questions.question: When is intervening during decoding better than filtering the finished reply?
questions.answer: Intervening during decoding is better when you want to steer the output before harmful content is committed, saving the cost and latency of generating a full reply only to discard it, and when you need fine-grained control such as suppressing specific tokens, steering with a safety direction, or guiding style and format continuously. It also helps when a late filter would produce an abrupt, unexplained refusal, since decoding-time control can yield a coherent safe completion rather than a hard block. Filtering the finished reply is simpler, model-agnostic, and better when you need a holistic judgment of the whole output or can only run moderation as a separate service. In short, decode-time intervention wins when control must be token-level, proactive, and latency-sensitive, while post-hoc filtering wins when the decision requires seeing the complete response or when you cannot modify the generation loop. In practice they are complementary and often combined.

questions.question: Design age assurance for a platform where the under-18 experience is fundamentally different.
questions.answer: Use a tiered approach matching assurance strength to risk rather than demanding hard identity proof from everyone upfront. Combine signals: self-declared age at signup, behavioral and content signals that estimate likely age, device and account signals, and escalate to stronger verification such as ID check or third-party age estimation only when stakes or uncertainty are high. Default ambiguous or likely-minor users into the safer under-18 experience and fail safe toward stricter protections, since the cost of exposing a minor to adult content outweighs the friction of a false positive. Minimize and protect any identity data collected, prefer privacy-preserving estimation over storing documents, and comply with regional legal requirements. Monitor for circumvention and re-evaluate accounts as behavior reveals more, because age assurance is probabilistic and ongoing, not a one-time gate.

questions.question: Write a service that proxies streaming TTS to a browser and cancels cleanly when the user navigates away.
questions.answer: The service opens a streaming connection to the upstream TTS provider and relays audio chunks to the browser over a streaming response (chunked HTTP or WebSocket) as they arrive, flushing promptly for low latency. To cancel cleanly on navigation, detect the client disconnect (the closed response stream or WebSocket close / ASGI disconnect event) and, in response, cancel the upstream TTS request and the relay task so you stop generating and paying for audio the user will not hear. Use structured cancellation (cancel the task group / propagate the abort to the upstream client) and release resources in a finally block so sockets and the TTS session are always closed. The hard parts are propagating cancellation across both legs, avoiding buffering that keeps audio flowing after disconnect, and handling partial chunks and backpressure.

questions.question: Serving real-time TTS is a different capacity problem from serving a text LLM. Why, and how do you plan capacity?
questions.answer: Real-time TTS is a streaming, strictly latency-bound workload: audio must be produced faster than real-time with very low and steady inter-chunk latency, so you cannot batch as aggressively or tolerate the queueing that a text LLM accepts. Each stream has a near-constant compute rate (frames or audio chunks per second) rather than the bursty prefill-then-decode profile of text, so capacity is about guaranteeing per-stream real-time throughput and bounded jitter, not maximizing tokens per second. You plan capacity by the number of concurrent streams each accelerator can sustain in real-time with headroom for the worst case, since dropping below real-time breaks the audio, whereas a text LLM can absorb bursts into latency. So I size for concurrent-stream capacity and tight tail latency, provisioning more headroom and smaller batches than a throughput-oriented text service.

questions.question: Design the safety stack for voice cloning: consent, watermarking and abuse response.
questions.answer: Gate cloning on verified, informed consent from the voice owner, requiring proof of identity and explicit authorization before a voice can be enrolled, and keep an auditable consent record. Embed imperceptible, robust watermarks in all generated audio and maintain detection tooling so synthetic speech can be identified downstream, and consider provenance signing of outputs. Build abuse response around detection and reporting: scan for attempts to clone high-risk or non-consenting voices such as public figures, rate-limit and monitor usage, provide a takedown and complaint channel, and retain logs to trace misuse. Prohibit clearly harmful use cases like fraud, impersonation for scams, and non-consensual intimate or political content, enforced by policy plus classifiers. The stack is consent at enrollment, watermarking and provenance at generation, and monitoring, detection, and takedown at the response layer.

questions.question: Budget the end-to-end latency for a real-time voice agent. Why is time-to-first-audio a different problem from an LLM's time-to-first-token?
questions.answer: End to end a turn spends time on endpointing silence after the user stops, streaming ASR finalization, LLM time-to-first-token plus the generation needed for the first speakable unit, TTS time-to-first-audio, and network round trips at each hop, and these partly overlap when you stream. Time-to-first-audio is different from an LLM's time-to-first-token because audio cannot start until you have a synthesizable chunk of text and the vocoder has produced playable samples, so it stacks the LLM's first-token latency, enough additional tokens to form a sentence or phrase, and the TTS model's own startup cost. You also need the audio to play continuously once it starts, so a jitter buffer and steady chunk cadence matter, whereas a text token can appear the instant it is decoded. Optimizing it therefore means not just faster first tokens but chunking generation so a short first phrase can be synthesized and streamed immediately while the rest is still being produced.

questions.question: Text normalisation is where TTS quality actually dies in production. Walk me through it.
questions.answer: Text normalization turns written text into the exact spoken form, and it breaks TTS when the model mispronounces anything it did not expand: numbers ('101' as one-oh-one versus one hundred one), currency and units, dates and times, phone numbers, abbreviations and acronyms (read as a word or spelled out), URLs and emails, and homographs whose pronunciation depends on context ('read', 'lead', 'St.' as street or saint). The pipeline typically tokenizes, classifies each token's semiotic type, expands it with rules or a neural normalizer, and does grapheme-to-phoneme conversion with a pronunciation lexicon and context disambiguation. The failure modes are silent: a wrong expansion sounds fluent but says the wrong thing, so you need verbalization tests, coverage of edge cases, and domain-specific lexicons for names, drugs, or codes. In production you often combine a fast rule-based normalizer for predictable classes with a learned model for ambiguous ones, plus the ability to inject pronunciation overrides.

questions.question: Design the dubbing pipeline: an English video becomes Spanish, same speakers, same timing.
questions.answer: Separate the pipeline into speech-to-text, translation, and resynthesis with timing and identity constraints. Transcribe the English with timestamps and diarization so each segment is attributed to a speaker, translate to Spanish while controlling length so the output duration roughly matches the source (isometric or length-constrained MT, with rephrasing when the literal translation is too long or short), then synthesize Spanish with a voice cloned from each original speaker so the same voices are preserved. Align the synthesized segments to the original timing with time-stretching or prosody control to keep lip-sync-friendly duration, and mix the dubbed speech back over the separated background audio and music. Add human review for translation quality, name and term handling, and timing, and optionally drive visual lip-sync if the video must match mouth movements.

questions.question: A hospital group schedules and confirms outpatient appointments by phone, manually, with three staff on a rota. Design what we would build for them.
questions.answer: I'd map their current call workflow and the scheduling system it writes to, then build a voice or messaging agent that handles the routine booking, confirmation, and reminder calls while escalating anything complex or clinical to staff. It needs reliable integration with their scheduling and EHR systems so it reads real availability and writes confirmed appointments, and it must handle interruptions, rescheduling, and no-shows gracefully. Given healthcare, I'd treat privacy, consent, and accurate identity verification as hard requirements, keep a human fallback, and log every interaction for audit. I'd pilot on one appointment type and a fraction of volume, measuring booking accuracy, completion rate, and patient satisfaction against the manual baseline before expanding. The three staff shift to handling exceptions rather than routine dialing.

questions.question: A contact centre wants to replace its IVR with voice agents. Run the engagement.
questions.answer: I'd start by analyzing their call data to find the high-volume intents that are genuinely automatable and the ones that must route to humans, because replacing the IVR wholesale on day one is how these fail. I'd design the voice agent for natural turn-taking with barge-in, backchannel handling, and fast latency, integrated with their backend systems so it can actually resolve issues like balances or status rather than just routing. Critically it needs a clean, fast escalation to a human with full context passed along, and clear measurement of containment rate, resolution, and caller satisfaction versus the old IVR. I'd pilot on one or two intents and a slice of traffic, tune on real transcripts, then expand intent by intent. I'd also set guardrails so the agent never guesses on high-stakes actions.

questions.question: Turn a conversation into billable diagnosis codes. What is the accuracy bar, and how do you build to it?
questions.answer: This is multi-label medical coding (e.g., ICD) from clinical dialogue, where the accuracy bar is driven by billing compliance and patient safety, so I would target high precision on billable codes while maintaining recall, and report per-code F1 and coder-agreement against expert-adjudicated labels rather than a single aggregate. Build it as a pipeline: robust ASR/transcription, clinical NLP or an LLM to extract diagnoses with evidence spans, and a mapping/normalization layer to the code ontology that respects coding rules and hierarchy. Keep a human coder in the loop with the model suggesting codes and surfacing supporting text, and gate deployment on calibration and audit against certified coders. Because errors have financial and regulatory consequences, favor conservative thresholds, strong evidence attribution, and continuous auditing over raw automation.

questions.question: The note should be ready before the clinician leaves the room. Build me the latency budget, and tell me where the money goes.
questions.answer: The budget runs from end of encounter to a finished note: audio capture and streaming ASR (can be near real-time), then the LLM summarization pass over a long transcript (prefill-heavy) plus decode of the structured note, then any formatting and review. The LLM stage dominates both latency and money, driven by the long transcript prefill and the generated note length, with ASR second. To hit before-the-clinician-leaves, I stream ASR during the visit so the transcript is ready at encounter end, start summarization incrementally, shorten/structure the prompt, use chunked prefill and streaming output, and size a quantized model that meets quality. Most of the cost is GPU time for the summarization LLM, so the levers are model size/quantization, prompt length, and batching across concurrent encounters.

questions.question: The patient's chart already lists their medications. How would you use that to improve transcription of drug names, and how would you keep it from backfiring?
questions.answer: The chart's medication list is a strong prior, so I use it to bias the speech recognizer toward those exact drug names via contextual biasing or a boosted vocabulary/phrase list, which sharply improves recognition of otherwise rare or acoustically ambiguous drug names. I can also post-process the transcript by matching likely drug mentions against the medication list and correcting near-misses. To keep it from backfiring I avoid over-biasing: the model must still be able to recognize new or changed medications not on the list, since patients start, stop, and switch drugs, so I cap the boost strength and never force a listed name over strong acoustic evidence of a different one. I validate that biasing improves accuracy on both listed and unlisted drugs and flag low-confidence or contradictory mentions for human review rather than silently rewriting them.

questions.question: Design a service that turns the conversation into draft orders: labs, imaging, referrals, prescriptions, via tool calls against the EHR.
questions.answer: The service listens to or ingests the clinical conversation, extracts candidate orders, labs, imaging, referrals, prescriptions, as structured intents, then maps each to the EHR's coded catalog and emits tool calls that create them as unsigned drafts for the clinician to review and sign. Grounding is critical: each proposed order cites the conversational evidence, and the system validates against the EHR's rules for allergies, interactions, dosing, and formulary before drafting. Nothing is finalized autonomously; the clinician must approve and sign, since orders are high-stakes and often irreversible, and every step is logged for audit. I would enforce patient-context safety so orders attach to the correct patient and encounter, handle ambiguity by surfacing low-confidence extractions for confirmation, and evaluate against clinician-reviewed transcripts for order precision and recall.

questions.question: Walk me through writing a finished note back into Epic. What goes wrong?
questions.answer: Writing a finished note back into Epic means mapping your structured note to the EHR's data model and interfaces (HL7/FHIR or the vendor's APIs), attaching it to the correct patient encounter with the right note type, author, and signing clinician, then committing it through the clinical workflow (draft, sign, or pend for review). What goes wrong: patient or encounter mismatches that attach a note to the wrong chart, authentication and authorization scoping (the note must be written under a licensed clinician's credentials, not the AI's), formatting and template mismatches that mangle structure, duplicate writes on retry without idempotency, and interface downtime or rejected messages that silently drop the note. Clinical and legal review is required before signing, since an unreviewed AI note is a safety and liability risk. Tradeoffs are automation (auto-pending notes) versus mandatory human sign-off, tight EHR integration versus brittleness to version and template changes, and strict idempotency and reconciliation versus the risk of lost or duplicated documentation.

questions.question: Two good clinicians write different notes for the same visit. So how do you evaluate note quality at all?
questions.answer: Because two good clinicians legitimately differ, evaluate note quality against clinically meaningful properties rather than exact-match to one reference: factual accuracy and faithfulness to the encounter, completeness of required elements, absence of hallucinated or dangerous content, and adherence to documentation standards. Use rubric-based human evaluation by clinicians measuring these dimensions, and quantify inter-rater agreement so you know the irreducible subjectivity and set metric ceilings accordingly. Prefer judging whether a note is clinically acceptable and safe over scoring stylistic similarity, and use multiple references or acceptability judgments instead of a single gold note. Automate with LLM-as-judge calibrated against clinician ratings for faithfulness and omission detection, with human review of a sample. Track downstream signals like clinician edits and corrections to ground the evaluation in real usage.

questions.question: Edit rate is the obvious measure of clinician trust. What does it hide, and what would you instrument instead?
questions.answer: Edit rate is appealing but hides a lot: a clinician may accept a flawed note without editing due to time pressure or trust fatigue, or heavily edit a good note for personal style, so low edits can mask unsafe content and high edits can reflect preference rather than error. It also treats all edits equally when a single dangerous omission matters far more than many cosmetic tweaks, and it says nothing about missing information the clinician never noticed. Instrument instead the type and severity of edits, distinguishing safety-critical corrections from stylistic ones, and measure factual accuracy and omission rate through clinician review against the encounter. Add acceptance without verification signals, time-to-finalize, downstream error reports, and targeted audits for hallucinations and missing findings. Combine these so trust is measured by clinical safety and correctness, not just whether text was changed.

questions.question: A generated note contains a medication the patient never mentioned. Treat that as a safety incident: how do you detect it before a clinician sees it?
questions.answer: Treat this as a hallucination that could cause patient harm and detect it by verifying every clinical entity in the note against the source conversation and record before clinician review. Extract medications, dosages, diagnoses, and other clinical entities from the generated note, then check that each is grounded in the transcript or structured data via span-level alignment and entailment; any medication not traceable to the source is flagged or removed and the note blocked or marked for mandatory correction. Reconcile extracted medications against the patient's known medication list to catch both invented and conflicting entries, and route high-risk discrepancies to a stricter review path. Measure the ungrounded-entity rate, especially for medications, as a tracked safety metric with alerting, and never let an unverified medication reach the note silently. The principle is span-level grounding plus clinical reconciliation as a hard gate before any human sees the note.

questions.question: Clinicians will not sign what they cannot verify. How would you build span-level provenance from every line of the note back to the conversation?
questions.answer: Generate the note so that each output span is produced with and bound to the specific transcript segments it derives from, recording these alignments as structured provenance rather than reconstructing them after the fact. Technically, carry source attributions through generation, for example with attention or retrieval-based grounding, and verify them with an entailment check that each note line is actually supported by its linked conversation spans, flagging any line that is not. Expose this in the clinician UI so every sentence can be clicked to highlight the exact passages in the transcript that justify it, enabling fast verification and correction. Store provenance per span with the note so it is auditable and persists in the record. This makes the note verifiable line by line, which is what lets a clinician confidently sign it.

questions.question: PHI is in every audio file, transcript and note you touch. How does that shape the architecture, and what can you send to a third-party model API?
questions.answer: Because PHI pervades the audio, transcripts, and notes, design for data minimization and strict control everywhere: encrypt at rest and in transit, enforce RBAC and access logging, segregate PHI, set retention limits, and keep processing within a HIPAA-compliant boundary with a business associate agreement covering every component. For third-party model APIs, only send data under a signed BAA that contractually prohibits training on the data and ensures appropriate safeguards; otherwise de-identify or redact PHI before sending, or keep inference in-house on self-hosted models. Prefer minimizing what leaves your boundary, passing only the fields a task needs, and avoid logging raw PHI in the API path. Maintain audit trails, patient consent, and the ability to honor access and deletion requests. The architecture is governed by least privilege, encryption, de-identification where possible, and contractual plus technical guarantees around any external processing.

questions.question: Our audio is a clinic room: two or three speakers, background noise, accents, and a vocabulary full of drug names. How would you build and improve the ASR for that?
questions.answer: Treat it as a far-field, multi-speaker, domain-specific ASR problem. On the front end add noise robustness and dereverberation, and if you have a mic array use beamforming; otherwise augment training with clinic-like noise and reverberation, and run diarization or speaker separation so overlapping speech from two or three speakers is attributed correctly. Adapt the acoustic model to the accents present with in-domain fine-tuning, and critically bias the language model toward the clinical vocabulary with a custom lexicon, pronunciation entries for drug names, and contextual biasing or shallow fusion so rare drug and condition names are recognized. Build an evaluation set from real clinic recordings with entity-level metrics (especially drug-name error rate), then iterate by mining the errors, expanding the lexicon, and retraining; add human-in-the-loop correction for high-stakes terms.

questions.question: Behaviour cloning on teleoperation data has a well-known failure mode. What is it, and what do you do about it on a real humanoid?
questions.answer: The failure mode is covariate shift (compounding error): a cloned policy makes small mistakes that take the robot into states absent from the expert data, where predictions degrade further, so errors accumulate and trajectories drift off-distribution. On a real humanoid, mitigate it with DAgger-style interactive data aggregation, querying the teleoperator to relabel states the policy actually visits and retraining on that enlarged distribution. Add noise and recovery demonstrations so the data covers off-nominal states, use history/temporal context and action chunking to reduce compounding, and apply safety constraints and shared autonomy during rollout. Fine-tuning with reinforcement learning or residual policies on real hardware further closes the gap between demonstrated and encountered states.

questions.question: A whole-body controller trained entirely in simulation has to run on real hardware. What transfers, what does not, and how do you close the gap?
questions.answer: Dynamics that are well modeled transfer reasonably, such as coarse kinematics and gross motion, but the sim-to-real gap appears in contact dynamics, friction, actuator latency and torque limits, sensor noise, and unmodeled compliance and delays. To close it, use domain randomization over physical parameters, masses, friction, latency, and sensor noise so the policy learns robustness, and system-identify the real robot to center the randomization distribution realistically. Add observation and actuation noise and delays in sim, prefer proprioceptive/robust state estimation, and fine-tune or adapt online on hardware with small amounts of real data. Conservative controllers, residual learning, and safety limits protect the hardware while the policy adapts.

questions.question: Where does reinforcement learning fit on top of imitation learning for manipulation, and what makes the reward the hard part?
questions.answer: Imitation learning gives a strong, safe prior from demonstrations but is capped by demonstration quality and suffers distribution shift, so RL layers on top to improve beyond the demonstrations, recover from off-distribution states, and optimize a task objective the demonstrations only approximate. A common recipe is to pretrain with behavior cloning, then fine-tune with RL (or use demonstrations to seed replay/regularize the policy, as in offline-to-online RL) to refine contact-rich skills. The reward is the hard part because manipulation success is sparse and delayed, true goals (grasp stability, no slip, no damage) are hard to sense, and naive dense rewards invite reward hacking. Practitioners use learned rewards, goal/success classifiers, demonstrations as implicit reward signals, and careful shaping plus safety constraints to make RL tractable.

questions.question: A colleague wants to move the semantic layer to the cloud so you can use a much bigger model. Walk me through the latency budget.
questions.answer: Moving the semantic layer to the cloud adds network round-trips and queueing on top of the larger model's own prefill and decode, so the budget becomes on-device capture plus upload latency, cloud queueing, prefill over the (possibly larger) context, decode, and the return trip. A bigger model raises per-token prefill and decode time and may increase TTFT, while the network leg adds tens to hundreds of milliseconds and variance that widens the tail. Whether it is worth it depends on whether the quality gain justifies the added latency and the loss of offline/private operation; I would quantify each leg and compare against the on-device baseline. Mitigations include streaming partial results, caching stable prefixes, keeping prompts short, regional endpoints to cut network latency, and routing only hard queries to the cloud model.

questions.question: Design the teleoperation data pipeline. Why is data collection the bottleneck in robotics rather than compute?
questions.answer: Collect teleoperation data by recording synchronized robot sensor streams (camera, proprioception, force) alongside the human operator's commanded actions during demonstrations, through a pipeline that timestamps and aligns modalities, validates quality, and stores episodes with metadata for training. Data collection is the bottleneck, not compute, because robot demonstrations are physical and real-time: each episode takes a human operator and a physical robot acting in the real world, cannot be parallelized the way GPU training can, and covers a vast space of tasks, objects, and conditions that must be sampled by actually performing them. Unlike text or images scraped from the web, embodied interaction data does not exist in abundance and must be generated through expensive, slow, hardware-bound teleoperation. Tradeoffs are demonstration quantity and diversity versus the cost and time of operators and robots, teleoperation fidelity versus throughput, and real-world collection (realistic but slow) versus simulation (cheap and parallel but suffers sim-to-real gap).

questions.question: You have 10 hours of demonstrations for a new task and budget for 50 more. How do you decide what to collect, and what return do you expect?
questions.answer: Spend the 50-hour budget where it most reduces policy error rather than collecting more of what you already have: analyze the current policy's failures on the task to find where it is weak (specific sub-tasks, object variations, lighting, failure-prone transitions) and prioritize demonstrations covering those gaps and the long tail, using diversity and coverage rather than repetition. Collect iteratively, retraining and re-evaluating after batches so later collection targets remaining errors (an active-learning loop), and include recovery and edge-case demonstrations that are underrepresented. Expect diminishing returns: the first demonstrations yield large gains and additional data helps sub-linearly, with the biggest improvements coming from covering previously unseen situations rather than redundant nominal runs. Tradeoffs are breadth (coverage of rare conditions) versus depth (reliability on common cases), and the overhead of iterative evaluate-then-collect versus collecting all 50 hours up front, which risks spending budget on data the policy did not need.

questions.question: How do you evaluate a manipulation policy when every trial costs robot time and every failure has physical consequences?
questions.answer: When each trial costs robot time and failures are physically risky, shift most evaluation into high-fidelity simulation validated against real hardware, and reserve scarce physical trials for the cases that matter most. Use simulation to screen policies broadly, quantify the sim-to-real gap on a small validated set, and prioritize real trials via active selection toward uncertain, safety-critical, or diverse conditions. Design physical tests with safety constraints, graduated difficulty, and hardware safeguards so failures are contained, and use statistical methods to estimate success and failure rates and their uncertainty from limited samples. Track not just task success but near-failures, force and safety-margin signals, and recovery behavior, since these leading indicators give more information per expensive trial. Gate deployment on both simulated breadth and a sufficient, stratified real-world sample rather than on simulation alone.

questions.question: You ship a policy to 300 robots. It works in the lab and degrades in the field. Debug it.
questions.answer: Lab-to-field degradation is a distribution-shift problem, so first characterize how the field differs from the lab: lighting, object and surface variation, calibration, wear, network latency, and operator and task differences across the 300 robots. Collect and compare telemetry and, where possible, logged observations and outcomes from field versus lab to see whether the policy fails on inputs outside its training distribution. Check for hardware drift and per-robot calibration differences, since degradation that varies by unit points to hardware rather than policy, while uniform degradation points to a systematic domain gap. Reproduce failing conditions in simulation or on a bench, measure the sim-to-real and lab-to-field gaps, and identify the dominant failure modes. Mitigate by adding field data to training or fine-tuning, improving robustness and calibration, and rolling fixes out via a monitored canary subset before the full fleet.

questions.question: Design the safety architecture for a learned whole-body policy operating near people.
questions.answer: Treat physical safety as the top priority and layer control so that no single learned-policy failure can injure a person. Keep the learned whole-body policy within a safety envelope enforced by independent, verifiable layers: a lower-level reactive safety controller and hardware limits that bound force, velocity, and workspace regardless of what the policy commands, plus a runtime monitor that can trigger a safe stop. Use proximity and force sensing to maintain safe margins around people, degrade speed and compliance as humans get closer, and design for graceful, compliant failure rather than rigid high-energy motion. Validate extensively in simulation and staged real-world testing, with out-of-distribution and uncertainty detection so the system becomes conservative or halts when inputs are unfamiliar. The principle is defense in depth: a capable but untrusted learned policy wrapped by independent, certifiable safety constraints and an always-available emergency stop.

questions.question: What is a vision-language-action model, and how is it different from an LLM with tools?
questions.answer: A vision-language-action model takes in visual (and often language) observations and directly outputs actions, such as robot joint commands or end-effector trajectories, learned end to end from demonstrations so perception and control share one representation. It differs from an LLM with tools in that the LLM reasons in text and invokes discrete, predefined APIs whose effects are symbolic, whereas a VLA produces continuous low-level control grounded in pixels and proprioception, closing the perception-action loop at high frequency. The VLA learns the mapping from raw sensory input to motor output rather than selecting from a fixed tool menu, which lets it handle dexterous, continuous, reactive behavior that would be hard to express as tool calls. Tool-using LLMs excel at high-level planning and symbolic tasks, while VLAs excel at embodied, physically grounded execution, and the two are often combined with the LLM planning and the VLA acting.

questions.question: Helix splits into a large slow model and a small fast one. Why not run a single end-to-end network?
questions.answer: Splitting into a large slow model and a small fast model is a frequency and latency trade: a single end-to-end network would have to run its whole heavy perception-and-reasoning stack at control rate, which is too slow for smooth high-frequency actuation, or run small enough to be fast but then too weak to understand the scene and instruction. The large model runs at low frequency to produce semantic understanding, plans, or a latent goal, while the small model runs at high frequency to turn that plus fresh observations into reactive, smooth motor commands. This mirrors slow deliberate cognition versus fast reflexes, lets each part be sized and trained for its job, and keeps the fast loop robust to latency in the slow one. It also allows the slow model to be shared or offloaded while the fast controller stays local and real-time.

questions.question: Explain action chunking. Why predict a sequence of future actions instead of the next one?
questions.answer: Action chunking means the policy predicts a short sequence of future actions in one inference step instead of a single next action. This reduces compounding error and the drift that comes from re-planning every step, produces smoother and more temporally consistent motion, and models the non-Markovian, multimodal structure of demonstrations better (committing to one coherent motion rather than averaging conflicting single-step choices). It also amortizes inference cost since one forward pass yields several actions, which helps meet real-time control rates, often combined with temporal ensembling or receding-horizon execution where you execute part of the chunk then re-predict. The trade-off is reduced reactivity within a chunk, so chunk length is tuned to balance smoothness against responsiveness to disturbances.

questions.question: In NumPy, compute minADE and minFDE for multi-modal trajectory predictions with variable-length ground truth. No Python loops.
questions.answer: Represent predictions as an array of shape (num_samples, num_modes, T, 2) and ground truth padded to T with a boolean validity mask of shape (num_samples, T) to handle variable lengths. Compute per-mode displacement errors as the Euclidean norm over the last axis between each predicted mode and the (broadcast) ground truth, giving (num_samples, num_modes, T). For minADE, average displacement over valid timesteps using the mask (sum of masked errors divided by valid count per sample) then take the min over the mode axis and mean over samples; for minFDE, take the error at each sample's last valid timestep (gather by the mask's final valid index) then min over modes. All of this is pure NumPy broadcasting plus masked reductions with no Python loops; the key trick is the validity mask to exclude padded steps and gathering the true final index per variable-length sample.

questions.question: Modular perception, prediction and planning, or end-to-end learned driving? Make the case, then tell me what you would actually build.
questions.answer: Modular stacks (perception, prediction, planning) are interpretable, independently testable, and easy to inject rules and safety constraints into, but suffer from hand-designed interfaces that lose information and from error compounding across stages. End-to-end learned driving can optimize the whole task jointly and exploit raw sensor richness, but is data-hungry, hard to verify, and opaque when it fails. In practice I would build a hybrid: keep modular interfaces and an interpretable, verifiable planner with safety constraints, but make perception and prediction heavily learned and trained with shared representations (e.g., a BEV feature space), and explore end-to-end or differentiable components where they measurably help. This preserves validation, debuggability, and safety fallbacks while capturing learning benefits, which matters for a safety-critical system.

questions.question: Design the output representation for a behaviour prediction model. What metrics would you gate it on?
questions.answer: The output should be multimodal and probabilistic: predict several plausible future trajectories per agent with associated probabilities, rather than a single mean path that averages distinct maneuvers into an implausible one. Represent trajectories as sequences of positions (or control points/polynomials) over a horizon, optionally decomposed into intent/maneuver mode plus a continuous refinement, and model joint/interactive futures across agents where interaction matters. Gate it on multimodal metrics like minimum-over-K average and final displacement error (minADE/minFDE), miss rate, and probabilistic scores such as negative log-likelihood, plus calibration of the predicted probabilities. Also gate on scene-level consistency (no collisions, map compliance) and downstream planning impact, not just per-agent geometric error.

questions.question: Where do vision-language models and foundation models genuinely help in an autonomy stack, and where are they a liability?
questions.answer: Vision-language and foundation models genuinely help with the long tail and semantic understanding: open-vocabulary recognition of rare objects and signs, scene and intent reasoning, auto-labeling and data mining, and natural-language interfaces for debugging and scenario search. They are a liability on the safety-critical real-time path because they are large and slow, poorly calibrated, prone to hallucination, hard to verify, and lack guarantees on latency and worst-case behavior. The pragmatic split is to use them offline (labeling, mining, evaluation, simulation) and as high-level advisory or redundancy signals, while keeping the low-latency perception-prediction-planning loop on specialized, validated, deterministic models. Any onboard use should be bounded, monitored, and never the sole authority for safety decisions.

questions.question: Budget the compute and latency for the onboard stack. What breaks when a model gets bigger?
questions.answer: The onboard budget is fixed memory, bandwidth, compute, and power, so I budget each stage (sensor pre-processing, model inference, post-processing) in milliseconds and the model's weights plus KV/activations in megabytes against the device limits. I keep the model quantized and small, use an efficient architecture, and reserve power/thermal headroom since sustained inference throttles. When the model grows, weights may no longer fit in memory, bandwidth-bound inference slows (lower frame rate / higher latency), and power and heat rise, so it can miss the real-time deadline or drain the battery. The fixes are re-quantizing or pruning, distilling back to a smaller model, lowering input resolution or frequency, or offloading the heavy part to a server, each trading capability or dependence for staying within the fixed onboard envelope.

questions.question: You have hundreds of millions of fleet miles. How do you find and use the rare scenarios that matter?
questions.answer: Treat it as a retrieval and mining problem over the fleet archive rather than random sampling: embed driving segments into a representation space (using sensor and perception features) and index them, then find rare safety-relevant scenarios via trigger detectors (disengagements, hard braking, near-misses, anomalies) and similarity search to gather more examples like a known hard case. Mine actively for where the current model is uncertain or wrong, curate and label those segments, and use them to retrain, plus build regression and scenario test suites so the rare cases become permanent evaluation gates. Because the valuable events are a tiny fraction of hundreds of millions of miles, efficient search and automated triggers beat brute-force labeling. Tradeoffs are trigger precision versus recall (missing rare events versus drowning in false positives), the cost of embedding and indexing the whole archive versus the value of findability, and over-weighting rare scenarios versus maintaining nominal-case performance.

questions.question: Design a system that finds driving segments similar to a given one across the entire fleet archive.
questions.answer: Embed each driving segment into a vector capturing its scene and dynamics (fusing perception outputs, trajectories, map context, and sensor features over the time window), index those vectors in an ANN store spanning the archive, and answer a similarity query by embedding the given segment and retrieving nearest neighbors. Precompute embeddings for the entire archive in a batch pipeline so query time is just one encode plus an ANN lookup, and support filtering by metadata (location, weather, maneuver) to scope results. Use these similar-segment retrievals to assemble training and test sets around rare scenarios and to audit how often a situation occurs across the fleet. Tradeoffs are the richness of the embedding (more faithful similarity) versus the cost of computing and storing vectors for hundreds of millions of miles, ANN recall versus speed and memory, and what notion of similarity to encode (visual scene versus behavioral dynamics), which determines whether retrieved matches are actually relevant.

questions.question: You are opening in a new city. Structure the safety case.
questions.answer: Structure the safety case for a new city as an explicit, evidence-backed argument that the system is acceptably safe to operate there, decomposed into claims (the vehicle handles the city's road types, traffic, weather, and rare events safely) each supported by evidence and bounded by the operational design domain you will restrict to initially. Gather evidence from mapping and data collection in the new city, simulation and closed-course testing of local scenarios, supervised on-road testing with safety drivers, and comparison against the known behavior from existing cities, identifying city-specific hazards (unique intersections, signage, pedestrian patterns) and showing mitigations. Define leading and lagging safety metrics, a staged rollout (safety driver, then limited autonomous, then expansion) with go/no-go gates, and continuous monitoring with the ability to roll back. Tradeoffs are the breadth of the operational design domain versus how quickly you can validate it, simulation and closed-course coverage versus expensive real-world miles, and speed of launch versus the confidence the evidence provides.

questions.question: Disengagement rate is a weak safety proxy. How would you actually measure whether the Driver is safe enough to ship?
questions.answer: Disengagement rate is weak because it mixes genuine safety needs with conservative or inconsistent operator behavior and is dominated by noise given how rare serious events are. Measure safety directly with a validated simulator estimating collision and near-miss rates per mile across scenario clusters, counterfactual analysis of whether a disengagement actually averted harm, and leading indicators like minimum time-to-collision, hard braking, rule violations, and safety-margin distributions. Stratify by operating conditions so a regression in one regime is not hidden, and use statistics to bound rare-event risk and the confidence of a safety claim given limited miles. Compare the candidate release against the prior one and a human-driver baseline on these metrics with confidence intervals, requiring review of every safety-critical event. Base the ship decision on converging evidence from simulation, closed-course, and monitored on-road exposure rather than a single proxy.

questions.question: How do you build a simulator you would trust to gate a release?
questions.answer: A release-gating simulator must be validated, meaning its outputs are shown to predict real-world outcomes, so first establish fidelity by replaying real logged scenarios and comparing simulated to actual behavior and quantifying the sim-to-real gap. Build it from a large, diverse scenario library mined from real driving plus synthesized rare and adversarial edge cases, with accurate sensor, dynamics, and agent-behavior models and realistic reactive other actors. Characterize where the simulator is and is not trustworthy, track its predictive calibration over time, and avoid letting the policy overfit to simulator quirks. Use it for broad screening and regression detection while confirming critical conclusions with closed-course and monitored real-world tests, so simulation gates breadth but not the final safety claim alone. Continuously expand and revalidate the scenario set as new real-world events appear so the simulator stays representative.

questions.question: Two days before a release decision, simulation shows a 15% increase in hard-braking events in one scenario cluster. Walk me through what you do.
questions.answer: Two days out, treat the 15% hard-braking increase as a potential regression and investigate before deciding, not panic or dismiss it. First confirm it is real and not a simulator or metrics artifact by checking the scenario cluster, the specific triggering conditions, and whether the change traces to the release or to a sim or scenario-set update. Compare against the prior release on the same cluster with confidence intervals to see if the increase is statistically significant and safety-relevant, and inspect individual trajectories to understand the mechanism and whether hard braking reflects safer or riskier behavior. Assess exposure and worst-case impact of that cluster in the real operating domain to judge severity. Based on evidence, either fix and re-validate, scope the release to exclude the affected conditions, or delay, erring toward safety rather than shipping an unexplained regression.

questions.question: Why carry lidar, radar and cameras rather than cameras alone? Where would you fuse them?
